title: The World Health Organization adult ADHD self-report scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population
plain_language: The six-question ASRS screener matched clinicians' diagnoses better than the full 18 questions, but it still missed about a third of people with ADHD in this community sample, so it is a first step, not a diagnosis.
key_finding: ASRS symptom items varied substantially in concordance with clinical ratings (Cohen's kappa 0.16-0.81). The unweighted six-question screener outperformed the unweighted 18-question ASRS in sensitivity (68.7% v. 56.3%), specificity (99.5% v. 98.3%), total classification accuracy (97.9% v. 96.2%) and kappa (0.76 v. 0.58); the authors conclude the unweighted screener should be preferred to the full ASRS until a weighted version is calibrated in larger samples.

title: The World Health Organization Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Self-Report Screening Scale for DSM-5
plain_language: A newer six-question version of the ASRS, built for the current DSM-5 criteria, caught over 90% of adults with ADHD in both community and clinic samples; in the clinic it also flagged more people who did not have ADHD.
key_finding: A 6-question DSM-5 screening scale derived by machine learning had sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 96.0%, AUC 0.94 and PPV 67.3% in weighted general-population data; in the NYU Langone clinical sample (57.7% prevalence) sensitivity was 91.9%, specificity 74.0%, AUC 0.83 and PPV 82.8%. The authors conclude it detects the vast majority of general population cases and could be used as a screening tool in specialty treatment settings.

title: Validation of the Expanded Versions of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale v1.1 Symptom Checklist and the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale
plain_language: Longer versions of two ADHD questionnaires add questions about planning, organisation and emotional control; these held together well and the authors suggest score ranges that point to likely adult ADHD.
key_finding: Cronbach's alphas were high for all sections of the expanded scales. 95% cutoff scores for ADHD controls were 70 (ASRS 31-item) and 23 (AISRS 18-item), and pilot normative histograms suggested 82 and 26; the authors conclude ASRS scores 70 to 82 and AISRS scores 23 to 26 suggest a high likelihood of adult ADHD and that the expanded versions have high validity for core DSM symptoms plus executive function deficit and emotional dyscontrol symptoms.

title: Structure and Diagnosis of Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Analysis of Expanded Symptom Criteria From the Adult ADHD Clinical Diagnostic Scale
plain_language: Inattention symptoms tend to last into adulthood more than hyperactivity, but inattention also shows up in other conditions; problems with planning and organising were better at singling out adult ADHD.
key_finding: Using the ACDS, 45.7% of respondents with childhood ADHD continued to meet full DSM-IV criteria for adult ADHD (94.9% of these with current attention-deficit disorder, 34.6% with current hyperactivity disorder); adult symptoms had a 3-factor structure (executive functioning, inattention/hyperactivity, impulsivity). Inattention was not specific to ADHD because it was strongly associated with other adult mental disorders, whereas executive-functioning problems were the most consistent and discriminating predictors, leading the authors to suggest more EF symptoms in DSM-V/ICD-11.

title: The Wender Utah Rating Scale: an aid in the retrospective diagnosis of childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Adults rate how they behaved as children; a score of 46 or more on 25 questions picked out most adults with ADHD and few people without it.
key_finding: From the 61-item WURS, the 25 items best separating ADHD from comparison subjects were analysed. A cutoff of 46 or higher correctly identified 86% of patients with ADHD, 99% of normal subjects and 81% of depressed subjects; WURS scores correlated moderately with parents' ratings. The authors conclude the WURS is sensitive in identifying childhood ADHD and may help recognise ADHD in patients with ambiguous adult psychopathology.

title: Criteria and Concurrent Validity of DIVA 2.0: A Semi-Structured Diagnostic Interview for Adult ADHD
plain_language: In 40 clinic patients, the free DIVA interview reached the same ADHD diagnoses as an established interview, but the study was small.
key_finding: DIVA 2.0 diagnoses agreed 100% with diagnoses from the CAADID interview, and DIVA scores correlated with the WURS (r = .544), ADHD-Rating Scale (r = .720) and Sheehan's Dysfunction Inventory (r = .674). The authors conclude DIVA 2.0 is a reliable tool for assessing and diagnosing adult ADHD and the only one offering free online access.

title: Self-ratings of ADHD symptoms in adults II: Reliability, validity, and diagnostic sensitivity
plain_language: The Conners' adult questionnaire gave consistent results over time and separated adults with and without ADHD correctly about 85% of the time.
key_finding: Coefficient alphas for the four CAARS factors ranged from .86 to .92 and median test-retest reliability was .89; all four factors correlated significantly with an established adult ADHD measure, and sensitivity and specificity were high with an overall diagnostic efficiency of 85%. The authors conclude the CAARS is psychometrically sound for evaluating current adult ADHD symptoms.

title: Validation of the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS)
plain_language: A clinician-rated ADHD symptom interview measured symptoms consistently and picked up improvement with medication.
key_finding: The AISRS showed high internal consistency, good convergent and discriminant validity, modest divergent validity and small ceiling and floor effects (<=1%), correlated highly with the CAARS-Inv:SV, had two confirmed subscales (hyperactivity-impulsivity and inattention) and was responsive to medication change. The authors conclude it is a robust, valid efficacy measure of adult ADHD symptoms.

title: Distinguishing sluggish cognitive tempo from attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults
plain_language: Some adults have a 'sluggish' pattern of daydreaming, mental fog and slowness that is related to but separable from ADHD; about half of people with one also had the other.
key_finding: SCT formed a distinct dimension from ADHD symptoms, unrelated to age, sex or ethnicity, and contributed unique variance to EF deficits and psychosocial impairment beyond ADHD symptoms; SCT was more impairing than ADHD alone in work and education. A threshold of 5 or more of 9 symptoms plus impairment would classify 5.1% of the population as having SCT. The authors conclude SCT may be a separate disorder from ADHD, with comorbidity in approximately half of all cases of each.

title: Sluggish cognitive tempo in adults: Psychometric validation of the Adult Concentration Inventory
plain_language: A 10-item questionnaire separates 'sluggish' attention problems (daydreaming, mental fog) from ADHD inattention and from anxiety or low mood in a large student sample.
key_finding: Factor analyses retained 10 ACI items with strong convergent and discriminant validity from anxiety/depressive and ADHD inattentive symptom dimensions. SCT was moderately to strongly correlated with daily life EF deficits, poorer socioemotional adjustment and functional impairment, remained uniquely associated with most of these beyond ADHD, and (with internalizing symptoms covaried) SCT but not ADHD inattention remained associated with poorer socioemotional adjustment. The authors conclude the findings support the ACI for studying adult SCT.

title: “Sluggish cognitive tempo in adults: Psychometric validation of the Adult Concentration Inventory”: Correction to Becker et al. (2017)
plain_language: A published correction to the ACI validation paper fixing the order of the questionnaire items in its main table.
key_finding: Correction notice for Becker et al.: in the original article the Table 1 item content was incorrectly ordered; the table and the text referencing it were corrected in all versions. The notice reproduces the original abstract (10 ACI items retained, N = 3,172).

title: Examining the Structural and External Validity of the Adult Concentration Inventory for Assessing Sluggish Cognitive Tempo in Adults
plain_language: In a mostly female adult sample, the ACI again separated 'sluggish' attention from ADHD inattention, and sluggishness went with poorer sleep, more daytime sleepiness and more anxiety/low mood.
key_finding: In a two-factor model with cross-loadings, 10 of the 16 SCT items loaded highly on SCT and low on ADHD inattention. SCT was uniquely associated with higher internalizing symptoms, time management and self-organization difficulties, poorer sleep quality, shorter sleep duration, lower sleep efficiency and more daytime sleepiness. The authors conclude the findings replicate and extend support for the ACI in adults.

title: Hyperfocusing as a dimension of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Adults with ADHD reported more 'getting stuck' in intense focus than students without ADHD, whether or not they took stimulant medication.
key_finding: Both ADHD groups scored higher than controls on the Hyperfocusing Scale and ASRS (p<0.001), with no difference between stimulant-naive and stimulant-treated patients. The authors conclude hyperfocusing is higher in adult ADHD and can be defined as a separate dimension of adult ADHD.

title: Validation of the dispositional adult hyperfocus questionnaire (AHQ-D)
plain_language: A 12-question hyperfocus questionnaire worked well, and people with more ADHD traits reported more hyperfocus, though this sample was not recruited for ADHD.
key_finding: The preregistered 12-item AHQ-D loaded on a single hyperfocus factor (loadings 0.57-0.81) with Cronbach's alpha 0.93. Hyperfocus correlated with CAARS ADHD-trait scores (r = 0.53), with another hyperfocus scale (r = 0.69) and with mind wandering (r = 0.39), weakly negatively with grit (r = -0.29), and not with extrasensory perception beliefs (r = 0.01). The authors conclude the AHQ-D is a valid way to measure hyperfocus in adults.

title: Multidimensional Assessment of Emotion Regulation and Dysregulation: Development, Factor Structure, and Initial Validation of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale
journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment
plain_language: This is the original paper describing the DERS, a questionnaire about difficulties managing emotions. No summary of its results was available to check.
key_finding: Paper reporting the development, factor structure and initial validation of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (per title, Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment). [no abstract available]

title: Development and Validation of a Brief Version of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale: The DERS-16
journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment
plain_language: A 16-question version of the emotion regulation questionnaire works about as well as the full 36-question version.
key_finding: The 16-item DERS-16 retained excellent internal consistency, good test-retest reliability and good convergent and discriminant validity, with minimal differences in validity compared with the original 36-item DERS. The authors conclude the DERS-16 is a valid, brief measure of overall emotion regulation difficulties.

title: Rejection sensitivity and disruption of attention by social threat cues
plain_language: People more sensitive to rejection were more distracted by, and looked away from, social threat cues; this was studied in general samples, not specifically in ADHD.
key_finding: Rejection sensitivity predicted disruption of goal-directed attention by social threat words (but not negative words) in an Emotional Stroop task, and attentional avoidance of threatening (but not pleasant) faces in a Visual Probe task; threat-avoidant attention was also associated with borderline personality features. The authors conclude this extends understanding of how rejection sensitivity contributes to a self-perpetuating cycle of interpersonal problems and distress.

title: Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP): reliability and validity
plain_language: The DRSP daily symptom diary gives consistent, valid ratings of premenstrual symptoms and impairment and can show change with treatment.
key_finding: DRSP items and Summary Scores had high test-retest reliability and high internal consistency in both studies, moderate to high correlations with other severity measures, and sensitivity to change and treatment differences. The authors conclude the DRSP provides sensitive, reliable and valid measures of PMDD symptoms and impairment criteria.

title: The premenstrual symptoms screening tool (PSST) for clinicians
plain_language: A short questionnaire that asks women to recall premenstrual symptoms and their impact, useful for flagging possible PMDD before daily tracking.
key_finding: The PSST translates categorical DSM-IV PMDD criteria into a severity rating scale; results in 519 primary care women were in line with prevalence rates from large prospective studies. The authors believe it establishes quickly whether women qualify for PMDD and is more practical than two cycles of prospective charting, describing it as an effective screening tool and starting point for further assessment.

title: Life between Clocks: Daily Temporal Patterns of Human Chronotypes
plain_language: A questionnaire about sleep on work days versus free days shows that 'night owls' build up sleep debt during the week and catch up at weekends, and that daylight shifts sleep earlier.
key_finding: The questionnaire documents sleep times, light exposure and self-assessed chronotype separately for work and free days. Sleep times differed greatly between work and free days except in extreme early types; late chronotypes accumulated sleep debt on workdays and compensated by sleeping several hours longer on free days; more time outdoors in daylight advanced sleep timing. The authors predict that most humans are sleep deprived during the workweek.

title: The Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness, Version 2 (MAIA-2)
plain_language: An improved, free 37-question survey of how people notice and relate to signals from inside their body.
key_finding: Five of six new items were added to two low-reliability MAIA scales, giving the 37-item MAIA-2; confirmatory factor analysis supported the 8-factor model (RMSEA = 0.055, SRMR = 0.064) with improved internal consistency reliability. The MAIA-2 is public domain.

title: The Generic BFRB Scale-8 (GBS-8): a transdiagnostic scale to measure the severity of body-focused repetitive behaviours
plain_language: An 8-question scale measures how severe and impairing skin picking, hair pulling and similar habits are, and gave consistent results 6 weeks apart.
key_finding: Factor analysis yielded two dimensions (symptom severity and impairment), test-retest reliability was satisfactory (r = .72) and concurrent validity with the RBFBS was good (r = .74). The authors conclude the GBS-8 appears reliable and valid as a global BFRB measure and recommend using it with specific BFRB scales.

title: The Skin Picking Scale-Revised: Factor structure and psychometric properties
journal: Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
plain_language: This is the paper describing the revised Skin Picking Scale. No summary of its results was available to check.
key_finding: Paper reporting the factor structure and psychometric properties of the Skin Picking Scale-Revised (per title, Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders). [no abstract available]

title: The Milwaukee Inventory for the Dimensions of Adult Skin Picking (MIDAS): Initial development and psychometric properties
journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
plain_language: A 12-question survey separates skin picking done without noticing from picking done deliberately.
key_finding: Exploratory factor analysis gave two 6-item factors, 'focused' and 'automatic' skin picking, with adequate internal consistency and good construct and discriminant validity in preliminary data. The authors conclude the MIDAS provides a reliable and valid assessment of automatic and focused picking.

title: Development and Validation of the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q)
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: A 25-question survey measures how much people hide or compensate for autistic traits in social situations, and it worked similarly across genders.
key_finding: Factor analyses supported three factors with 25 items, with equivalent factor structure across gender and diagnostic group; internal consistency was α = 0.94 and preliminary test-retest reliability r = 0.77, with convergent validity against autistic traits, wellbeing, anxiety and depression. The authors conclude the study provides robust psychometric support for the CAT-Q.

title: Relations Between Social Camouflaging, Life Satisfaction, and Depression Among Polish Women Diagnosed with ADHD
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Women with ADHD who reported more masking of their symptoms also reported lower life satisfaction and more depression; the study cannot show which causes which.
key_finding: Social camouflaging, measured with novel CAT-Q-inspired items tailored for ADHD, was negatively associated with life satisfaction and positively correlated with depressive symptoms after controlling for demographic variables. Limitations were self-report measures, cross-sectional design and self-reported diagnosis; the authors suggest masking efforts may link to lower life satisfaction and more depressive symptoms in women with ADHD.

title: Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Treatments for Suicidality in People Living with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): A Systematic Review
journal: Administration and Policy in Mental Health and Mental Health Services Research
plain_language: Across 18 studies, people with PMDD or related premenstrual disorders more often reported suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts than comparison groups, but the studies defined PMDD and suicidality in different ways, many had quality problems, and no study has yet tested a treatment aimed at suicidality in PMDD.
key_finding: Systematic review (narrative synthesis, no meta-analysis) of 18 studies (n = approximately 2,600,000); MMAT appraisal flagged issues with 70% of studies. Eight suicidality-related indicators/outcomes were significantly associated with PMDD and/or premenstrual disorders (PMDs). Reported prevalences varied widely: 16%-30.47% for 'suicidality', 26%-86% for suicidal ideation, 11.5%-41.5% for suicide planning and 7.1%-60.7% for suicide attempts. Common risk factors were other psychiatric comorbidities, high impulsivity/aggression/hopelessness scores and hormonal factors. No studies evaluated treatments for suicidality in PMDD. The authors conclude that, despite clinical and methodological heterogeneity, people with PMDD are at increased risk of suicidality.

title: The female side of pharmacotherapy for ADHD—A systematic literature review
plain_language: Women and girls may respond to ADHD medicines somewhat differently from men and boys, but the studies are few and the differences inconsistent.
key_finding: Girls received significantly fewer ADHD prescriptions than boys in all 7 prescription studies, a gap no longer seen in adults (with one exception); each of the 14 effect studies found at least one sex difference in medication effects. The authors suggest single daily methylphenidate may not be optimal for girls and atomoxetine may be promising for girls and women, but say robustness needs further investigation.

title: Sex Differences in the Effect of Atomoxetine on the QT Interval in Adult Patients With Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: In a very small study, atomoxetine slightly lengthened a heart-rhythm measure in women but not men, so heart checks may matter more for women.
key_finding: In 24 adults with pre- and post-treatment ECGs, only women had a prolonged Bazett-corrected QT interval after atomoxetine, and in women QTcB correlated with atomoxetine dose (r = 0.631); there was no such correlation in men.

title: The suppression of appetite and food consumption by methylphenidate: the moderating effects of gender and weight status in healthy adults
plain_language: In adults without ADHD, a single dose of methylphenidate reduced appetite in women and normal-weight men, but not in men with obesity.
key_finding: In a placebo-controlled challenge, methylphenidate (0.5 mg/kg) reduced appetite, cravings and snack-food intake in all groups except obese men, showing gender differences in the appetite response to methylphenidate. Participants did not have ADHD.

title: Extended-release methylphenidate for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults
plain_language: Long-acting methylphenidate reduces adult ADHD symptoms by a small-to-moderate amount and causes more side effects than placebo; Cochrane rated the evidence very low certainty.
key_finding: Extended-release methylphenidate improved self-rated (SMD -0.37) and investigator-rated ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.42), had a small effect on quality of life (SMD -0.15), no effect on days missed at work or serious adverse events, and increased the risk of any adverse event (RR 1.27). All evidence was rated very low certainty, mainly because of high risk of bias, short trials and limited generalisability.

title: Immediate-release methylphenidate for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults
plain_language: Short-acting methylphenidate has been poorly studied in adults; what trials there are show more stomach upset and appetite loss than placebo.
key_finding: Evidence that immediate-release methylphenidate reduces adult ADHD symptoms was low to very low certainty; it increased gastrointestinal complications (RR 1.96) and loss of appetite (RR 1.77) vs placebo, and adverse events were poorly assessed and reported.

title: Amphetamines for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults
plain_language: Amphetamine-type medicines, including lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse/Elvanse), reduce adult ADHD symptoms in the short term, but more people stop them because of side effects; most trial participants were men.
key_finding: Amphetamines reduced clinician-rated (SMD -0.90) and patient-rated (SMD -0.51) ADHD symptoms in the short term, with lisdexamfetamine SMD -1.06, but did not improve retention in treatment and increased withdrawal due to adverse events (RR 2.69). Doses at study completion did not appear to differ in efficacy. Evidence was low or very low quality; most participants were male (57.2%).

title: Atomoxetine for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in the adulthood: a meta‐analysis and meta‐regression
plain_language: Atomoxetine, a non-stimulant, helps adult ADHD a little, but more people stop taking it than stop placebo.
key_finding: Atomoxetine had modest efficacy in adults (patient-rated SMD -0.33; clinician-rated SMD -0.40), but all-cause discontinuation (OR 1.39) and adverse-event discontinuation (OR 2.57) were higher than with placebo; the authors judge its benefit-risk balance poor and the recommendation weak.

title: A Phase III, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial Assessing the Efficacy and Safety of Viloxazine Extended-Release Capsules in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Viloxazine, a newer non-stimulant, modestly reduced adult ADHD symptoms in one trial; trouble sleeping, tiredness and nausea were the commonest side effects.
key_finding: Viloxazine ER (mean dose 504 mg) reduced investigator-rated ADHD symptoms more than placebo at 6 weeks (AISRS -15.5 vs -11.7) with effects significant by week 2; common adverse events were insomnia (14.8%), fatigue (11.6%), nausea (10.1%), decreased appetite (10.1%), dry mouth (9.0%) and headache (9.0%), and 9.0% vs 4.9% discontinued for adverse events.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Guanfacine Extended-Release in the Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Adults
plain_language: Guanfacine helped adult ADHD symptoms in a Japanese trial, but 19.8% stopped it because of side effects such as sleepiness and dizziness.
key_finding: Guanfacine ER (titrated to 4-6 mg/d) improved ADHD-RS-IV scores more than placebo at week 10 (effect size 0.52), but more patients had adverse events (81.2% vs 62.0%) and discontinued because of them (19.8% vs 3.0%); main adverse events were somnolence, thirst, low blood pressure, postural dizziness and constipation.

title: ADHD medication discontinuation and persistence across the lifespan: a retrospective observational study using population-based databases
plain_language: About half of adults who start ADHD medication have stopped within a year, and women and men are similar in this.
key_finding: Within 1 year of starting ADHD medication, only 48% of adults aged 25 or over and 39% of young adults remained on treatment; at 5 years, 30-40% of adolescents and adults were covered by treatment in most countries when reinitiation was counted. Patterns were similar across sex.

title: Drug survival and risk factors for ADHD medication discontinuation in adults: A Danish Nationwide Registry ‐based cohort study
plain_language: In Denmark, women were slightly more likely than men to stay on ADHD medication over five years, and people who tried more than one medicine were more likely to stay on treatment.
key_finding: Five-year drug survival was 29% in women vs 23.5% in men (men's discontinuation OR 1.26); adults aged 31-50 and those who switched medication two or more times were less likely to discontinue (OR 0.53 for two switches; 0.26 for three or more).

title: Psychiatric and neurological predictors of early ADHD medication discontinuation across the lifespan: a multinational study
plain_language: How often adults stop ADHD medication early varies hugely between countries, which suggests health-system factors matter more than individual illness features; men and women were similar.
key_finding: Early discontinuation (180 days or more without dispensing) varied widely, from 38% to 68% in adults; few clinical predictors were consistent from adolescence onwards, sex differences were limited, and marked cross-country variation pointed to system-level influences.

title: Further evidence of low adherence to stimulant treatment in adult ADHD: an electronic medical record study examining timely renewal of a stimulant prescription
plain_language: In one US health system, fewer than half of adults refilled their first stimulant prescription on time.
key_finding: In electronic medical records from a US healthcare system, only 42% of adults renewed their first stimulant prescription in a timely enough fashion to be considered consistently medicated.

title: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder medication shortage in the United States: a qualitative assessment of Reddit posts
plain_language: During the US stimulant shortage, people on Reddit described struggling to function, battling pharmacies and doctors, and rationing doses or using caffeine and nicotine to cope.
key_finding: Qualitative analysis of r/ADHD posts during the US shortage found cognitive, emotional and functional impacts, access barriers (complex systems, unsupportive providers, cost), and coping by changing or skipping doses, saving medication, caffeine, nicotine, meditation and exercise; the community provided support and resource-sharing.

title: “Everything’s a Challenge”: An Interview Study of ADHD Individuals in the Midst of the Prescription Stimulant Shortage
plain_language: People with ADHD interviewed during the shortage said it disrupted their work and lives, and that rules against misuse made getting medication harder.
key_finding: Interviewees described major difficulty accessing ADHD medication during the stimulant shortage, with knock-on harms to work, study and personal life; controls aimed at reducing non-medical use worsened access, and some sought medication through unofficial channels.

title: Elevated levels of hoarding in ADHD: A special link with inattention
plain_language: About 20% of adults attending an ADHD clinic had significant hoarding problems, compared with 2% of people without ADHD, and this was linked to inattention.
key_finding: Clinically significant hoarding was found in about 20% of adults with ADHD vs 2% of controls, and hoarding severity was higher even in the remaining patients (d = 0.89); inattention was the only significant predictor of hoarding severity, and about half of those with hoarding were male.

title: Who really hoards? Hoarding symptoms in adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and healthy controls
plain_language: Hoarding disorder was more common among adults with ADHD than among people with OCD, the condition hoarding used to be linked to.
key_finding: Hoarding disorder was more common in adults with ADHD (32.1%) than in OCD (8%) or healthy controls (4%), as were hoarding symptoms.

title: IS ADHD IN CHILDHOOD ASSOCIATED WITH LIFETIME HOARDING SYMPTOMS? AN EPIDEMIOLOGICAL STUDY
plain_language: In a general-population survey, adults who recalled childhood inattention were much more likely to have hoarding symptoms.
key_finding: Lifetime hoarding symptoms were more common in people reporting childhood ADHD symptoms (8.9% vs 2.7%); childhood inattention, not hyperactivity, was associated with hoarding (OR 6.04) independent of obsessive-compulsive symptoms. ADHD symptoms were reported retrospectively.

title: Relationships among compulsive hoarding, trauma, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: People who hoard reported more ADHD symptoms and more trauma than people who do not.
key_finding: Compared with controls, people who hoard reported more types and more frequent trauma, more inattention and hyperactivity symptoms, and greater comfort from possessions.

title: Impact of ADHD on Household Chores
plain_language: Parents of children with ADHD said ADHD made everyday chores harder; there is no similar study in adult women.
key_finding: Most parents believed ADHD affected their child's ability to complete self-care and family-care chores independently and satisfactorily; the study concerns children and relies on parent report.

title: Understanding phenomenological experiences of autistic inertia using online community discourse
plain_language: Autistic people online describe "inertia" as being stuck either unable to start or unable to stop, which can be both enjoyable and very disabling; research on it is only beginning.
key_finding: Reflexive thematic analysis of autistic Reddit discourse described inertia as "all or nothing" extremes of staying at rest or in motion, worsened by intersecting factors, with impacts from joyful to highly disabling and a "vicious cycle" with fatigue; the findings corroborated earlier interview studies, and the authors note the topic is scarcely acknowledged in academic literature.

title: Premature mortality in autism spectrum disorder
plain_language: In Sweden, autistic people were about two and a half times as likely as others to die during the study period, from many different causes.
key_finding: During follow-up 2.60% of autistic people died vs 0.91% of the general population (OR 2.56, 95% CI 2.38-2.76). Mortality was raised for almost all cause categories and was partly moderated by gender and intellectual ability; the authors conclude premature mortality was markedly increased owing to many medical conditions.

title: Suicidal ideation and suicide plans or attempts in adults with Asperger's syndrome attending a specialist diagnostic clinic: a clinical cohort study
plain_language: Two in three adults diagnosed with autism in adulthood at a specialist clinic said they had thought about suicide at some point.
key_finding: In adults newly diagnosed with Asperger syndrome, 66% (243/367) self-reported lifetime suicidal ideation, 35% (127/365) plans or attempts and 31% (116/368) depression; lifetime ideation was more likely than in a general UK population sample (OR 9.6, 95% CI 7.6-11.9). The authors identify depression as an important potential risk factor.

title: The combination of autism and exceptional cognitive ability is associated with suicidal ideation
plain_language: Among autistic children, those with higher IQ were more likely to have had thoughts of suicide, according to parents; this has not been tested in adults.
key_finding: In a clinic for gifted/talented youth, parent-reported suicidal ideation was in excess among autistic youth with IQ >= 120 (OR 5.9). In SPARK vs ABCD, autistic children had more suicidal thoughts (OR 6.8), and autistic children with suicidal thoughts had higher cognitive ability than those without; polygenic scores for cognitive performance were associated with suicidal thoughts (Z = 2.16, p = 0.03). The authors suggest rising cognitive ability is an unexpected risk factor in autism.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of suicidality in autistic and possibly autistic people without co-occurring intellectual disability
plain_language: Across 36 studies, about a third of autistic or possibly autistic people without intellectual disability had thought about suicide and about a quarter had attempted it or harmed themselves with suicidal intent.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence was 34.2% for suicidal ideation, 21.9% for suicide plans and 24.3% for suicide attempts and behaviours, with high heterogeneity (I2 > 75). Estimates did not differ between autistic and possibly autistic samples. The authors conclude suicidality is highly prevalent in both groups and possibly autistic people need more clinical attention.

title: Suicidality in autistic youth: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: About one in four autistic young people had had suicidal thoughts; childhood adversity raised the risk and resilience lowered it.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence in autistic youth was 25.2% for suicidal ideation, 8.3% for attempts and 0.2% for suicide deaths; self-reports gave higher estimates than parent reports, and heterogeneity was substantial. Adverse childhood experiences were strong risk factors and resilience was protective.

title: Predicting the diagnosis of autism in adults using the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) questionnaire
plain_language: In adults referred for an autism assessment, the AQ questionnaire was poor at telling who would be diagnosed; many autistic people scored below the cut-off.
key_finding: AQ scores did not significantly predict who received an autism diagnosis: sensitivity 0.77, specificity 0.29, negative predictive value 0.36, so 64% of those scoring below the cut-off were false negatives. Generalized anxiety disorder may mimic autism and inflate AQ scores. The authors say guidance supporting the AQ in adult assessment (e.g. NICE) may need reconsidering.

title: Brief Report: An Evaluation of the AQ-10 as a Brief Screening Instrument for ASD in Adults
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: In a study comparing people already known to be autistic with people who were not, the 10-question AQ worked about as well as the full 50-question version.
key_finding: In diagnosed autistic adults vs controls, the AQ-10, the abridged AQ and the full AQ-50 performed similarly well as screens, with very similar sensitivity, specificity and area under the curve at suggested cut-offs. The authors conclude the AQ-10 is potentially useful as a brief screen.

title: The Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R): A Scale to Assist the Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults: An International Validation Study
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: The RAADS-R questionnaire separated autistic adults from others very well in its first study, which compared clearly defined groups.
key_finding: The 80-item RAADS-R distinguished autistic adults from comparison groups (p < .0001), with sensitivity 97%, specificity 100% and test-retest reliability r = .987. The authors conclude it is a useful adjunct diagnostic tool for adults.

title: Common polygenic risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with cognitive ability in the general population
plain_language: Genes linked to autism were linked, very slightly, to higher thinking-test scores in ordinary people; genes linked to ADHD were not.
key_finding: Polygenic risk for autism was positively associated with general cognitive ability (beta = 0.07, r2 = 0.003), logical memory and verbal intelligence, replicated as a positive association with full-scale IQ in a twin sample (beta = 0.07). Evidence for ADHD polygenic risk was inconsistent, with one negative correlation with IQ at age 11 (beta = -0.08).

title: Genome-wide association meta-analysis in 269,867 individuals identifies new genetic and functional links to intelligence
plain_language: A very large genetic study found that genes for higher intelligence seem to lower, not raise, the chance of ADHD.
key_finding: A genome-wide meta-analysis identified 205 loci and 1,016 genes for intelligence. Mendelian randomization suggested protective effects of intelligence for Alzheimer's disease and ADHD, and bidirectional causation with pleiotropic effects for schizophrenia.

title: Giftedness and Overexcitability
plain_language: Gifted people scored somewhat higher on "overexcitability" questionnaires, mainly for intellectual curiosity and imagination; differences in emotional and sensory intensity were small.
key_finding: Gifted samples had higher mean overexcitability scores, but the effect for psychomotor OE was not significant, emotional and sensual OEs were small, and intellectual and imaginational OEs were medium. The authors note important limitations.

title: Openness to Experience Rather Than Overexcitabilities
plain_language: What gifted-education writers call "overexcitabilities" looked statistically like the ordinary personality trait "openness to experience".
key_finding: Structural equation models fitted better and were interpretable when each overexcitability and the matching openness-to-experience facet loaded on a joint factor, suggesting openness encompasses OEs. The authors recommend the field use the five-factor openness construct instead of OEs.

title: High intelligence: A risk factor for psychological and physiological overexcitabilities
plain_language: A survey of Mensa members found they reported more mental and physical health conditions than national averages, but the sample was self-selected.
key_finding: Mensa members self-reported higher rates of diagnosed or suspected mood and anxiety disorders, ADHD, autism, allergies, asthma and autoimmune disease than national averages. The authors interpret this as implicating high IQ as a potential risk factor and as preliminary support for a "hyper brain/hyper body" association.

title: Bright, but allergic and neurotic? A critical investigation of the “overexcitable genius” hypothesis
plain_language: A second Mensa survey found more autism, fatigue, depression and anxiety but not more allergies, and the authors say that may be about who joins Mensa rather than IQ.
key_finding: Compared with the general population, European Mensa members had raised prevalence of autism (RR 2.25), chronic fatigue syndrome (RR 5.69), depression (RR 4.38), generalized anxiety (RR 3.82) and IBS (RR 3.76), but not asthma, allergies or autoimmune disease. The authors found little evidence for immunological explanations and say sample selectiveness rather than high IQ itself may explain the effects.

title: High intelligence is not associated with a greater propensity for mental health disorders
plain_language: In half a million UK adults, very high scorers on intelligence tests had less anxiety and PTSD than average scorers, though slightly more allergies.
key_finding: People with high general intelligence had less generalized anxiety (OR 0.69) and PTSD (OR 0.67), lower neuroticism, less social isolation and fewer reported childhood and adult stressors, but more allergies (OR 1.13-1.33). The authors conclude highly intelligent people do not have more mental health disorders, and high intelligence may protect against anxiety and PTSD.

title: Childhood IQ and Adult Mental Disorders: A Test of the Cognitive Reserve Hypothesis
plain_language: In a New Zealand birth cohort, children with lower IQ were more likely to develop depression and anxiety as adults; higher IQ was linked only to more mania.
key_finding: Lower childhood IQ was associated with higher risk of schizophrenia spectrum disorder, adult depression and anxiety, more comorbidity and more persistent depression; higher childhood IQ predicted increased risk of adult mania.

title: Intelligence in Early Adulthood and Subsequent Hospitalization for Mental Disorders
plain_language: In over a million Swedish men, those with higher test scores at conscription were less likely to be hospitalised later for any mental disorder.
key_finding: Risk of hospital admission for every category of mental disorder rose as IQ fell; per standard deviation decrease in IQ, hazard ratios were 1.50 for mood disorders and 1.51 for neurotic disorders (range 1.49-1.85 across categories). The authors conclude lower intelligence is a risk factor for the whole range of mental disorders.

title: Behavioral and Socio-Emotional Disorders in Intellectual Giftedness: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Studies disagree on whether gifted children have more emotional or behavioural problems; the evidence is too mixed to say.
key_finding: Findings were mixed: socio-emotional problems were found in 3 of 8 studies, internalizing disorders in 5 of 9 and externalizing disorders in 3 of 5; ADHD was the most studied comorbidity. The authors say no single conclusion can be drawn and that age and verbal-nonverbal discrepancy should be considered.

title: Good social skills despite poor theory of mind: exploring compensation in autism spectrum disorder
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Some autistic teenagers with higher IQ looked socially typical on assessment despite underlying difficulties, and they reported more anxiety.
key_finding: Autistic adolescents who compensated (good ADOS social scores despite poor theory-of-mind performance) had better IQ and executive function but more self-reported anxiety than low compensators. The authors conclude well-compensated individuals are not experiencing a milder form of autism.

title: Age at autism spectrum disorder diagnosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis from 2012 to 2019
plain_language: On average autism is diagnosed at about five years old, and studies disagree about which factors make diagnosis later.
key_finding: Mean age at autism diagnosis was 60.48 months (range 30.90-234.57). Factors that may affect age at diagnosis, such as diagnosis type, additional diagnoses and gender, were reported by 46 studies, often with conflicting or inconclusive results.

title: Demographic and Cognitive Profile of Individuals Seeking a Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adulthood
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Among adults seeking an autism assessment, those diagnosed and those not had similar rates of other mental health conditions; ability and coping seemed to soften the effects of autistic traits.
key_finding: Psychiatric comorbidity was high in both those diagnosed (58%) and not diagnosed (59%). Within the autistic group, older age went with higher self-rated autistic traits and better cognitive performance; the authors suggest cognitive ability and coping may mitigate the effects of traits without reducing them.

title: Cognitive Profile in Autism and ADHD: A Meta-Analysis of Performance on the WAIS-IV and WISC-V
plain_language: Autistic people often score much lower on speed tasks than on reasoning; people with ADHD show a flatter pattern; neither pattern can diagnose the condition.
key_finding: Autistic children and adults scored in the typical range for verbal and nonverbal reasoning but about 1 SD below the mean on processing speed, with slightly lower working memory. People with ADHD scored mostly at age-expected levels with slightly lower working memory. The authors conclude the profiles are not sensitive or specific enough for diagnosis.

title: Cognitive profile analysis in school psychology: History, issues, and continued concerns
plain_language: Using gaps between a person's IQ sub-scores to make diagnoses has long been questioned and the evidence still does not support it.
key_finding: Reviews the history of cognitive profile analysis (using strengths and weaknesses across IQ index scores to make diagnostic or treatment decisions) and summarises evidence raising new and continued concerns about its use, including newer methods.

title: Cognitive characteristics of intellectually gifted children with a diagnosis of ADHD
plain_language: Gifted children with ADHD tended to have high reasoning scores but lower working-memory and speed scores, unlike other gifted children.
key_finding: Gifted children (GAI >= 125) made up 8.8% of a large ADHD sample, about twice the expected proportion. They showed lower working memory and processing speed scores typical of ADHD, which the authors argue shows this is not misdiagnosis; the pattern resembled gifted children with specific learning disorder but not typically developing gifted children.

title: Cognitive, Adaptive, and Psychosocial Differences Between High Ability Youth With and Without Autism Spectrum Disorder
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Bright autistic young people were slower on speed tasks and had more everyday and emotional difficulties than equally bright non-autistic peers.
key_finding: Compared with high-ability peers, high-ability autistic youth had poorer processing speed, adaptive skills and parent- and teacher-rated psychological functioning.

title: The Identification and Performance of Gifted Students With Learning Disability Diagnoses
plain_language: Research on "gifted with a learning disability" students used very different definitions, and many of those labelled were not actually struggling academically.
key_finding: Across 46 studies of "gifted/learning disabled" students, identification criteria varied widely, learning-disability identification often relied on dubious methods, and the identified students often lacked academic impairment.

title: The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ): Evidence from Asperger Syndrome/High-Functioning Autism, Males and Females, Scientists and Mathematicians
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Autistic traits were higher among maths and science students and maths prize-winners, but not among university students in general.
key_finding: Autistic adults scored a mean AQ of 35.8 vs 16.4 in controls. Cambridge students overall did not differ from controls, but science and maths students scored higher than humanities students, and Mathematics Olympiad winners scored higher than male humanities students.

title: Health Conditions and Functional Status in Adults with Autism: A Cross-Sectional Evaluation
plain_language: Young autistic adults reported more epilepsy, depression, high blood pressure and allergies than the general population.
key_finding: Young autistic adults (18-29) had higher prevalence than the general population of seizure disorder (11.2% vs 1.4%), depression (16.4% vs 6.4%), hypertension (12.9% vs 6.3%) and allergies (39.7% vs 8.4%). The authors conclude adults with autism have high rates of seizures and depression but low rates of STIs, tobacco and alcohol misuse.

title: A meta-analysis of the relation of intolerance of uncertainty to symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder
plain_language: People who find uncertainty hard to bear tend to have more symptoms of generalised anxiety, depression and OCD. The link was similar for all three, a little stronger for generalised anxiety.
key_finding: Using the GAD-derived definition, intolerance of uncertainty correlated .57 with GAD, .53 with MDD and .50 with OCD symptoms; it was more strongly related to GAD than to OCD only under that definition, and no other differences between the three syndromes were found.

title: Exposing Worry's Deceit: Percentage of Untrue Worries in Generalized Anxiety Disorder Treatment
plain_language: In a small study, about nine in ten worries of people with generalised anxiety did not come true, and people who saw this most clearly improved most in treatment.
key_finding: 91.4% of recorded worry predictions did not come true, and participants' expected likelihoods were much greater than the observed likelihoods; a higher percentage of untrue worries predicted greater symptom reduction during treatment. The authors conclude worries in GAD were mostly inaccurate.

title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety in autism: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Autistic people who find uncertainty hard to tolerate tend to be more anxious, much as in non-autistic people, so uncertainty-focused therapy may help.
key_finding: Autistic participants reported high levels of anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty; nine of 10 studies with relevant statistics found a significant link between the two, of about the same strength as in non-autistic samples.

title: When the world becomes 'too real': a Bayesian explanation of autistic perception
plain_language: A theory that autistic people's perception leans less on expectations built from past experience, so the world may feel more raw and detailed.
key_finding: Proposes that attenuated Bayesian priors ('hypo-priors') may underlie autistic perception, so that perception is less modulated by prior experience, and that this could explain sensory and other non-social features of autism.

title: Precise minds in uncertain worlds: Predictive coding in autism
plain_language: A theory that autistic brains treat every small surprise as important and find it hard to let minor mismatches go, which could make sameness feel safer.
key_finding: Argues that autism involves giving prediction errors a uniform, inflexibly high weight, so people cannot learn when to ignore errors; insistence on sameness and repetitive behaviour are framed as attempts to obtain a sense of predictive success.

title: An aberrant precision account of autism
plain_language: A theory that autistic brains weigh incoming sensory information too heavily compared with expectations.
key_finding: Develops the view that autistic perception reflects aberrant encoding of precision within hierarchical predictive coding, in particular an imbalance in the precision given to sensory evidence relative to prior beliefs, and reviews findings consistent with it.

title: Prediction in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review of Empirical Evidence
plain_language: Across 47 studies, autistic people often found it harder to learn what predicts what, especially when the clues were faint or inconsistent.
key_finding: Studies suggest differences in predictive learning and predictive response in autism, with challenges detecting predictive relationships especially when cues have low salience or consistency, and low-level predictive processing differences; the authors say the broad hypothesis still needs to be better defined and tested.

title: Death anxiety and its role in psychopathology: Reviewing the status of a transdiagnostic construct
plain_language: Fear of death seems to sit underneath many anxiety problems, including health anxiety and panic, and may be worth treating directly.
key_finding: Reviews theory, measures and studies and concludes death anxiety appears to be a basic fear at the core of a range of disorders, including hypochondriasis, panic disorder, and anxiety and depressive disorders; large controlled treatment studies are needed.

title: The relationship between death anxiety and severity of mental illnesses
plain_language: In 200 people in treatment, those with more fear of death had more severe symptoms across many disorders. The study cannot show which causes which.
key_finding: Death anxiety strongly predicted psychopathology, including number of lifetime diagnoses, medications, hospitalisations and distress, not accounted for by neuroticism, with large to very large correlations with symptom severity across 12 disorders; the authors note experimental research is needed to establish causality.

title: Death anxiety and its relationship with obsessive-compulsive disorder
plain_language: In people with OCD, more fear of death went with worse OCD, and being reminded of death made people with washing compulsions wash more.
key_finding: Fear of death correlated moderately to strongly with OCD severity, hospitalisations, medications and lifetime anxiety diagnoses; in an experiment, reminders of death increased hand-washing in OCD washers but not in non-washers.

title: Adrenal fatigue does not exist: a systematic review
plain_language: A review of 58 studies found no good evidence that 'adrenal fatigue' is a real medical condition.
key_finding: Studies of cortisol and fatigue gave almost systematically conflicting results, with heterogeneous, mostly descriptive designs and methods not endorsed by endocrinologists; the authors conclude there is no substantiation that 'adrenal fatigue' is an actual medical condition.

title: Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: putative role of epigenetic mechanisms
plain_language: Animal studies suggest stress effects can pass to offspring through gene regulation, but in humans this has not been shown, and many other routes are possible.
key_finding: The most compelling evidence for epigenetically mediated intergenerational effects comes from animal models; given the paucity of human studies and methodological challenges, intergenerational effects in humans cannot yet be attributed to a single set of biological or other determinants.

title: Are children of Holocaust survivors less well-adapted? A meta-analytic investigation of secondary traumatization
plain_language: Studies of children of Holocaust survivors found that, outside clinic samples, they were not more traumatised than other people.
key_finding: In adequately designed non-clinical studies there was no evidence that parents' traumatic Holocaust experiences affected their children; secondary traumatisation appeared only in studies of clinical participants, who were stressed for other reasons.

title: A critical view on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans
plain_language: Passing on gene-regulation changes across generations is seen in some plants and animals, but in humans it is hard to prove because families also share genes, surroundings and culture.
key_finding: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is seen in plants, nematodes and fruit flies, but its occurrence in mammals and humans is controversial because it is confounded by genetic, ecological and cultural inheritance, which makes conclusive proof difficult.

title: The Long-Term Health Consequences of Child Physical Abuse, Emotional Abuse, and Neglect: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Children who were neglected or emotionally abused were about two to three times as likely to have depression as adults.
key_finding: Neglect was associated with depressive disorders (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.61-2.77), drug use (OR 1.36) and suicide attempts (OR 1.95); emotional abuse with depressive disorders (OR 3.06). The authors conclude the evidence suggests a causal relationship between non-sexual child maltreatment and a range of mental disorders.

title: Child maltreatment and depression: A meta-analysis of studies using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire
plain_language: Across nearly 69,000 people, emotional neglect and emotional abuse in childhood were among the experiences most strongly linked to later depression.
key_finding: Higher Childhood Trauma Questionnaire scores were associated with depression diagnosis (g = 1.07) and symptoms; every maltreatment type was associated with depression, with emotional abuse and emotional neglect showing the strongest associations.

title: Prospective Association between Childhood Behavioral Inhibition and Anxiety: a Meta-Analysis
journal: Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology
plain_language: Young children who are very shy and wary of new things are nearly three times as likely to develop anxiety later, especially social anxiety.
key_finding: Childhood behavioural inhibition prospectively increased the odds of anxiety (OR 2.80, 95% CI 2.03 to 3.86), from small for specific phobia (OR 1.49) to large for social anxiety disorder (OR 5.84).

title: Behavioral Inhibition and Risk for Developing Social Anxiety Disorder: A Meta-Analytic Study
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Very inhibited young children were over seven times as likely to develop social anxiety disorder.
key_finding: Behavioural inhibition was associated with a greater than sevenfold increase in risk of social anxiety disorder (OR 7.59); the authors note 15% of children show extreme inhibition and almost half of them eventually develop social anxiety disorder.

title: Behavioral manifestations of autism in the first year of life
plain_language: Some babies later diagnosed autistic were unusually quiet and inactive at 6 months, then became very easily distressed by 12 months.
key_finding: By 12 months, siblings later diagnosed with autism could be distinguished by specific behavioural markers and a temperament pattern of marked passivity and decreased activity at 6 months, followed by extreme distress reactions and less positive affect by 12 months.

title: Waking up is the hardest thing I do all day: Sleep inertia and sleep drunkenness
plain_language: Grogginess after waking is a real, measurable state, worst when waking during your body's night. It is more severe in some sleep and mood disorders.
key_finding: Sleep inertia is a distinct state after waking with performance impairment and sleepiness, most intense on awakenings during the biological night; prolonged 'sleep drunkenness' is common in hypersomnolence disorders, and difficulty waking is commonly endorsed in mood disorders. Evidence-based treatment guidance is not yet available.

title: Pathological demand avoidance in children and adolescents: A systematic review
plain_language: Research on 'pathological demand avoidance' is thin: definitions are unclear, it relies on parents' reports, and other explanations such as anxiety have rarely been tested.
key_finding: All studies based identification of PDA on Newson's original descriptions, whose development was not clearly described; most relied only on parent report, generally failed to consider alternative explanations such as anxiety, and none asked people with PDA themselves. Definition and measurement problems limit any conclusions.

title: Development of the 'Extreme Demand Avoidance Questionnaire' (EDA-Q): preliminary observations on a trait measure for Pathological Demand Avoidance
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: A parent questionnaire for extreme demand avoidance picked out children whose parents reported PDA, as a research tool rather than a diagnosis.
key_finding: The EDA-Q scored higher in children with parent-reported PDA than in all comparison groups (sensitivity .80, specificity .85), whereas the SDQ did not separate PDA from autism with disruptive behaviour; females scored higher than males. The authors present it as a tool for future research.

title: Identifying features of 'pathological demand avoidance' using the Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders (DISCO)
plain_language: In a clinic sample, children with many demand-avoidant features were almost all autistic and often anxious.
key_finding: Eleven DISCO items were selected to index PDA; the high-scoring group showed lack of co-operation, apparently manipulative and socially shocking behaviour, difficulties with others, anxiety and sudden mood changes, and all but one met autism criteria.

title: Intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety as explanatory frameworks for extreme demand avoidance in children and adolescents
plain_language: Children with demand avoidance found uncertainty especially hard, and avoiding demands may partly be a way to make life more predictable and less frightening.
key_finding: Children with a PDA diagnosis scored higher on parent-reported intolerance of uncertainty; demand avoidance could be conceptualised in part as an attempt to increase certainty and predictability to reduce anxiety. All PDA behaviour features were predicted by intolerance of uncertainty, and only meltdown was mediated by anxiety.

title: Fundamental challenges and likely refutations of the five basic premises of the polyvagal theory
plain_language: A detailed critique argues that the biology behind polyvagal theory, the source of much 'freeze' and 'shutdown' language, does not hold up.
key_finding: Argues that each of the five basic premises of polyvagal theory is either untenable or highly implausible given the scientific literature, and that treating respiratory sinus arrhythmia as equivalent to vagal tone is a category mistake.

title: Einstein and dyslexia: Is giftedness more frequent in children with a specific learning disorder than in typically developing children?
plain_language: Children with learning disorders are rarely 'gifted' by full IQ but more often by reasoning scores alone, and they score lower than other gifted children on memory and speed.
key_finding: Fewer than 1% of children with learning disorders had full-scale IQ above 130 (vs 2.28% expected), but 3.75% met the gifted criterion on the General Ability Index; gifted children with learning disorders scored higher on working memory and processing speed than other children with learning disorders but lower than equally gifted typically developing children.

title: Diagnostic Utility of WISC-IV General Abilities Index and Cognitive Proficiency Index Difference Scores Among Children With ADHD
plain_language: A big gap between reasoning scores and speed/memory scores did not reliably identify children with ADHD.
key_finding: Areas under the curve for the GAI-CPI discrepancy ranged from .46 to .64, so the discrepancy method had low accuracy in identifying children with ADHD.

title: Depression, Stress, and Anhedonia: Toward a Synthesis and Integrated Model
plain_language: Long-term stress may dull the brain's reward and motivation system, which could explain loss of interest in depression. This is a model, mostly based on animal studies.
key_finding: Presents a heuristic model in which anhedonia arises from dysfunctional interactions between stress and brain reward systems, supported by animal data that stress negatively affects mesocorticolimbic dopamine pathways involved in incentive motivation.

title: Children's Understanding of Death: A Review of Three Components of a Death Concept
plain_language: Most children understand that death is permanent, stops the body working and happens to everyone by about age 5 to 7.
key_finding: Most healthy children in modern urban-industrial societies understand all three components of death (irreversibility, non-functionality and universality) between 5 and 7 years of age.

title: The Context and Process of Theory Development: The Story of Ambiguous Loss
plain_language: The originator of 'ambiguous loss' explains how she named this kind of unclear, unresolved loss and how the idea has been developed since.
key_finding: Boss describes coining the term 'ambiguous loss' to name a previously unidentified family stressor, and notes that the theory is being tested and broadened across cultures, disciplines and types of loss.

title: Differential Behavioral Effects of Gonadal Steroids in Women with and in Those without Premenstrual Syndrome
plain_language: When hormones were switched off and then given back at normal levels, women with premenstrual syndrome got their symptoms back and other women did not, which suggests the issue is how some brains react to ordinary hormone changes rather than abnormal hormone levels.
key_finding: In women with PMS, leuprolide ovarian suppression reduced symptoms versus placebo, and adding back estradiol or progesterone brought symptoms back in the 10 responders, whereas 15 women without PMS showed no mood change on the same regimen. The authors conclude PMS symptoms are an abnormal response to normal hormonal changes.

title: The ESC/E(Z) complex, an effector of response to ovarian steroids, manifests an intrinsic difference in cells from women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: Cells grown in a lab dish from women with PMDD handled some hormone-responsive genes differently from other women's cells, a small early hint that the difference may be built in at the cell level.
key_finding: Untreated cell lines from women with PMDD over-expressed ESC/E(Z) gene-silencing complex mRNA (significant for MTF2, PHF19, SIRT1) but had decreased protein for those genes; progesterone increased several ESC/E(Z) transcripts only in controls, while estradiol decreased them in PMDD cells.

title: Allopregnanolone and mood disorders
plain_language: This review suggests that in some women a calming brain chemical made from progesterone has the opposite, upsetting effect at the levels reached before a period.
key_finding: This review proposes that PMDD mood symptoms are a paradoxical reaction to allopregnanolone acting at GABA-A receptors: negative mood occurs at luteal-phase-like concentrations on an inverted-U curve. It notes such paradoxical reactions to GABA-A modulators occur in 3-8% of people exposed, similar to the 3-8% PMDD prevalence in fertile-age women.

title: 5α-Reductase Inhibition Prevents the Luteal Phase Increase in Plasma Allopregnanolone Levels and Mitigates Symptoms in Women with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: In a small trial, a drug that stops progesterone being turned into a particular brain chemical eased PMDD symptoms at a high dose, supporting the idea that this chemical is involved.
key_finding: High-dose dutasteride (2.5 mg/day), which blocks progesterone-to-allopregnanolone conversion, significantly reduced irritability, sadness, anxiety, food cravings and bloating versus placebo in women with PMDD; 0.5 mg/day had no effect, and dutasteride did not affect mood in controls.

title: Allopregnanolone in premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD): Evidence for dysregulated sensitivity to GABA-A receptor modulating neuroactive steroids across the menstrual cycle
plain_language: This review pulls together evidence that, in PMDD, the brain's calming system does not adjust well to normal monthly hormone swings, which can also make stress hit harder before a period.
key_finding: This review argues that PMDD reflects impaired GABA-A receptor responses to normal fluctuations of allopregnanolone across the cycle, drawing on rodent and human evidence, with poor allopregnanolone-GABA control of the stress (HPA) axis raising luteal stress sensitivity; SSRI and GABA-A-targeting treatments are cited as supporting evidence.

title: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder Symptoms Following Ovarian Suppression: Triggered by Change in Ovarian Steroid Levels but Not Continuous Stable Levels
plain_language: In a small study, PMDD symptoms came back when hormone levels went up but faded once levels held steady, suggesting the change itself is the trigger.
key_finding: Among 12 women whose PMDD remitted on leuprolide, symptoms rose significantly in the first month of continuous estradiol/progesterone but not in months 2-3 or during the placebo month. The authors conclude that the change in levels from low to high, not the steady-state level, was associated with onset of PMDD symptoms.

title: Estrogen Shapes Dopamine-Dependent Cognitive Processes: Implications for Women's Health
plain_language: In healthy women, whether higher oestrogen helped or hurt working memory depended on their natural dopamine level, which may explain why hormone effects on thinking differ between people.
key_finding: Natural estradiol fluctuations affected working memory, and the direction of the effect depended on baseline prefrontal dopamine (indexed by COMT Val158Met genotype and enzyme activity); fMRI patterns fitted a dopamine 'cortical efficiency' account.

title: Associations Between Symptoms of Premenstrual Disorders and Polygenic Liability for Major Psychiatric Disorders
plain_language: Women whose genes carry more risk for ADHD and other mental health conditions were somewhat more likely to report premenstrual mood symptoms, suggesting a shared genetic background.
key_finding: Self-reported premenstrual depression/irritability (21.7% of 56,725 women) was associated with polygenic risk scores for depression (beta 0.13), schizophrenia (0.11), bipolar disorder (0.07), ADHD (0.07, P=1.58e-9) and autism (0.03), but not height; results held in women without a psychiatric diagnosis.

title: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: Evidence for a New Category for DSM-5
plain_language: Experts reviewed the research and agreed PMDD is a real, well-defined condition that deserves its own place in the main psychiatric diagnostic manual.
key_finding: The DSM-5 Mood Disorders Work Group review concluded that evidence on PMDD diagnosis, treatment and validity had matured enough to move it from the DSM-IV research appendix to a full DSM-5 category; it cites PMDD affecting 2%-5% of premenopausal women.

title: Toward the Reliable Diagnosis of DSM-5 Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: The Carolina Premenstrual Assessment Scoring System (C-PASS)
plain_language: A scoring system for daily symptom diaries diagnoses PMDD almost as well as an expert, and shows that remembering symptoms afterwards is not a reliable way to tell whether you have PMDD.
key_finding: The C-PASS standardises DSM-5 PMDD diagnosis from 2 or more months of DRSP daily ratings; in 200 women it agreed with expert clinical diagnosis with an estimated 98% correct classification, and retrospective reports of premenstrual worsening poorly predicted prospective diagnosis.

title: Towards a consensus on diagnostic criteria, measurement and trial design of the premenstrual disorders: the ISPMD Montreal consensus
plain_language: An international group of experts agreed on shared rules for diagnosing and studying premenstrual disorders.
key_finding: An international expert group (founding the ISPMD, Montreal 2008) set out unified recommendations on diagnostic criteria for premenstrual disorders, how to quantify them, and clinical-trial design, intended to inform ICD-11 and DSM-5.

title: The prevalence of premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: When PMDD is confirmed with daily symptom tracking over two cycles, 3.2% of women have it (1.6% in community samples); studies without that tracking give 7.7%, likely an overestimate.
key_finding: Pooled PMDD point prevalence was 3.2% (95% CI 1.7-5.9) with confirmed diagnosis and 7.7% (5.3-11.0) with provisional diagnosis; community samples with confirmed diagnosis gave 1.6% (1.0-2.5) with low heterogeneity (I2=26%). Heterogeneity was high across all studies (I2=99%); studies relying on provisional diagnosis are likely to produce artificially high prevalence rates.

title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: SSRI antidepressants reduce premenstrual symptoms whether taken every day or only in the luteal phase, though side effects such as nausea and low energy are relatively frequent.
key_finding: SSRIs reduced premenstrual symptoms more than placebo (moderate dose: SMD -0.65 from end scores, low-quality evidence; SMD -0.36 from change scores, moderate-quality evidence), with no clear difference between luteal-only and continuous dosing. Adverse effects were dose-related, most often nausea (NNH 7) and low energy (NNH 9).

title: Ulipristal Acetate for Treatment of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: A Proof-of-Concept Randomized Controlled Trial
plain_language: A drug that blocks progesterone's effects reduced PMDD mood symptoms in one trial, but it needs repeating before it can be relied on.
key_finding: Ulipristal acetate 5 mg/day for three cycles improved premenstrual DRSP scores by 41% vs 22% on placebo (difference -18%, 95% CI -29 to -8), with effects on depressive and anger/irritability subscales but not physical symptoms; remission occurred in 50.0% vs 21.1%.

title: The effectiveness of GnRHa with and without 'add-back' therapy in treating premenstrual syndrome: a meta analysis
journal: BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
plain_language: Medicines that switch off the ovaries' cycle appear effective for premenstrual syndrome, and adding back hormones to reduce side effects does not reduce the benefit.
key_finding: GnRH analogues were more effective than placebo for premenstrual syndrome (SMD -1.19, 95% CI -1.88 to -0.51; OR 8.66), and adding hormonal add-back therapy did not reduce efficacy (SMD 0.12, -0.35 to 0.58).

title: A randomized, double-blind study on efficacy and safety of sepranolone in premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: An experimental PMDD drug did not beat a dummy treatment on its main measure, though some later, less reliable analyses looked more promising.
key_finding: The prespecified primary endpoint (DRSP Sum21) showed large improvement in all arms but no significant difference from placebo; distress improved significantly (p=0.037). A post-hoc per-protocol analysis of 9 premenstrual days favoured sepranolone 10 mg (p=0.008).

title: Premenstrual Exacerbations of Mood Disorders: Findings and Knowledge Gaps
plain_language: Many women with depression or bipolar disorder notice their usual symptoms get worse before a period, which is different from PMDD and may need a different treatment approach.
key_finding: Around 60% of women with mood disorders report premenstrual exacerbation (PME) in community and clinical studies, and PME predicts a more severe course; treatments that help PMDD show less or no efficacy in PME, and evidence is sparse and mostly from small studies and case reports.

title: Effects of acute estradiol and progesterone on perimenstrual exacerbation of suicidal ideation and related symptoms: a crossover randomized controlled trial
plain_language: In a small trial, keeping hormone levels steady around the period reduced suicidal thoughts in women whose thoughts worsened at that time, suggesting the hormone drop itself plays a part.
key_finding: Buffering perimenstrual hormone withdrawal with transdermal estradiol plus oral progesterone reduced perimenstrual suicidal ideation, planning, hopelessness, rejection sensitivity and perceived burdensomeness versus placebo; delayed withdrawal from the hormones brought back SI, hopelessness and rejection sensitivity. No participant met full PMDD criteria, but 93% had peak SI perimenstrually.

title: Suicidal Risk in Women with Premenstrual Syndrome and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Women with PMDD are more likely to have suicidal thoughts and attempts, which is why doctors should ask about this.
key_finding: Across 10 meta-analysed studies, women with PMDD had higher odds of suicide attempt (OR 6.97, 95% CI 2.98-16.29) and suicidal ideation (OR 3.95, 2.97-5.24); women with PMS had raised ideation (OR 10.06, 95% CI 1.32-76.67) but not attempts.

title: Mortality Risk Among Women With Premenstrual Disorders in Sweden
plain_language: Women with premenstrual disorders do not die earlier overall, but they do have a higher risk of suicide, especially if diagnosed young.
key_finding: Women with clinically diagnosed premenstrual disorders had no higher all-cause mortality (aHR 0.91, 0.82-1.02) but higher death from non-natural causes (HR 1.59) and suicide (HR 1.92, 1.43-2.60); diagnosis before age 25 was linked to higher all-cause (HR 2.51) and suicide (HR 3.84) mortality.

title: Reproductive steroids and ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle
plain_language: In a small diary study of young women, ADHD-type symptoms rose on days after oestrogen fell while progesterone or testosterone rose, with increases just after a period starts and just after ovulation.
key_finding: Lower estradiol together with higher progesterone or testosterone predicted more ADHD symptoms the next day, particularly in women high in trait impulsivity; phase analyses suggested symptom increases in the early follicular and early luteal (post-ovulatory) phases.

title: Female-specific pharmacotherapy in ADHD: premenstrual adjustment of psychostimulant dosage
plain_language: Nine women whose ADHD medicine seemed to wear off before their period felt better when their doctor raised the dose that week, but this is early evidence and should only be done with a doctor.
key_finding: In 9 consecutive women with ADHD and premenstrual worsening, raising the psychostimulant dose in the premenstrual week improved ADHD and mood symptoms (inattention, irritability, energy) with minimal adverse events over 6-24 months, and all chose to continue.

title: Prevalence of hormone-related mood disorder symptoms in women with ADHD
plain_language: Many women attending an adult ADHD clinic reported PMDD symptoms, postnatal depression and difficult menopause symptoms, but they were compared only with general-population figures.
key_finding: In 209 consecutive women with ADHD, the prevalence of PMDD symptoms (MINI-Plus) and postpartum depression after first birth (EPDS) was high compared with the general population, and climacteric anxiety, depression, sexual dysfunction, vasomotor and somatic scores were raised; comparison was with general-population figures rather than a matched control group.

title: Increased risk of provisional premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) among females with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): cross-sectional survey study
plain_language: Young women with ADHD screened positive for possible PMDD more often (31.4% with a reported diagnosis, 41.1% by symptom scale) than those without ADHD (9.8%), though the screen was a one-off questionnaire, not daily tracking.
key_finding: Provisional PMDD (PSST screen) was present in 31.4% of those with self-reported clinical ADHD and 41.1% with ASRS-based ADHD versus 9.8% without ADHD; risk was highest with ASRS-based ADHD plus depression/anxiety (RR 4.53, 3.10-6.61).

title: Association of ADHD/ASD traits with premenstrual dysphoric disorder among full-time employed women in Japan: A cross-sectional study
plain_language: Working women with more ADHD traits were much more likely to report PMDD symptoms, while autistic traits were not linked.
key_finding: Among 2,000 Japanese employed women not using contraception and with no history of pregnancy, ADHD traits (ASRS) were associated with PMDD (adjusted OR 6.49, 4.10-10.2) while autism traits (AQ-10) were not; PMDD prevalence was 5.1% on a Japanese scale based on DSM-IV-TR research criteria.
