title: The monthly spectrum: Premenstrual symptoms across ADHD and autism
plain_language: Women with ADHD and autistic women both reported more severe premenstrual problems than other women.
key_finding: Both ADHD and autistic women had significantly higher provisional PMDD rates (PSST) than controls, with no difference between the two groups; premenstrual symptoms rose with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and social difficulties, and sensory hypersensitivity did not independently explain them. The authors warn prevalence depends on recruitment.

title: ADHD and Sex Hormones in Females: A Systematic Review
plain_language: A small body of research hints that ADHD symptoms shift with hormone changes such as puberty and the menstrual cycle, but more research is needed.
key_finding: Eleven studies gave largely suggestive evidence linking ADHD symptoms to sex hormones in females, mainly in puberty and across the menstrual cycle, but studies were few, small and heterogeneous; the authors call for research on other milestones including menopause.

title: Research advances and future directions in female ADHD: the lifelong interplay of hormonal fluctuations with mood, cognition, and disease
plain_language: ADHD experts describe how puberty, periods, pregnancy and menopause can make ADHD and mood harder, and point out that treatments for women at these times have barely been studied.
key_finding: This expert review concludes that hormonal transitions exacerbate ADHD symptoms and mood disturbances while pharmacological research and tailored treatments are lacking, and that undiagnosed women have increased vulnerability to PMDD, postpartum depression and cardiovascular disease in perimenopause.

title: Association of Hormonal Contraception With Depression
plain_language: Women, especially teenagers, who started hormonal contraception were somewhat more likely to start antidepressants later, though this shows a link rather than proof of cause.
key_finding: Compared with non-users, hormonal contraceptive users had higher rates of first antidepressant use: combined pill RR 1.23, progestogen-only pill 1.34, patch 2.0, vaginal ring 1.6, LNG-IUS 1.4; adolescents 15-19 on the combined pill had RR 1.8.

title: Association of Hormonal Contraception With Suicide Attempts and Suicides
plain_language: In Denmark, hormonal contraception use was linked to a higher risk of suicide attempts and suicide, with the link for attempts peaking after two months of use and teenagers at highest relative risk.
key_finding: Current or recent hormonal contraceptive use was associated with first suicide attempt (HR 1.97, 1.85-2.10) and suicide (HR 3.08, 1.34-7.08) versus never-use; the association with attempts peaked after 2 months of use and adolescents had the highest relative risk.

title: Hormonal Contraceptive Use and Risk of Depression Among Young Women With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Young women with ADHD who used the contraceptive pill were more likely to be diagnosed with depression than pill users without ADHD, which is worth discussing when choosing contraception.
key_finding: Women with ADHD had a 3-fold higher depression risk irrespective of contraception (aHR 3.69); combined oral contraceptive users with ADHD had aHR 5.19 versus non-users without ADHD and 6.10 versus combined-pill users without ADHD; progestogen-only pill users with ADHD had aHR 5.00. Non-oral methods were similarly moderately raised in both groups.

title: Depression and anxiety disorders during the postpartum period in women diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: New mothers with ADHD had prevalence ratios of 5.09 for depression and 5.41 for anxiety diagnoses in the year after birth compared with mothers without ADHD.
key_finding: In the year after delivery, 16.76% of women with ADHD were diagnosed with depression (PR 5.09, 4.68-5.54) and 24.92% with anxiety (PR 5.41, 5.06-5.78), beyond other risk factors; surveillance bias is possible.

title: Perimenopausal symptoms in women with and without ADHD: A population-based cohort study
plain_language: Women with ADHD reported more severe perimenopause symptoms, starting at younger ages, than women without ADHD.
key_finding: Women with ADHD had higher total perimenopausal symptom scores (18.0 vs 13.0) and severe perimenopausal symptoms were more common (54.2% vs 30.1%; PR 1.80, 1.64-1.98) across psychological, somatic and urogenital domains; the score gap was largest at ages 35-39 (19.0 vs 12.5), which the authors interpret as an earlier onset of perimenopause in ADHD.

title: Effects of Estradiol Withdrawal on Mood in Women With Past Perimenopausal Depression
plain_language: Women who had been depressed around menopause became low again when their oestrogen was quietly stopped, while other women did not, suggesting some women are especially sensitive to oestrogen dropping.
key_finding: After 3 weeks of open-label estradiol, blinded switch to placebo raised depression scores in women with past perimenopausal depression (CES-D 2.4 to 8.8; HAM-D 3.0 to 6.6; P=.0004) but not in controls or those continuing estradiol, despite similar estradiol levels on placebo.

title: Premenstrual disorders
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: A clinical review says diagnosing premenstrual disorders needs two months of daily symptom tracking; SSRIs and contraceptive pills taken with little or no break work best, and hormone-suppressing GnRH treatment may help women who do not respond.
key_finding: Clinical review: premenstrual disorders include premenstrual syndrome, PMDD and premenstrual worsening of another medical condition; diagnosis rests on a careful medical history and daily symptom monitoring across 2 menstrual cycles; the most efficacious treatments for PMS and PMDD include serotonin reuptake inhibitors and contraceptives with a shortened or no hormone-free interval, and women who do not respond may benefit from GnRH agonist treatment.

title: The efficacy of fluoxetine in improving physical symptoms associated with premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: PMDD is not only emotional: breast tenderness, bloating and headaches are among its most common physical symptoms, and they improved more with daily fluoxetine than with placebo in a trial of 320 women.
key_finding: In a randomised, double-blind trial, daily fluoxetine (20 or 60 mg) was superior to placebo for the common physical symptoms of PMDD, including breast tenderness, bloating and headache, with no difference between the two doses.

title: Menstrual migraine is caused by estrogen withdrawal: revisiting the evidence
plain_language: Some women get migraines tied to their period, widely thought to be triggered by the drop in oestrogen beforehand, but the evidence for that explanation is still limited.
key_finding: Menstrual migraine affects about 6% of reproductive-age women. The widely accepted idea that the premenstrual drop in estrogen triggers attacks is plausible but rests on limited evidence, with small samples and inconsistent definitions.

title: Gastrointestinal symptoms before and during menses in healthy women
plain_language: Most healthy women in this study noticed gut symptoms around their period, and women with low mood or anxiety, and those with tiredness, were more likely to have several gut symptoms.
key_finding: 73% of healthy women had at least one GI symptom in the 5 days before or during menses, most often abdominal pain (58% before; 55% during) and diarrhoea (24%; 28%). Women with emotional symptoms were more likely to have multiple GI symptoms, and fatigue was common and tied to GI symptoms.

title: Symptoms across the menstrual cycle in women with irritable bowel syndrome
plain_language: For women with IBS, gut symptoms and whole-body symptoms rise and fall with the menstrual cycle.
key_finding: Using a daily diary across one cycle, women with IBS had more severe GI, somatic and psychological symptoms than controls, and many symptoms, not only gut symptoms, varied with menstrual cycle phase, with the strongest cycle effect in somatic and menstrual symptoms.

title: Adolescent body dysmorphic disorder: Insight, executive function, and rates of ADHD and Autistic traits
plain_language: In a small study of teenagers with body dysmorphic disorder, nearly all had autistic traits and more than a third had ADHD, but the sample was very small.
key_finding: Most adolescents with body dysmorphic disorder (96%) had autistic traits and 39% met criteria for ADHD; 73% had poor or delusional insight.

title: Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone for premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: A specific pill (drospirenone with low-dose oestrogen) eased PMDD symptoms more than placebo over three months, though placebo helped a lot too and side effects such as nausea, spotting and breast pain were more common.
key_finding: In two placebo-controlled trials in women with PMDD, drospirenone 3 mg plus ethinyl estradiol 20 μg reduced premenstrual symptoms after three months (MD -7.92; 95% CI -11.16 to -4.67) and improved productivity, social activities and relationships; nausea, intermenstrual bleeding and breast pain were more common (ORs 3.15, 4.92, 2.67). The placebo also had a large effect, and it is unknown whether the pill works beyond three cycles, helps milder symptoms, or beats other pills.

title: Efficacy of a New Low-Dose Oral Contraceptive With Drospirenone in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: In 450 women, the drospirenone pill taken 24 days on and 4 days off helped PMDD symptoms more than placebo; about 1 in 8 women benefited because of the pill rather than placebo.
key_finding: In a multicentre double-blind RCT, a 24/4 regimen of drospirenone 3 mg/ethinyl estradiol 20 μg reduced total DRSP scores more than placebo (-37.49 vs -29.99; adjusted difference -7.5, 95% CI -11.2 to -3.8), with response (50% decrease) in 48% vs 36% (relative risk 1.7), a number-needed-to-treat of 8.

title: Treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder with a new drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive formulation
plain_language: In a small trial where each woman tried both the pill and placebo, the drospirenone pill helped PMDD symptoms more than placebo.
key_finding: In a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, drospirenone 3 mg/ethinyl estradiol 20 μg (24/4) reduced total DRSP scores more than placebo (-12.47, 95% CI -18.28 to -6.66); 61.7% vs 31.8% responded on the Clinical Global Impressions-Improvement scale.

title: Efficacy of combined oral contraceptives for depressive symptoms and overall symptomatology in premenstrual syndrome: pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomized trials
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: Across 9 trials, the combined pill helped premenstrual symptoms overall but did not clearly help low mood specifically, and no one brand stood out as better than the rest.
key_finding: In pairwise and network meta-analysis, combined oral contraceptives beat placebo for overall premenstrual symptoms (SMD 0.41; 95% credible interval 0.17-0.67) but not for premenstrual depressive symptoms specifically (SMD 0.22; -0.06 to 0.47), and no combined pill was more effective than any other.

title: Continuous oral levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol for treating premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: Taking a pill continuously with no break helped some PMDD measures more than placebo, but not all of them.
key_finding: Continuous daily levonorgestrel 90 μg/ethinyl estradiol 20 μg for 112 days reduced late-luteal DRSP scores more than placebo in the first cycle (-30.52 vs -22.47) and the worst 5 days of the last cycle (-26.77 vs -20.89), but other primary end points were not significant; 52% vs 40% responded.

title: An overview of four studies of a continuous oral contraceptive (levonorgestrel 90 mcg/ethinyl estradiol 20 mcg) on premenstrual dysphoric disorder and premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: Studies of a no-break pill for PMDD and PMS gave mixed results, and placebo also helped a lot, so the benefit is uncertain.
key_finding: Across four studies of continuous levonorgestrel 90 μg/ethinyl estradiol 20 μg, premenstrual symptoms improved by 30% to 59% in controlled trials and 56% to 81% in an open-label substudy, but results were not consistent between studies and the placebo effect was large.

title: Comparison of premenstrual dysphoric disorder treatment with antidepressants and combined oral contraceptives: a systematic review with network meta-analysis
plain_language: When studies were compared indirectly, both SSRIs and the pill helped PMDD; there are no direct head-to-head trials yet.
key_finding: A network meta-analysis concluded that both SSRIs and combined oral contraceptives are effective for PMDD, with continuous paroxetine and the 24/4 drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol regimen the most effective in their classes; the authors call for direct head-to-head trials between the two classes.

title: Continuous or Intermittent Dosing With Sertraline for Patients With Severe Premenstrual Syndrome or Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: Taking sertraline only in the two weeks before a period worked about as well as taking it every day, and it worked within the first month; women who also had symptoms after their period ended did less well.
key_finding: In a double-blind RCT of sertraline 50-100 mg/day, both continuous and luteal-phase dosing improved premenstrual symptoms more than placebo, with improvement occurring swiftly in the first month; premenstrual dosing did not differ from continuous dosing. Placebo improved gradually to a similar level by the third month, and women with more postmenstrual symptoms remained more symptomatic whichever regimen they took.

title: Efficacy of intermittent, luteal phase sertraline treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: Taking sertraline only in the second half of the cycle helped 50% of women with PMDD within the first cycle, compared with 26% on placebo.
key_finding: Luteal-phase sertraline (50-100 mg) beat placebo over three cycles (responders 50% vs 26% by cycle 1); about 8% on sertraline and less than 1% on placebo stopped because of adverse events.

title: Symptom-Onset Dosing of Sertraline for the Treatment of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: Taking sertraline only on symptom days gave mixed results: it helped on some measures but missed the main one. Stopping it each month didn't cause withdrawal symptoms.
key_finding: Starting sertraline (50-100 mg/day) at symptom onset and stopping in the first days of menses did not beat placebo on the primary outcome (PMTS difference 1.88; P = .06) but did on depression, total DRSP and anger/irritability scores, with response in 67.0% vs 52.4%; the authors conclude women "may or may not benefit" depending on the scale. Abrupt stopping caused no discontinuation symptoms.

title: Psychological Intervention for Premenstrual Syndrome: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
plain_language: Cognitive behavioural therapy may ease premenstrual anxiety and low mood, but the trials were small and low quality.
key_finding: Low-quality evidence suggests CBT reduces anxiety (ES -0.58; NNT 5) and depression (ES -0.55; NNT 5) in premenstrual syndrome, with possible benefits on behaviour and interference with daily life; monitoring alone had limited support and education appeared ineffective.

title: Internet-Based Cognitive-Behavioural Intervention for Women with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial
plain_language: An 8-week online CBT programme with therapist support reduced how much PMDD interfered with daily life, and the benefits lasted at least 6 months.
key_finding: Eight weeks of therapist-guided internet CBT reduced functional and psychological impairment, everyday-life interference, symptom intensity and disability compared with a waitlist, with effects stable at 6 months; the authors conclude iCBT was highly effective.

title: Evaluation of the relative efficacy of a couple cognitive-behaviour therapy (CBT) for Premenstrual Disorders (PMDs), in comparison to one-to-one CBT and a wait list control: A randomized controlled trial
plain_language: CBT, either alone or with a partner, reduced premenstrual distress; doing it as a couple helped partners understand and improved coping.
key_finding: Both one-to-one and couple CBT reduced premenstrual symptoms, emotional reactivity and distress compared with a waitlist; couple CBT gave greater active behavioural coping, and partner understanding and relationship improvement were reported most in the couple condition.

title: Efficacy of psychological interventions for premenstrual syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
plain_language: Across 20 trials, talking therapies reduced premenstrual symptoms and related low mood, anxiety and irritability, though most trials were in PMS rather than confirmed PMDD.
key_finding: Psychological interventions reduced PMS severity (after excluding an outlier trial, SMD -1.57) and PMS-related depressive (SMD -1.08), anxiety (SMD -1.03) and anger/irritability symptoms (SMD -0.85); the authors conclude they "may" help.

title: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues for premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
plain_language: Medicines that switch off the ovaries work well for severe premenstrual symptoms but cause menopause-like side effects; adding hormones back to protect the body is under-tested and progestogen may bring symptoms back.
key_finding: GnRH agonists without add-back improved global premenstrual symptoms vs placebo (SMD -1.23; high-certainty) but raised withdrawal due to adverse events (RR 4.24). With add-back, evidence was low certainty (1 RCT, 31 women), and oestrogen plus cyclical progestogen add-back may worsen symptoms (SMD 0.90). Authors: menopausal side effects preclude long-term use; GnRH agonists can give a short-term break, and long-term add-back data are lacking.

title: What’s Stopping Us? Using GnRH Analogs With Stable Hormone Addback in Treatment-Resistant Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: A how-to guide for clinicians: track symptoms daily, try SSRIs and then the pill, and consider ovary-suppressing injections with hormone add-back if those fail.
key_finding: Practical guidance recommending prospective symptom ratings for diagnosis, SSRIs and oral contraceptives as first- and second-line treatments, and GnRH analogues with hormone add-back when these fail; it identifies poor provider knowledge and cost as barriers to access.

title: Hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy for severe premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: Most women who had their womb and ovaries removed for severe premenstrual syndrome, and then took HRT, said their cyclical symptoms had gone, but this was a small look-back study with no comparison group.
key_finding: Of 47 women who had hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for severe PMS, 96% were satisfied or very satisfied and 93.6% reported complete resolution of cyclical symptoms; 93.6% continued HRT. Women had suffered for a mean of 9.68 years before surgery. This was a retrospective structured-interview series without a comparison group.

title: The effect of hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy in women with severe premenstrual syndrome
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: In 14 women whose severe premenstrual syndrome had not responded to other treatments, removing the womb and ovaries (with oestrogen afterwards) ended the cyclical symptoms.
key_finding: In 14 women with severe, treatment-resistant PMS confirmed by prospective charting, hysterectomy, oophorectomy and continuous oestrogen replacement abolished the cyclic symptom pattern at 6 months, with improved mood and quality of life; the authors say surgery is indicated for a small, selected group.

title: The effect of hysterectomy or levonorgestrel‐releasing intrauterine system on premenstrual symptoms in women treated for menorrhagia: secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
plain_language: Removing the womb but keeping the ovaries reduced premenstrual symptoms no more than a hormonal coil did, in women treated for heavy periods.
key_finding: In women treated for heavy periods (not diagnosed with PMS), premenstrual symptoms decreased similarly after hysterectomy (ovaries kept) or a levonorgestrel IUS by six months; the authors state the effect on premenstrual syndrome remains unsettled.

title: ISPMD consensus on the management of premenstrual disorders
plain_language: International experts agree that PMDD treatment starts with a careful diagnosis, and that the main options either act on serotonin or switch off ovulation; CBT, calcium and chasteberry need more study.
key_finding: ISPMD consensus: management rests on careful diagnosis; options act either on central serotonin (SSRIs) or by suppressing ovulation (oral contraceptives, GnRH agonists, danazol, estradiol), with oophorectomy considered; CBT, calcium and Vitex agnus castus are named as warranting further exploration.

title: Fourth consensus of the International Society for Premenstrual Disorders (ISPMD): auditable standards for diagnosis and management of premenstrual disorder
plain_language: Experts set standards for good PMDD care: two months of symptom diaries before diagnosis, SSRIs as the first treatment, and clear explanation of side effects.
key_finding: ISPMD auditable standards: diagnosis should rest on an accurate history and 2 months of symptom diaries showing premenstrual symptoms relieved by menstruation; for treatment, the top standards were SSRIs as first line, an evidence-based approach, and proper explanation of SSRI side effects.

title: The treatment of premenstrual syndrome with preparations of Vitex agnus castus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: Chasteberry looked helpful for PMS in pooled trials, but the studies were poor quality and probably overstate the benefit; PMDD was barely studied.
key_finding: Vitex agnus castus had a large pooled effect vs placebo on PMS symptoms (Hedges g -1.21), but most trials had high risk of bias, heterogeneity was extreme (I² 91%) and publication bias was likely; the authors say this precludes a definitive conclusion and the effect is "at best" an overestimate.

title: Vitex agnus-castus in premenstrual syndrome: A meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials
plain_language: In the three best-reported trials, specific chasteberry extracts helped PMS symptoms more than placebo; most other trials were too poorly reported to count.
key_finding: Restricting to double-blind trials of properly characterised extracts (Ze 440, BNO 1095), women taking vitex were 2.57 times more likely than placebo to have remission of PMS symptoms; most of the 21 trials could not be used because of incomplete reporting.

title: Vitex agnus castus for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder: a systematic review
plain_language: All eight trials found chasteberry helped, but most were in PMS, used different products and measures, and so are hard to compare.
key_finding: All 8 RCTs were positive for vitex in PMS or PMDD and it was well tolerated, but most focused on PMS, diagnostic criteria changed over time, three different preparations were tested and outcome measures varied; the authors consider it a safe and efficacious alternative.

title: Calcium carbonate and the premenstrual syndrome: Effects on premenstrual and menstrual symptoms
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: In a large trial of women with PMS, daily calcium cut premenstrual symptoms by about half, compared with about a third on placebo.
key_finding: In a multicentre double-blind RCT in women with moderate-to-severe PMS, 1200 mg/day elemental calcium (as calcium carbonate) for 3 cycles reduced luteal symptom scores by 48% from baseline vs 30% with placebo by the third cycle, with all 4 symptom factors reduced.

title: Efficacy of vitamin B-6 in the treatment of premenstrual syndrome: systematic review
plain_language: Vitamin B6 at up to 100 mg a day may ease premenstrual symptoms, but most of the trials were poor quality.
key_finding: Vitamin B6 improved overall premenstrual symptoms vs placebo (OR 2.32) and premenstrual depression (OR 1.69; 4 trials, 541 patients); conclusions are limited by the low quality of most trials, and doses up to 100 mg/day are "likely to be of benefit".

title: A Synergistic Effect of a Daily Supplement for 1 Month of 200 mg Magnesium plus 50 mg Vitamin B 6 for the Relief of Anxiety-Related Premenstrual Symptoms: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Crossover Study
journal: Journal of Women's Health & Gender-Based Medicine
plain_language: In 44 women with mild premenstrual symptoms, magnesium on its own did not help; magnesium plus B6 slightly eased anxiety-type symptoms.
key_finding: In a one-cycle crossover RCT, no single treatment differed overall, but magnesium 200 mg plus B6 50 mg reduced anxiety-related premenstrual symptoms (p = 0.040); the effect was "small" and "modest", and the authors say further studies are needed before recommendations; absorption from magnesium oxide was poor.

title: The Association Between Serum Magnesium and Premenstrual Syndrome: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
plain_language: Women with PMS do not reliably have lower magnesium levels than other women.
key_finding: There was no overall association between serum or red-cell magnesium and PMS, except lower luteal serum magnesium in a subgroup of studies done outside the USA; the authors call for well-designed trials of magnesium.

title: Effect of nutritional interventions on the psychological symptoms of premenstrual syndrome in women of reproductive age: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
plain_language: Across 31 trials, B6, calcium and zinc helped premenstrual mood symptoms; magnesium, vitamin D and special diets lacked good evidence, and almost all trials had quality problems.
key_finding: Vitamin B6, calcium and zinc consistently improved psychological PMS symptoms, while evidence was insufficient for vitamin B1, vitamin D, whole grains, soy, fatty acids, magnesium, multivitamins or PMS-specific diets; only 1 trial had low risk of bias.

title: Exercise for premenstrual syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
plain_language: Regular exercise may ease premenstrual symptoms, but the trials were mostly low quality.
key_finding: Exercise for at least 8 weeks reduced global PMS symptoms vs comparators (SMD -1.08) with substantial heterogeneity (I² 87%), and 87% of trials were at high risk of bias; the authors conclude exercise "may be" effective but uncertainty remains.

title: Premenstrual Syndrome as a Predictor of Menopausal Symptoms
plain_language: Premenstrual syndrome tended to fade during the run-up to menopause, but women who had it were more likely to get hot flushes, low mood and poor sleep in that transition.
key_finding: Premenstrual syndrome decreased with age and with changes in bleeding status during the menopause transition, but women with PMS at baseline were more likely to report hot flushes (OR 2.09), depressed mood (OR 2.34), poor sleep (OR 1.72) and decreased libido (OR 1.54).

title: Menstrual cycle phase, menopausal transition stage, self-reports of premenstrual syndrome and symptom severity: observations from the Seattle Midlife Women's Health Study
plain_language: Premenstrual mood symptoms were not worse in the early menopause transition than in the late reproductive years in this study.
key_finding: Daily diaries showed dysphoric mood, neuromuscular and somatic symptoms rose from post-menses to pre-menses and were amplified by current PMS, but late reproductive and early menopausal-transition stage had no effect on any symptom group.

title: Patient Experiences of Health Care Providers in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: Examining the Role of Provider Specialty
plain_language: In a survey of 2,512 people seeking PMDD care, different types of clinician had different strengths, and gynaecologists were the most likely to ask for daily symptom tracking.
key_finding: In the IAPMD global survey, psychotherapists were rated highest on interpersonal factors, gynaecologists and psychiatrists highest on PMDD awareness and knowledge, and gynaecologists were most likely to ask patients to track symptoms daily; authors call for more PMDD training.

title: Patient Perspectives of Healthcare for Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder in Australia: A Mixed-Methods Study
plain_language: Australians seeking PMDD care saw about five clinicians on average; 54% reported medical gaslighting, 56% misdiagnosis, and only 19% were diagnosed in line with DSM recommendations.
key_finding: Participants had seen an average of 5.1 healthcare providers seeking a PMDD diagnosis and judged 51% to have poor PMDD awareness; 54% reported medical gaslighting and 56% misdiagnosis, and only 19% had diagnostic methods consistent with DSM recommendations. Diagnosis was described as bringing better coping and self-compassion.

title: Medical gas-lighting, diagnostic odyssey and self-advocacy among women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder from nine countries
plain_language: Women with PMDD in nine countries described being dismissed, long roads to diagnosis and having to advocate for themselves, whatever their health system.
key_finding: Interviews generated four themes (medical gas-lighting and the importance of diagnosis, diagnostic odyssey, access to healthcare, self-advocacy); negative experiences delayed diagnosis and fostered mistrust, and were similar across countries.

title: Women’s experiences of receiving a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder: a qualitative investigation
plain_language: UK women described years of misdiagnosis before PMDD was recognised, and diagnosis as life-changing.
key_finding: Four themes emerged: a broken woman, misdiagnosis and the lost decades, a life transformed, and negotiating the aftermath; the authors stress accurate, timely detection and clinician training.

title: Barriers to Diagnosis and Treatment for Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): A Scoping Review
plain_language: A review found many barriers to getting PMDD diagnosed and treated, including stigma, clinicians' limited knowledge and fragmented health services.
key_finding: Barriers to PMDD diagnosis and treatment were individual (stigma, medical mistrust, shame, side effects), medical (limited provider knowledge, non-adherence to guidelines, negative interactions), cultural and structural (fragmented care, limited access).

title: The experiences and psychological impact of living with premenstrual disorders: a systematic review and thematic synthesis
plain_language: Women's accounts describe PMDD as taking over their lives, leaving them to manage it and push for care largely on their own.
key_finding: Women described premenstrual disorders as intense, life-changing and life-controlling ("controlled by PMDs"; "a woman and life left broken"); they carried responsibility for understanding and managing their condition and advocating for themselves in healthcare.

title: Women’s experiences of living with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) or premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD): A scoping review
plain_language: Studies of women with PMS or PMDD describe feeling like two different people, strain on relationships and a lack of understanding from those around them.
key_finding: Scoping review themes: lack of understanding or support, dual identity, impact on relationships, and difficulty reaching diagnosis; women reported a lack of understanding from family, friends and medical practitioners.

title: Prevalence of lifetime self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in a global sample of 599 patients reporting prospectively confirmed diagnosis with premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: In an online survey of people with confirmed PMDD, most had had suicidal thoughts and about a third had made an attempt in their lifetime.
key_finding: Among respondents with PMDD diagnosed using two months of daily ratings, lifetime rates were high for active suicidal ideation (72%), planning (49%), attempt (34%) and non-suicidal self-injury (51%); 70% reported at least one comorbid psychiatric diagnosis.

title: Cannabis, Psychedelics, and Other Substance Use to Manage Premenstrual Symptoms: A Survey Study
plain_language: About half of people with PMDD in this survey used cannabis to cope with premenstrual mood symptoms; whether it helps has not been tested.
key_finding: To manage premenstrual mood symptoms, respondents most often used cannabis (30.0%), alcohol (16.1%) and psychedelics (5.9%), higher in PMDD (51.5% cannabis, 16.2% psychedelics); cannabis and psychedelics were used more in the luteal phase. Efficacy was not assessed and the authors call for research.

title: Interoceptive awareness in patients with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: In a very small study, adults with ADHD were less accurate at counting their own heartbeat, suggesting reduced awareness of internal body signals.
key_finding: On a heartbeat-counting task, 14 adults with ADHD performed significantly worse than 16 controls, which the authors interpret as reduced awareness of internal bodily signals.

title: Interoceptive awareness in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: In another small study, adults with ADHD sensed their heartbeat as well as everyone else, so whether ADHD affects body awareness is still unsettled.
key_finding: 24 adults with ADHD and 23 controls performed strikingly similarly on both a heartbeat perception task and an interoception questionnaire, suggesting preserved interoceptive awareness in adult ADHD.

title: Knowing your own heart: Distinguishing interoceptive accuracy from interoceptive awareness
plain_language: How well you actually sense your body, how well you think you do, and how well those two match are three different things.
key_finding: In 80 healthy adults, interoceptive accuracy (heartbeat-task performance), sensibility (self-report) and awareness (confidence-accuracy correspondence) were distinct and dissociable; the dimensions corresponded only in the subgroup with the highest accuracy.

title: Interoception and Mental Health: A Roadmap
journal: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
plain_language: Experts agreed that how we sense signals from inside the body matters for many mental health conditions, and set out how to research it better.
key_finding: Consensus overview from the 2016 Interoception Summit on assessing interoception, how it is integrated, and its role in psychopathology (anxiety, mood, eating, addictive and somatic symptom disorders), with a roadmap for future research.

title: Predicting Impairment in Major Life Activities and Occupational Functioning in Hyperactive Children as Adults: Self-Reported Executive Function (EF) Deficits Versus EF Tests
plain_language: Questionnaires about everyday organising and planning predicted real-life problems at work and home better than lab puzzles did.
key_finding: Self-reported EF deficits predicted impairment across 10 major life-activity domains and 12 occupational measures better than EF tests did; most adults with persistent ADHD were impaired on EF ratings but few on EF tests.

title: Practitioner Review: Do performance-based measures and ratings of executive function assess the same construct?
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Lab tests of 'executive function' and questionnaires about daily life barely agree; they seem to measure different things.
key_finding: Across 20 studies only 68 of 286 correlations (24%) between EF tests and EF rating scales were significant (median r=.19); the authors conclude they measure different constructs, cognitive efficiency versus success in goal pursuit.

title: Functional Impairments in Adults With Self-Reports of Diagnosed ADHD: A Controlled Study of 1001 Adults in the Community
plain_language: Adults with ADHD in a US survey had more difficulty with school, work and relationships than similar adults without ADHD.
key_finding: Compared with 501 matched controls, 500 adults with self-reported community ADHD diagnoses were less likely to have finished high school (83% vs 93%), hold a college degree (19% vs 26%) or be employed (52% vs 72%), changed jobs more (5.4 vs 3.4 in 10 years), and were more often arrested (37% vs 18%) or divorced (28% vs 15%).

title: The risk of eating disorders comorbid with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: People with ADHD are several times more likely to have an eating disorder, and people with eating disorders are more likely to have ADHD.
key_finding: ADHD was associated with any eating disorder (pooled OR 3.82, 2.34-6.24; AN 4.28, BN 5.71, BED 4.13), more strongly when ADHD was diagnosed by clinical interview (5.89) than self-report (2.23); people with eating disorders had higher odds of ADHD (OR 2.57), 5.77 in binge-eating cohorts.

title: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and disordered eating behaviour: A systematic review and a framework for future research
plain_language: ADHD, especially impulsivity, is linked to overeating and binge-type eating.
key_finding: Across 75 studies there was moderate-strength evidence for a positive association between ADHD and disordered eating, especially overeating; impulsivity was consistently linked to overeating and bulimia, with more limited evidence linking hyperactivity to restrictive eating in males but not females.

title: Associations between Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Eating Disorders by Gender: Results from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication
plain_language: In a nationally representative US survey, women with binge eating, bulimia or anorexia were more likely to have ADHD, which usually started first.
key_finding: In both sexes, lifetime and past-year binge eating and binge-eating disorder were associated with higher ADHD prevalence; in women, bulimia nervosa and lifetime anorexia nervosa were also associated with ADHD, and ADHD invariably began before the eating disorder.

title: Association Between ADHD and Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Adults with ADHD are more likely to live with obesity, and those taking ADHD medication did not show this higher risk.
key_finding: ADHD was associated with obesity in adults (OR 1.55, 1.32-1.81) and children (OR 1.20); adult obesity prevalence was 28.2% with ADHD vs 16.4% without. Gender did not moderate the association, and individuals medicated for ADHD were not at higher risk.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Lisdexamfetamine for Treatment of Adults With Moderate to Severe Binge-Eating Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
plain_language: An ADHD stimulant medicine reduced binge eating in adults with binge-eating disorder, though side effects were common.
key_finding: Lisdexamfetamine 50 and 70 mg/day, but not 30 mg/day, reduced binge-eating days versus placebo; 4-week binge cessation was 42.2% (50 mg) and 50.0% (70 mg) vs 21.3% on placebo. Adverse events occurred in 84.7% on drug vs 58.7% on placebo.

title: Emotion regulation and other psychological models for body-focused repetitive behaviors
plain_language: Hair-pulling, skin-picking and nail-biting may work as a way of managing uncomfortable feelings.
key_finding: Review of the emotion-regulation model of body-focused repetitive behaviours (hair-pulling, skin-picking, nail-biting), covering comorbidity, naturalistic and experimental studies, subtypes and treatment trials, alongside psychodynamic and cognitive-behavioural models.

title: Association of nail biting and psychiatric disorders in children and their parents in a psychiatrically referred sample of children
journal: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
plain_language: Most children seen at a mental health clinic for nail biting also had ADHD.
key_finding: Among 63 referred children with nail biting, the most common comorbidities were ADHD (74.6%), oppositional defiant disorder (36%) and separation anxiety (20.6%); nail-biting severity and frequency were not associated with any comorbid disorder.

title: Comorbid trichotillomania and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults
plain_language: About one in seven adults with hair-pulling disorder also had ADHD, and ADHD medication did not seem to make hair pulling worse.
key_finding: Of 308 adults with trichotillomania, 47 (15.3%) met the ADHD threshold and had higher impulsivity on all subscales; ADHD did not change hair-pulling severity, quality of life or functioning, and stimulant use did not appear to affect severity.

title: Skin Picking Disorder
plain_language: Skin picking disorder is fairly common and can be treated with a specific type of behaviour therapy and some medicines.
key_finding: Clinical review of skin picking disorder: community prevalence 1.4%-5.4%; treatment should include CBT (habit reversal or acceptance-enhanced behaviour therapy) and medication options (SRIs, N-acetylcysteine, naltrexone).

title: The efficacy of habit reversal therapy for tics, habit disorders, and stuttering: A meta-analytic review
plain_language: A behaviour therapy called habit reversal training works well for habits like nail biting.
key_finding: Across 18 studies (575 participants), habit reversal therapy had a large effect versus control (d=0.80) for repetitive behaviours including tics, stuttering, nail biting, thumb sucking and TMD.

title: Treating trichotillomania: A meta-analysis of treatment effects and moderators for behavior therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors
plain_language: For hair pulling, behaviour therapy showed large effects and serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor medicines moderate effects.
key_finding: Across 11 RCTs for trichotillomania, behaviour therapy had a large pooled effect (ES 1.41) and SRIs a moderate one (ES 0.41); BT effects were larger with more contact hours and with mood-enhancing techniques.

title: N-Acetylcysteine, a Glutamate Modulator, in the Treatment of Trichotillomania: A Double-blind, Placebo-Controlled Study
plain_language: In one small trial, the supplement N-acetylcysteine helped about half of people with hair-pulling disorder.
key_finding: N-acetylcysteine 1200-2400 mg/day: 56% much or very much improved vs 16% on placebo (P=.003), with significant improvement first seen after 9 weeks and no adverse events in the NAC group.

title: N-acetylcysteine Versus Placebo for Treating Nail Biting, a Double Blind Randomized Placebo Controlled Clinical Trial
journal: Anti-Inflammatory & Anti-Allergy Agents in Medicinal Chemistry
plain_language: N-acetylcysteine reduced nail biting in children for a short time only.
key_finding: In 42 children and adolescents, NAC 800 mg/day increased nail length more than placebo after 1 month (5.21 vs 1.18 mm) but not at 2 months; two NAC participants stopped because of adverse events.

title: Atypical sensory profiles as core features of adult ADHD, irrespective of autistic symptoms
plain_language: Many adults with ADHD, especially women, are unusually sensitive or under-sensitive to sound and other sensations, and this is not explained by autism.
key_finding: 116 adults with ADHD had more sensory hyper- and hyposensitivity than norms, related to ADHD severity in a dose-response way but not to autistic symptoms; 43% of women vs 22% of men reported atypical sensitivity.

title: Fatigue in an adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder population: A trans-diagnostic approach
plain_language: Most adults with ADHD in this clinic study reported serious fatigue.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD were significantly more fatigued than healthy controls, with 62% meeting fatigue caseness; people with CFS had more ADHD symptoms than controls, and ADHD and CFS groups did not differ on functional impairment, mood or self-efficacy.

title: Meta-analysis: Altered Perceptual Timing Abilities in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: People with ADHD tend to judge short time intervals less accurately in lab tasks.
key_finding: Across 55 studies, people with ADHD had more difficulty discriminating very brief (sub-second) durations, more variable estimation of multi-second durations, and time-estimation/production errors indicating an accelerated internal clock.

title: Risk of accidents and unintentional injuries in men and women with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder across the adult lifespan
plain_language: Adults with ADHD have more accidents and injuries throughout life, and women with ADHD have the most minor injuries.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD had raised risk of both mild (outpatient) and severe (inpatient) accidents and injuries across adulthood; women with ADHD had the highest risk of mild incidents at all ages, and comorbid anxiety, psycholeptics and ADHD medication were associated with lower risk.

title: Association Between Medication Use for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Risk of Motor Vehicle Crashes
plain_language: People with ADHD, including women, had fewer car crashes during months when they were taking ADHD medication.
key_finding: Within the same individuals, months on ADHD medication carried lower risk of emergency visits for motor vehicle crashes: 42% lower in women (OR 0.58, 0.53-0.62) and 38% lower in men (OR 0.62); up to 22.1% of crashes might have been avoided with continuous medication.

title: Serious Transport Accidents in Adults With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and the Effect of Medication: A Population-Based Study
plain_language: Adults with ADHD had more serious traffic accidents; medication seemed to help men in this study, but the result for women was unclear.
key_finding: Men (HR 1.47) and women (HR 1.45) with ADHD had higher risk of serious transport accidents; medication was associated with a 58% reduction in men (HR 0.42) but no significant association in women.

title: Life expectancy and years of life lost for adults with diagnosed ADHD in the UK: matched cohort study
plain_language: UK adults diagnosed with ADHD were estimated to live several years less on average, which the authors think is likely due to preventable risk factors and unmet support needs.
key_finding: Among 30,039 UK adults with diagnosed ADHD, estimated life expectancy was 6.78 years (95% CI 4.50-9.11) shorter for men and 8.64 years (6.55-10.91) for women; the authors believe this is likely due to modifiable risk factors and unmet support needs.

title: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society Expert Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Postural Tachycardia Syndrome, Inappropriate Sinus Tachycardia, and Vasovagal Syncope
plain_language: The main international cardiology statement says POTS means a big heart-rate jump on standing plus symptoms, mostly affects young women, and should be treated first with exercise, fluids, salt and compression; drug evidence is weak.
key_finding: Defines POTS as frequent symptoms on standing, a heart-rate rise of ≥30 bpm on moving from lying to standing held for more than 30 seconds (≥40 bpm at age 12-19), and no orthostatic hypotension. Prevalence is given as approximately 0.2%, most patients present between 15 and 25 years, and more than 75% are female. Non-drug measures come first; a structured, progressive exercise programme 'can be effective' (Class IIa); 2-3 L water and 10-12 g salt daily, fludrocortisone, pyridostigmine, midodrine and low-dose propranolol are weaker (Class IIb) options; drugs that block the norepinephrine reuptake transporter 'can worsen symptoms in patients with POTS and should not be administered' (Class III). Modafinil 'may be considered' for brain fog but can worsen tachycardia.

title: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Position Statement on Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) and Related Disorders of Chronic Orthostatic Intolerance
plain_language: Canadian heart specialists say POTS is a pattern with several possible causes, not one disease, and that the label is sometimes given to people who don't actually meet the criteria.
key_finding: Canadian Cardiovascular Society position statement using a GRADE systematic review. It describes POTS as a heterogeneous syndrome 'and not a specific disease', requiring excessive orthostatic tachycardia without substantial orthostatic hypotension plus orthostatic-intolerance symptoms that worsen upright and improve lying down. It flags that many patients are given a POTS label incorrectly (symptoms without tachycardia, tachycardia without symptoms, or tachycardia with another overt cause) and proposes a new nomenclature for orthostatic intolerance syndromes.

title: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS): State of the science and clinical care from a 2019 National Institutes of Health Expert Consensus Meeting - Part 1
plain_language: US experts agree POTS mostly affects young women, often starts in the teens, sometimes after an infection, and has no approved drug; lifestyle and non-drug measures come first.
key_finding: Summary of a 2019 NIH expert meeting. A typical patient with POTS is a woman of child-bearing age who often first has symptoms in adolescence, and onset may follow immunological stressors such as a viral infection. Fatigue, exercise intolerance and gastrointestinal symptoms are common. Management begins with education and non-drug treatment; there are no FDA-approved medicines for POTS and evidence for many medicines used 'is not robust'.

title: The face of postural tachycardia syndrome – insights from a large cross‐sectional online community‐based survey
plain_language: In 4,835 people with POTS, almost all were women, many first got ill as teenagers, diagnosis took about two years, and almost everyone reported trouble concentrating.
key_finding: In 4835 survey respondents with physician-diagnosed POTS, 94% were female and 93% white, about half developed symptoms in adolescence (mode 14 years), and median diagnostic delay was 24 months (IQR 6-72), with frequent misdiagnosis. Common symptoms included lightheadedness (99%), tachycardia (97%), presyncope (94%), headache (94%) and difficulty concentrating (94%).

title: What is brain fog? An evaluation of the symptom in postural tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: Almost everyone with POTS in this survey described 'brain fog' as forgetfulness and trouble focusing, made worse by tiredness, poor sleep, standing and dehydration.
key_finding: Of 138 respondents with POTS, 132 reported brain fog, described mainly as 'forgetful', 'cloudy' and 'difficulty focusing, thinking and communicating'. Common triggers were fatigue (91%), lack of sleep (90%), prolonged standing (87%), dehydration (86%) and feeling faint (85%); brain fog persisted after lying down. The authors conclude brain fog is best described as a cognitive complaint and that factors other than upright posture may sustain it.

title: Attention and executive function are impaired during active standing in postural tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: People with POTS did worse on attention and planning tests when standing up than people without POTS.
key_finding: In 87 people with POTS and 39 controls matched for age, sex and education, those with POTS had lower executive function (Stroop t-score 48 ± 11 vs 55 ± 10; p = 0.009) and worse attention (reaction speed 2.78 ± 0.11 vs 2.69 ± 0.06; p < 0.001) while standing.

title: Efficacy of Therapies for Postural Tachycardia Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
plain_language: Across studies, fluids, salt, compression-type measures, heart-rate drugs and exercise each helped about half to three-quarters of people, but the research is small and weak.
key_finding: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies (25 case series, 3 small RCTs). Treatments that increase blood volume, increase vascular tone, control heart rate or improve exercise tolerance showed moderate efficacy (range 51%-72%), with few comparative data and high heterogeneity. The authors conclude the evidence base for managing POTS 'is extremely limited'.

title: Propranolol Decreases Tachycardia and Improves Symptoms in the Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: A small dose of propranolol eased the racing heart and symptoms in the short term; a bigger dose slowed the heart more but people felt worse.
key_finding: In a randomised crossover trial in 54 patients, propranolol 20 mg lowered supine and standing heart rate and improved symptoms at 2 hours more than placebo (median -4.5 vs 0). In 18 patients, 80 mg lowered standing heart rate more than 20 mg, but symptoms improved more with the low dose (-6 vs -2). Low-dose propranolol helped; higher doses did not further improve, and may worsen, symptoms.

title: Exercise Training Versus Propranolol in the Treatment of the Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: In a small trial of mostly women, a 3-month exercise programme improved daily functioning, while propranolol slowed the heart but did not make people feel better.
key_finding: In 19 patients (18 women), both 4 weeks of propranolol and 3 months of exercise training lowered standing heart rate, but only training improved quality of life (SF-36 physical functioning 33 ± 10 to 50 ± 9; social functioning 37 ± 9 to 48 ± 6) and modestly increased the aldosterone:renin ratio. The authors conclude exercise training is superior to propranolol for upright haemodynamics and quality of life.

title: Randomized Trial of Ivabradine in Patients With Hyperadrenergic Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
plain_language: In a small trial, ivabradine lowered heart rate and improved daily functioning in one subtype of POTS without major side effects.
key_finding: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with hyperadrenergic POTS (95.5% women), ivabradine significantly reduced heart rate and improved physical (p = 0.008) and social (p = 0.021) functioning, with no significant bradycardia or hypotension.

title: Outcomes of Adolescent-Onset Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: Most teenagers diagnosed with POTS were better or much better about five years later, though few were completely free of symptoms; their mental health scores were normal.
key_finding: Of 172 responders diagnosed with POTS at ages 13-18 at Mayo Clinic, surveyed a mean 5.4 years later, 19% reported complete resolution, 51% persistent but improved symptoms and 16% intermittent symptoms (86% resolved, improved or intermittent). Physical health scores were below population norms (36.6 vs 50), whereas mental health scores were normal (50.1).

title: Renin-Aldosterone Paradox and Perturbed Blood Volume Regulation Underlying Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: In a small study, people with POTS had less blood volume than expected, and the hormones that normally correct this did not rise.
key_finding: Patients with POTS (n = 15) had larger deficits in plasma volume (334 vs 10 mL), red blood cell volume (356 vs 218 mL) and total blood volume (689 vs 228 mL) than controls (n = 14), yet plasma renin activity was not raised and aldosterone was paradoxically low (190 vs 380 pmol/L).

title: Psychiatric profile and attention deficits in postural tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: People with POTS were not more likely to have anxiety disorders, but they did have ADHD-like attention problems that had not been there in childhood.
key_finding: Patients with POTS (n = 21) did not have more lifetime major depression or anxiety disorders (including panic disorder) than the general population; they scored as moderately anxious on the Beck Anxiety Inventory but did not have high anxiety sensitivity. They scored significantly higher than controls on inattention and ADHD subscales, but these symptoms were not present in childhood. The authors conclude inattention may be an important source of disability in POTS.

title: Autonomic Dysfunction in Autism Spectrum Disorder
plain_language: In autistic people sent to specialist autonomic clinics, most had an autonomic problem such as POTS, and most of those were also hypermobile.
key_finding: Among 28 autistic people referred to two UK autonomic centres, 20 had a diagnosed autonomic condition, most often POTS (9 POTS alone, others POTS with vasovagal syncope or other combinations), and 16 of these 20 had hEDS. Autistic participants had higher basal heart rate and orthostatic responses, with impaired sympathetic vasoconstriction. The authors conclude autonomic dysfunction was over-represented in autism with a strong hEDS association.

title: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and task-related heart rate variability: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: People with ADHD showed slightly lower heart rate variability during tasks, a small and inconsistent sign of different nervous-system regulation.
key_finding: Across 13 studies (869 with ADHD, 909 controls), people with ADHD had lower vagally mediated heart rate variability after a task demand, a small effect (Hedges' g = 0.20; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.40), with high heterogeneity (I² = 77%) and some evidence of small-study effects.

title: Is autonomic nervous system function atypical in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)? A systematic review of the evidence
plain_language: Studies tend to find the body's 'arousal' system is under-active rather than over-active in ADHD, though about half of studies found no difference.
key_finding: A systematic review of 55 studies (electrodermal, heart rate, pupillometry) found autonomic dysfunction in ADHD more often in the direction of hypo-arousal than hyper-arousal, particularly at rest and during tasks needing sustained attention; almost half of findings were null. Stimulants increased autonomic activity.

title: The effects of stimulant and non-stimulant medications on the autonomic nervous system (ANS) functioning in people with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: ADHD medicines, especially stimulants, raise heart rate and blood pressure.
key_finding: In a systematic review and meta-analysis (29 studies on blood pressure, 32 on heart rate), stimulants, and to a lesser degree non-stimulants, increased heart rate and blood pressure in people with ADHD; stimulants also increased electrodermal activity and pupil size.

title: Heart rate variability in individuals with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis
plain_language: Autistic people on average showed lower heart rate variability, especially during social stress.
key_finding: Across 34 studies, autistic individuals had lower baseline parasympathetic heart rate variability (Hedges' g = -0.5168) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (g = -0.5860), and lower HRV reactivity under social stress (g = -0.4647); RSA reactivity under social stress showed the largest effect (g = -0.7246).

title: The Relationship Between Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS), Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS)
plain_language: A review found almost no solid research showing that hEDS, POTS and MCAS form a linked 'triad'; the idea rests mainly on overlapping symptoms.
key_finding: A structured literature review found only 4 (narrow search) and 9 (broad search) original research articles, none combining all three conditions. The authors conclude that an evidence-based shared mechanism between any two, 'much less all three', has not been described; studies proposing a relationship are biased or use outdated criteria, and the purported association stems from overlapping vague, subjective symptoms.

title: Prevalence of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: About a third of people with POTS in this study met the formal criteria for hypermobile EDS, and a quarter more were hypermobile.
key_finding: Using the 2017 hEDS criteria, 28 of 91 POTS participants (31%) met criteria for hEDS, and an additional 24% had generalised joint hypermobility without meeting hEDS criteria.

title: Mast Cell Activation Disorder and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome: A Clinical Association
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
plain_language: Some people with POTS who also had allergy-type, skin or gut symptoms had blood or urine results hinting at mast cell activation, but single abnormal tests do not prove it.
key_finding: Of 69 patients meeting POTS criteria, 44 (64%) had additional non-orthostatic symptoms (migraine, allergic, skin or gastrointestinal); 29 of these (66%) had at least one laboratory abnormality suggesting mast cell activation disorder, mostly elevated prostaglandins or histamine markers. The authors note solitary abnormal results are not definitive.

title: Prevalence of mast cell activation disorders and hereditary alpha tryptasemia among patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: A systematic review
plain_language: A systematic review found no studies that properly tested whether mast cell disorders are more common in POTS or EDS.
key_finding: A systematic search found no study that diagnosed any mast cell activation disorder or hereditary alpha tryptasemia alongside POTS and/or EDS using pre-specified diagnostic criteria, so the review could not confirm a relationship; one study came close to full MCAS criteria.

title: Menstrual Cycle Affects Renal-Adrenal and Hemodynamic Responses During Prolonged Standing in the Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: In a small study, women with POTS coped worse with standing just after their period started than in the second half of the cycle.
key_finding: In 10 women with POTS, stroke volume and cardiac output were lower in the early follicular phase than the mid-luteal phase after 30 minutes standing, and plasma renin activity and aldosterone were lower in the early follicular phase. Presyncope was more common in the early follicular phase than the mid-luteal phase in both groups. The authors suggest the high estrogen and progesterone of the mid-luteal phase improve late-standing tolerance.

title: Gynecologic disorders and menstrual cycle lightheadedness in postural tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: Women with POTS felt more lightheaded throughout the cycle, worst during their period, and reported more gynaecological conditions.
key_finding: Women with POTS (n = 65) reported more lightheadedness than controls (n = 95) across all menstrual phases; both groups reported most lightheadedness during menses and less in the follicular phase. Women with POTS reported more gynaecological disease.

title: Menstrual cycle phase does not affect sympathetic neural activity in women with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: In a small study, the menstrual cycle changed blood pressure but not heart rate, nerve activity or fainting on tilt in women with POTS.
key_finding: In 10 women with POTS studied in the early follicular and mid-luteal phases, muscle sympathetic nerve activity did not differ between phases, but blood pressure and total peripheral resistance were higher in the mid-luteal phase; heart rate and presyncope incidence were the same in both phases.

title: Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome during pregnancy: A systematic review of the literature
plain_language: Limited studies suggest women with POTS can have healthy pregnancies; symptoms may get better or worse.
key_finding: A systematic review of 11 articles rated the evidence quality as poor. It concluded POTS should not be a contraindication to pregnancy, symptoms vary in pregnancy and postpartum, continuing pre-conception medication may help with no significant risks reported, and POTS did not appear to affect the rate of adverse events.

title: Low iron storage and mild anemia in postural tachycardia syndrome in adolescents
plain_language: In a small group of teenagers with POTS, half had low iron stores, more than in teenagers generally.
key_finding: Among 24 children with POTS (aged 12-18; 71% female), low iron storage (ferritin ≤25 μg/L) was more common than in the US paediatric population (50% vs 14%), as was iron deficiency (25% of teenage girls vs 9%) and anaemia (18% of girls vs 1.5%).

title: Comparative cardiovascular safety of medications for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
plain_language: All main ADHD medicines except guanfacine raise heart rate a few beats per minute on average; stimulants are not worse than non-stimulants on this.
key_finding: In a network meta-analysis of 102 short-term RCTs, amphetamines, atomoxetine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate and viloxazine raised blood pressure and pulse. In adults, pulse rose by 4.37 bpm (methylphenidate) to 5.8 bpm (viloxazine) versus placebo (very low certainty). Stimulants were not associated with larger increases than atomoxetine or viloxazine; guanfacine lowered values. The authors advise monitoring blood pressure and pulse with any ADHD medication, not stimulants only.

title: Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases Associated With Medications Used in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Large studies found no clear rise in heart disease with ADHD medicines, though a small increase in heart-rhythm problems can't be ruled out.
key_finding: Across 19 observational studies (3 931 532 participants), ADHD medication was not significantly associated with any cardiovascular disease in children/adolescents (RR 1.18), young or middle-aged adults (RR 1.04) or older adults (RR 1.59), nor for stimulants (RR 1.24). A modest increase could not be ruled out, especially for cardiac arrest or tachyarrhythmias (RR 1.60; 95% CI 0.94-2.72); evidence in female patients and those with pre-existing CVD needs further study.

title: Effects of Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibition on Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
plain_language: One dose of atomoxetine, an ADHD medicine, made the heart race more on standing and worsened symptoms in people with POTS.
key_finding: In a randomised crossover trial in 27 POTS patients, a single 40 mg dose of atomoxetine increased standing heart rate compared with placebo (121 ± 17 vs 105 ± 15 bpm; p = 0.001) and worsened symptom scores (+4.2 vs -3.5 au; p = 0.028). The authors note POTS patients commonly have ADHD and similar comorbidities treated with norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors.

title: Use of Methylphenidate in the Treatment of Patients Suffering From Refractory Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: In a small uncontrolled study, most people with hard-to-treat POTS reported feeling better on methylphenidate.
key_finding: In a retrospective uncontrolled series of 24 patients with POTS refractory to usual drugs who were started on methylphenidate, 2 stopped because of side effects and 18 completed 6 months; 14 of 18 (77%) reported marked symptom improvement, and 9 of 12 with recurrent syncope had none at 6 months. Response was assessed subjectively.

title: Hemodynamic Profiles and Tolerability of Modafinil in the Treatment of Postural Tachycardia Syndrome
plain_language: A single low dose of modafinil did not make the heart race more or worsen POTS symptoms, and slightly raised blood pressure.
key_finding: In a randomised crossover trial in 54 patients, modafinil 100 mg did not significantly change standing heart rate or symptom burden over 4 hours compared with placebo (14 vs 14), and raised seated systolic blood pressure (109 vs 104 mm Hg). The authors suggest modafinil could be tested for cognitive impairment in POTS.

title: Cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction in post-COVID-19 syndrome: a major health-care burden
plain_language: Problems with heart-rate and blood-pressure control are common in long COVID, and many severely affected people meet criteria for POTS.
key_finding: Cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction is an important component of long COVID and might affect one-third of highly symptomatic patients; many severely affected patients meet criteria for POTS or inappropriate sinus tachycardia.

title: Excessive heart rate response to orthostatic stress in postural tachycardia syndrome is not caused by anxiety
plain_language: People with POTS reported more anxiety, but their racing heart on standing was explained by blood pooling, not by anxiety.
key_finding: During graded venous pooling, heart rate rose 39 ± 5 bpm in POTS vs 19 ± 3 bpm in controls; sham pooling produced no rise, and heart-rate responses to mental stress did not differ (18 ± 2 vs 19 ± 1 bpm). Anxiety, somatic vigilance and catastrophic thoughts were higher in POTS but were not related to heart-rate responses. The authors conclude the tachycardia is a physiological response, not caused by anxiety.

title: The genesis and presentation of anxiety in disorders of autonomic overexcitation
plain_language: People with POTS were less accurate at sensing their heartbeat and their worry was focused on body symptoms rather than on social fears or past trauma.
key_finding: Compared with 23 controls, patients with POTS (21), vasovagal syncope (20) and essential hyperhidrosis (20) reported more somatic anxiety but not more social anxiety or trauma. Their heartbeat-tracking accuracy was diminished and consistently underestimated; in POTS and syncope, accuracy correlated positively with somatic anxiety. The authors conclude affective symptoms appear driven by anxiety and vigilance about physical sensations rather than trauma or neurosis.

title: Prevalence of co-occurring mental health diagnoses in the autism population: a systematic review and meta-analysis
key_finding: Pooled prevalence of ADHD in autistic people was 28% (95% CI 25-32), the most common co-occurring diagnosis, ahead of anxiety disorders (20%) and depressive disorders (11%). Heterogeneity was very high (I2 >95%), and estimates varied with age, gender and intellectual functioning.

title: Identifying the lost generation of adults with autism spectrum conditions
key_finding: Describes a "lost generation" of adults missed under older, narrower criteria. First diagnosis in adulthood is hard because there may be no developmental informant, learnt or camouflaging strategies hide traits, and co-occurring disorders are common. Possible misdiagnosis, especially in women, should be explored.

title: What Is the Male-to-Female Ratio in Autism Spectrum Disorder? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
key_finding: The pooled male-to-female odds ratio was 4.20 overall but 3.25 in studies that screened the general population, against 4.56 in studies relying on existing diagnoses. The authors conclude that the true ratio is closer to 3:1 and that there is a diagnostic gender bias against girls.

title: The Experiences of Late-diagnosed Women with Autism Spectrum Conditions: An Investigation of the Female Autism Phenotype
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
key_finding: Qualitative framework analysis. Late-diagnosed women described 'pretending to be normal', professionals missing their autism because of their gender, and conflicts between autism and a traditional feminine identity. Experiences of sexual abuse were widespread in the sample. Mid-tier: a first-person qualitative account of the female autism phenotype.

title: Autistic spectrum disorder symptoms in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytical review
key_finding: Pooled 21% of children and adolescents with ADHD met threshold for ASD, with no significant difference between community (19%) and clinical (24%) samples. Dimensional ASD traits were much higher in ADHD than non-ADHD youth (d = 1.23).

title: The familial co-aggregation of ASD and ADHD: a register-based cohort study
key_finding: Individuals with ASD had much higher odds of ADHD (OR 22.33). The association was stronger in ASD without intellectual disability. Co-aggregation fell from monozygotic twins (OR 17.77) to dizygotic twins (4.33) and full siblings (4.59), consistent with shared genetic liability.

title: Genomic Relationships, Novel Loci, and Pleiotropic Mechanisms across Eight Psychiatric Disorders
key_finding: In a cross-disorder genome-wide analysis of 8 psychiatric disorders including ADHD and ASD, genetic correlations grouped the disorders into three groups. Meta-analysis found 109 loci associated with at least two disorders, in genes with heightened brain expression beginning prenatally and with roles in neurodevelopment. The abstract does not give the specific ADHD-ASD correlation.

title: Conceptualising compensation in neurodevelopmental disorders: Reflections from autism spectrum disorder
key_finding: Proposes a transdiagnostic definition of compensation: the processes behind an observed mismatch between apparently improved behaviour and persisting cognitive or neural differences. It reviews possible cognitive and neural mechanisms, using autism as the example.

title: Compensatory strategies below the behavioural surface in autism: a qualitative study
key_finding: Qualitative online study. Adults described multiple distinct social compensatory strategies, with positive outcomes (relationships, independence, employment) and negative ones (poor mental health, late diagnosis). Undiagnosed adults used strategies qualitatively similar to diagnosed adults, which may keep them below the diagnostic threshold.

title: “Putting on My Best Normal”: Social Camouflaging in Adults with Autism Spectrum Conditions
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
key_finding: Thematic analysis produced a three-stage model of camouflaging: motivations (fitting in, connection), techniques (masking plus compensation), and consequences (exhaustion, challenging stereotypes, threats to self-perception). Mid-tier, qualitative.

title: Risk markers for suicidality in autistic adults
key_finding: 72% of autistic adults scored above the SBQ-R cut-off for suicide risk, against 33% of general-population adults. Within autistic adults, camouflaging, non-suicidal self-injury and the number of unmet support needs significantly predicted suicidality. The authors conclude camouflaging and unmet support needs appear to be risk markers unique to autism. Mid-tier (Molecular Autism), cross-sectional survey.

title: Mixed emotions: the contribution of alexithymia to the emotional symptoms of autism
key_finding: Argues that emotional-processing difficulties seen in some autistic people are due to co-occurring alexithymia (reduced ability to identify and describe one's own emotions), not to autism itself. Alexithymia is also elevated in eating disorders, anxiety and other conditions.

title: Investigating alexithymia in autism: A systematic review and meta-analysis
key_finding: 49.93% of autistic people met alexithymia criteria, against 4.89% of neurotypical people. Autistic groups scored significantly higher on all TAS scores. Alexithymia is common but not universal in autism.

title: Reasoning on the Autism Spectrum: A Dual Process Theory Account
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
key_finding: The authors conclude that higher autistic traits, and an ASD diagnosis, are characterised by a consistent bias towards deliberative reasoning (and potentially away from intuition) under dual-process theory. Small study; the clinical sample was all male. The abstract states no earlier study had examined these reasoning styles in autism.

title: Update of a Meta-analysis of Sensory Symptoms in ASD: A New Decade of Research
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
key_finding: Effect sizes for sensory over-responsivity, under-responsivity and seeking were large compared with typical controls. Compared with other clinical groups, only over-responsivity was significantly elevated; the authors highlight the core nature of sensory symptoms, particularly over-responsivity, in autism. Mid-tier (JADD) meta-analysis.

title: Sensory perception in autism
key_finding: Reviews sensory processing in autism, brought into focus by the recent revision of the autism diagnostic criteria. It covers computational and neurobiological insights, implications for animal and computational models, and how sensory difficulties may relate to the other behavioural domains of autism.

title: Sensory over-responsivity in adults with autism spectrum conditions
key_finding: Autistic adults reported more sensory over-responsivity than controls across visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory and proprioceptive domains. Over-responsivity correlated positively with AQ scores both across and within groups.

title: High Prevalence of Self-Reported Photophobia in Adult ADHD
key_finding: Self-reported photophobia was reported by 69% of respondents with ADHD (symptoms) against 28% without, and the ADHD group wore sunglasses longer during daytime in all seasons. The authors suggest photophobia may relate to dopamine and melatonin systems. Mid-tier online survey.

title: “Having All of Your Internal Resources Exhausted Beyond Measure and Being Left with No Clean-Up Crew”: Defining Autistic Burnout
key_finding: Community-based participatory thematic analysis. Autistic burnout was characterised by chronic exhaustion, loss of skills and reduced tolerance to stimulus, arising from cumulative life load plus barriers to support. Participants linked it to suicidal behaviour, and to recovery through acceptance, reduced expectations and unmasking. The authors conclude it appears to be distinct from occupational burnout and clinical depression.

title: Defining autistic burnout through experts by lived experience: Grounded Delphi method investigating #AutisticBurnout
key_finding: A Grounded Delphi consensus defined autistic burnout as exhaustion, withdrawal, problems with thinking, reduced daily living skills and increased manifestation of autistic traits. The authors say clinicians should be aware it differs from depression and that depression treatments could potentially worsen it, while noting research is still needed to show it is separate from depression, chronic fatigue and non-autistic burnout.

title: Measuring and validating autistic burnout
key_finding: Psychometric evaluation of the 27-item AASPIRE Autistic Burnout Measure (ABM) and the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory. EFA gave a 4-factor ABM structure, but further models indicated a unidimensional overarching 'Autistic Burnout' construct. The ABM and CBI-P correlated strongly with depression, anxiety, stress and fatigue, and only moderately with camouflaging. The ABM and the CBI-P Emotional Exhaustion subscale were judged valid preliminary screening tools.

title: Understanding the burnout experience: recent research and its implications for psychiatry
