key_finding: Reviews burnout as an occupationally specific dysphoria: its measures, models, causes and consequences. Highlights open issues about links between burnout and mental illness, attempts to reduce burnout to exhaustion alone, and the lack of intervention research.

title: Is Burnout a Depressive Condition? A 14-Sample Meta-Analytic and Bifactor Analytic Study
key_finding: The meta-analytic disattenuated correlation between exhaustion (burnout's core) and depressive symptoms was r = .80, which the authors call problematically strong for discriminant validity. Bifactor models consistently showed burnout overlapping with depression across countries and measures. (Abstract retrieved from Crossref; not in Europe PMC.)

title: Long-Term Outcomes of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Conduct Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
key_finding: Childhood ADHD was longitudinally associated with failure to complete high school (OR 3.7), depression (OR 2.3) and unemployment (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.0-3.9), among other adverse outcomes.

title: Executive function deficits mediate the relationship between employees' ADHD and job burnout
key_finding: In 171 employees, those with ADHD reported higher job burnout, and the effect was mediated by executive-function deficits: self-management to time for physical fatigue, and self-organisation/problem-solving for emotional exhaustion and cognitive weariness. Mid-tier, single field study.

title: Prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: A meta-analysis
plain_language: Around four in ten autistic people also meet criteria for ADHD at some point.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence of ADHD in autistic people was 38.5% current (95% CI 34.0-43.2) and 40.2% lifetime (95% CI 34.9-45.7). Age, intellectual disability, recruitment setting and diagnostic criteria significantly influenced the current prevalence estimate.

title: Changing ASD-ADHD symptom co-occurrence across the lifespan with adolescence as crucial time window: Illustrating the need to go beyond childhood
plain_language: Autism and ADHD traits overlapped most in the teenage years; the authors suggest this is when life asks most of planning and social skills.
key_finding: ASD/ADHD symptom constellations peak in adolescence and are lower in early childhood and old age. The authors hypothesise that co-occurrence is highest at the transition to independent adulthood, where social adaptation and executive-function skills matter most.

title: Autism Spectrum Disorders and ADHD: Overlapping Phenomenology, Diagnostic Issues, and Treatment Considerations
plain_language: Autism and ADHD overlap a lot but are still different conditions, and treatment works best when both are recognised.
key_finding: ASD and ADHD share genetic heritability and both involve social and executive-function impairment, with quantitative and qualitative differences in how these present. Comorbid ADHD should be considered for ASD interventions to work well, and vice versa. The authors conclude the two remain distinct enough to warrant separate diagnoses.

title: Co-occurring ADHD symptoms in autistic adults are associated with less independence in daily living activities and lower subjective quality of life
plain_language: Autistic adults with more ADHD symptoms found everyday tasks harder and rated their quality of life lower.
key_finding: Autistic adults who self-rated more ADHD symptoms reported less independence in activities of daily living and lower subjective quality of life. The authors describe this as the first study to show these associations in autistic adults.

title: Individual risk and familial liability for suicide attempt and suicide in autism: a population-based study
plain_language: Autistic women who also have ADHD have a much higher risk of suicide attempts than the general population, and getting help for other mental health conditions matters.
key_finding: Suicidal behaviour risk was highest in ASD without intellectual disability with comorbid ADHD: suicide attempt OR 7.25 (6.79-7.73) and suicide OR 13.09 (8.54-20.08). Females with ASD without ID had generally higher risk than males. Among females with ASD+ADHD, the OR was 10.27 for attempts and 14.26 for suicide. Adjusting for psychiatric comorbidity attenuated the risks.

title: Assessment of Suicidal Behaviors Among Individuals With Autism Spectrum Disorder in Denmark
plain_language: Autistic people, especially women, are at higher risk of suicide, mostly when they also have other mental health conditions.
key_finding: People with ASD had higher rates of suicide attempt (aIRR 3.19, 95% CI 2.93-3.46) and suicide (aIRR 3.75, 2.85-4.92). Among those with ASD, females had a 4.41-fold higher attempt rate than males. ASD alone gave aIRR 1.33 (0.99-1.78) for attempt, against 9.27 (8.51-10.10) with other psychiatric comorbidity. More than 90% of those who attempted or died by suicide had another diagnosis.

title: Autism and autistic traits in those who died by suicide in England
plain_language: Autism, including signs of undiagnosed autism, was found much more often among people who died by suicide in two English regions than expected.
key_finding: Evidence of autism was found in 10.8% of suicide deaths against 1.1% expected (OR 11.08, 95% CI 3.92-31.31). In the interview subsample, adding undiagnosed possible autism raised this to 41.4% (OR 19.76, 2.36-165.84).

title: Delayed autism spectrum disorder recognition in children and adolescents previously diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Getting an ADHD diagnosis first can delay an autism diagnosis by years, especially for girls.
key_finding: Children and adolescents first diagnosed with ADHD received their ASD diagnosis on average 1.8 years later than ASD-only peers. The delay was 1.5 years in boys and 2.6 years in girls. No significant delay or gender difference was found in the adult sample, which the authors say should be read with caution.

title: Timing of the Diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Autism Spectrum Disorder
plain_language: Children diagnosed with ADHD first tended to get their autism diagnosis about three years later.
key_finding: About 20% of children with ASD were first diagnosed with ADHD. They received their ASD diagnosis about 3 years later (95% CI 2.3-3.5) and were nearly 30 times more likely to be diagnosed with ASD after age 6 (95% CI 11.2-77.8), independent of ASD severity.

title: Gender Differences in Misdiagnosis and Delayed Diagnosis among Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder with No Language or Intellectual Disability
plain_language: Women with autism were diagnosed later than men and were more often given the wrong diagnosis first.
key_finding: 75.4% received their ASD diagnosis on average 8 years after first contact with mental health services. Compared with men, women had a longer delay before referral, were older at ASD diagnosis, and were less likely to be correctly diagnosed and more likely to be misdiagnosed at first evaluation.

title: ‘I was exhausted trying to figure it out’: The experiences of females receiving an autism diagnosis in middle to late adulthood
plain_language: Women diagnosed with autism after 40 described years of pretending to be "normal", and found diagnosis helped them be kinder to themselves.
key_finding: Four themes emerged: a hidden condition (pretending to be normal; mental health mislabelling), the process of acceptance, the impact of others after diagnosis, and a new autistic identity. Several participants described diagnosis as a shift from self-criticism to self-compassion and greater agency, though painful to adjust to so late.

title: The Female Autism Phenotype and Camouflaging: a Narrative Review
journal: Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Autism may often look different in women, partly because many hide their traits, but the research is still young.
key_finding: The review weighs the "female protective effect" against underdiagnosis because females express autism in ways that do not meet current criteria. It concludes that evidence so far supports a female-typical autism presentation, including camouflaging, but that its characteristics and impact across genders and ages need more study.

title: Is There a Bias Towards Males in the Diagnosis of Autism? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: On standard tests autistic women can look 'less autistic' than men, and they reported more masking, which may partly explain this.
key_finding: Autistic males showed more severe core symptoms and social-interaction difficulties on standard clinical measures. Females showed more cognitive and behavioural difficulties. In a separate meta-analysis, females used more compensation and masking camouflaging strategies than males.

title: Camouflaging in autism: A systematic review
plain_language: People who hide their autistic traits more tend to have worse mental health, though the studies are limited.
key_finding: Three preliminary conclusions: adults with more self-reported autistic traits report more camouflaging, sex and gender differences in camouflaging exist, and higher self-reported camouflaging is associated with worse mental health. The research base was limited in participant characterisation and representativeness.

title: Is camouflaging unique for autism? A comparison of camouflaging between adults with autism and ADHD
plain_language: Adults with ADHD also hide their differences, but less than autistic adults, and heavy masking tracks autistic traits more than ADHD traits.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD scored higher than comparison adults on total camouflaging and the assimilation subscale, but lower than autistic adults on total, compensation and assimilation scores. Autism traits, but not ADHD traits, predicted camouflaging regardless of diagnosis.

title: Is Camouflaging Autistic Traits Associated with Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviours? Expanding the Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide in an Undergraduate Student Sample
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Students who hid autistic-type traits more often felt they did not belong and were more likely to have had suicidal thoughts.
key_finding: Camouflaging autistic traits was associated with greater thwarted belongingness and lifetime suicidality, in line with the Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicide.

title: Methylphenidate for children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder
plain_language: In autistic children, methylphenidate might help hyperactivity and there was no evidence it worsens autism, but the studies are small and short.
key_finding: High-dose methylphenidate improved teacher-rated hyperactivity (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -1.13 to -0.43) with low-quality evidence. There was no evidence of harm to, or benefit for, core autism symptoms. Reduced appetite was more likely (RR 8.28). Adverse-event evidence was very low quality because trials were short and excluded intolerant children.

title: A prospective open-label trial of long-acting liquid methylphenidate for the treatment of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in intellectually capable adults with autism spectrum disorder
journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
plain_language: In a small trial without a placebo group, a stimulant seemed to help ADHD symptoms in autistic adults.
key_finding: Extended-release liquid methylphenidate was associated with significant improvement in clinician-rated ADHD severity (AISRS mean change -22.8 ± 8.8). The authors conclude their findings suggest it is effective and well tolerated.

title: Towards the measurement of autistic burnout
plain_language: Early tests of a questionnaire for autistic burnout found it was linked to depression and could not reliably tell current from past burnout.
key_finding: Autistic burnout was associated with masking and depression. The AASPIRE Autistic Burnout Measure correlated with depression but not with masking, and did not distinguish well between current and past burnout. Burnout involved exhaustion, withdrawal and cognitive problems linked to everyday stress.

title: What Is Autistic Burnout? A Thematic Analysis of Posts on Two Online Platforms
plain_language: Autistic people online described burnout as recurring and tied to masking and to living in a world that does not understand autism.
key_finding: Eight themes, including a chronic or recurrent condition, direct impact on health, "a life unlived", and masking ("damned if you do, damned if you don't"). The overarching theme was that pervasive lack of autism awareness and stigma underlie burnout. Self-awareness and personal control were described as influencing risk and recovery.

title: A conceptual model of risk and protective factors for autistic burnout
plain_language: A proposed model of how too many demands and too few resources lead to autistic burnout. It has not been tested yet.
key_finding: Proposes the Conceptual Model of Autistic Burnout (CMAB), built on the social-relational model of disability, the Job Demands-Resources model and Conservation of Resources theory. Individual, social and environmental risk and protective factors are hypothesised to cause or buffer burnout. The authors stress that the field is in its infancy.

title: ADHD at the workplace: ADHD symptoms, diagnostic status, and work-related functioning
plain_language: Adults with ADHD often feel they fall short of their potential at work even when they are not failing visibly.
key_finding: Work problems were found in community adults with ADHD symptoms and in diagnosed adults. These problems mainly took the form of not meeting their own standards and potential, and less often negative evaluations or job loss. Inattention symptoms were strongly associated with work problems, and neuropsychological test scores did not predict work functioning.

title: Disclosure and workplace accommodations for people with autism: a systematic review
plain_language: Autistic workers who disclose can get helpful changes like quiet space or flexible hours, but disclosure can also bring stigma.
key_finding: Rates of disclosure and of receiving accommodations varied widely. Disclosure brought acceptance and accommodations but also risked stigma and discrimination. Reported accommodations included interview changes, flexible schedules or working from home, environmental changes (lighting, quiet space), communication support, and colleague awareness training.

title: Work organization and mental health problems in PhD students
plain_language: About a third of PhD students were at risk of a common mental health problem, linked to how their work is organised.
key_finding: 32% of PhD students were at risk of having or developing a common psychiatric disorder (GHQ-12), especially depression, significantly higher than highly educated general-population, employee and student comparison groups. Work-family interface, job demands and job control, supervisor leadership style, team decision-making culture and perception of a career outside academia were linked to mental health problems.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation among Ph.D. students
plain_language: About one in four PhD students has significant depression symptoms and about one in six has significant anxiety.
key_finding: Pooled proportion of PhD students with clinically significant depression symptoms was 0.24 (95% CI 0.18-0.31; I2 = 98.75%) and with anxiety 0.17 (95% CI 0.12-0.23; I2 = 98.05%). Data were too limited to pool suicidal ideation.

title: Understanding the mental health of doctoral researchers: a mixed methods systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-synthesis
plain_language: PhD researchers report more stress than the general population; isolation and being female were the clearest risk factors, and support from others and a good supervisor relationship helped.
key_finding: Doctoral researchers reported significantly higher stress levels than population norm data. Across meta-analysis and meta-synthesis, the risk factors with the strongest evidence base were isolation and identifying as female; social support, viewing the PhD as a process, a positive student-supervisor relationship and self-care were the best-established protective factors. The authors call for better-coordinated data collection before clinically meaningful conclusions can be drawn.

title: “Life is Much More Difficult to Manage During Periods”: Autistic Experiences of Menstruation
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Many autistic women find that their sensory and emotional difficulties get worse around their period.
key_finding: Autistic respondents described distinct, sometimes distressing menstrual experiences, especially a cyclical amplification of autism-related challenges, including sensory differences and difficulty regulating emotion and behaviour, with significant negative impact on their lives.

title: Menstruation and menopause in autistic adults: Periods of importance?
plain_language: Autistic women in this study did not have clearly more PMDD, but they did report a harder menopause.
key_finding: PMDD prevalence was not found to be increased in autistic women (14.3% vs 9.5% non-autistic). Autistic women reported more menopausal complaints, associated with depression and autistic traits. In non-autistic women, menopausal complaints were associated with ADHD traits and depression.

title: Prevalence of Premenstrual Syndrome in Autism: A Prospective Observer-rated Study
plain_language: In a small group of autistic women with learning disabilities in residential care, premenstrual symptom worsening was very common.
key_finding: Over three prospectively observer-rated cycles, late luteal phase dysphoric disorder (a premenstrual increase of 30% or more in DSM-IV symptoms) was found in 92% of the autism group against 11% of controls.

title: ‘When my autism broke’: A qualitative study spotlighting autistic voices on menopause
plain_language: Some autistic women found menopause made their autism much harder to manage and harder to hide.
key_finding: Participants reported that autism-related difficulties (sensory sensitivity, socialising, communicating needs) worsened during menopause, sometimes so much that they could no longer mask. They also described extreme meltdowns, anxiety, depression and suicidal feelings, and very little available support.

title: Large-scale neural network compensation associated with camouflaging in trait autism and its potential mental health costs
plain_language: In young adults from a mostly non-clinical sample, those with more autistic traits who said they masked more showed stronger links between certain brain networks at rest, and this was tied to more anxiety and low mood.
key_finding: In 110 healthy young adults, greater self-reported camouflaging was associated with increased resting-state connectivity between the default mode and cingulo-opercular networks (and within the cingulo-opercular network), but only among those with higher autistic traits. This DMN-CON hyperconnectivity statistically mediated the link between camouflaging and depression/anxiety scores; the authors note the non-clinical sample, cross-sectional design and resting-state-only data as limitations.

title: Neural self-representation in autistic women and association with 'compensatory camouflaging'
plain_language: In autistic women, those who masked more showed a stronger response in a brain area used for thinking about oneself.
key_finding: Autistic men showed reduced right TPJ (mentalizing) and vmPFC (self-representation) responses compared with typically developing men, but autistic women did not differ from typically developing women. In autistic women only, more camouflaging was associated with a heightened vmPFC self-representation response during a task-based fMRI paradigm.

title: Listening Effort Among Adults With and Without Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
plain_language: Young adults with ADHD had to put in more mental effort to follow speech while doing another task, even though they understood it just as well.
key_finding: Using a dual-task paradigm, listening effort was greater in 19 young adults with ADHD than in 20 controls, although speech perception itself did not differ. The authors suggest that people with ADHD may expend much more effort to process the same information and so may be more prone to fatigue; the abstract reports no ratio such as 'twice'.

title: A Pilot Study of Behavioral, Physiological, and Subjective Responses to Varying Mental Effort Requirements in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Teenage boys with ADHD did worse on memory tasks but did not find them harder than other boys did.
key_finding: Across five N-back difficulty levels, boys with ADHD performed worse at every level but rated the tasks as equally difficult and discounted effort similarly to controls; only subtle differences in pupil dilation were seen. The behavioural results did not support mental effort problems in ADHD.

title: The long-term financial outcome of children diagnosed with ADHD
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
plain_language: People diagnosed with ADHD as children were, by 30, earning and saving much less than their peers, and the gap was growing.
key_finding: At age 30, adults with childhood ADHD had worse outcomes on most financial indicators than controls, even when they no longer endorsed DSM symptoms, and the gap widened between 25 and 30. Extrapolated, male probands were projected to earn $1.27 million less over their working lives and reach retirement with up to 75% lower net worth.

title: The economic burden of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: A sibling comparison cost analysis
plain_language: Adults diagnosed with ADHD later in life had noticeably lower income and higher costs than their own brothers or sisters.
key_finding: Compared with their own same-sex siblings, adults first diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood had lower disposable income, paid less tax, received more benefits and had higher health, social-care and crime costs, averaging 20,134 euros more per person in 2010.

title: Diminished Interoceptive Accuracy in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Most, but not all, small studies suggest people with ADHD are somewhat less accurate at sensing signals from inside their bodies.
key_finding: Of five studies comparing people with and without ADHD, three found reduced interoception in ADHD; across twelve general-population studies, lower interoception was associated with more inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, emotional dysregulation and executive dysfunction. Studies were of moderate quality with small samples.

title: Interoceptive abilities in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Adults with ADHD were less accurate at counting their own heartbeats, and this wasn't explained by autism traits or depression.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD showed lower heartbeat-counting accuracy, lower confidence and lower self-reported interoceptive accuracy than controls, even after controlling for autistic traits, alexithymia, depression and other variables. The authors urge caution because of the small sample and narrow age range.

title: Interoception in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Autistic adults did not differ significantly from other adults in sensing their heartbeat; findings on other kinds of body awareness are mixed.
key_finding: A meta-analysis of five adult studies found no significant difference in cardiac interoceptive accuracy between autistic and non-autistic adults (μ = -.21, SE = .11, p = .06). Findings for interoceptive sensibility and awareness, and in children and adolescents, were inconsistent.

title: Burnout as experienced by autistic people: A systematic review
plain_language: Across 48 studies, autistic people described burnout as crushing exhaustion, and said that rest, time alone, sensory relief and understanding themselves helped them recover.
key_finding: Autistic burnout consisted of debilitating exhaustion and increased disability, sometimes chronic with intermittent crises. Sensory and social overwhelm, camouflaging, stigma, everyday life challenges and alexithymia contributed. Recovery was helped by a more accurate framework for self-understanding, meeting needs for rest, solitude and sensory relief, and individual and community support. Samples were mostly White, female, late-diagnosed adults.

title: How does 'autistic burnout' feel? A qualitative study exploring experiences of earlier and later-diagnosed autistic adults
plain_language: People diagnosed with autism as adults found burnout more confusing and longer-lasting, partly because they didn't know why it was happening.
key_finding: Burnout was described as a powering down and/or an over-activation of mind and body, leading to a craving for sensory and social rest. For those diagnosed in adulthood, burnout seemed more chronic and confusing; some used substances to cope, and not knowing why it was happening took a sometimes dangerous toll.

title: Special interests and subjective wellbeing in autistic adults
plain_language: Special interests were linked to feeling better for autistic adults, though extremely intense involvement was linked to feeling worse.
key_finding: About two-thirds of autistic adults reported a special interest. Wellbeing did not differ between those with and without one, but among those with special interests, motivation to engage was associated with higher subjective wellbeing and life satisfaction; very high intensity of engagement was negatively related to wellbeing.

title: 'People should be allowed to do what they like': Autistic adults' views and experiences of stimming
plain_language: Autistic adults said stimming helps them calm down and express strong feelings, and that it should not be trained away.
key_finding: Autistic adults described stimming as a self-regulatory mechanism that helps soothe or communicate intense emotions or thoughts, and as lacking social acceptance. They objected to treatment aimed at eliminating it.

title: Does Camouflaging Predict Functioning, Distress, and Quality of Life for Autistic Adults?
plain_language: Masking went along with worse mental health, but once social anxiety was taken into account it added little on its own.
key_finding: Camouflaging (CAT-Q) correlated with poorer mental health and quality of life but did not predict depression, distress or disability beyond social responsiveness and social anxiety. The authors suggest current camouflaging measures may capture overlapping constructs.

title: Psychological Stress and Mitochondria: A Conceptual Framework
plain_language: This paper proposes that long-term stress may change how the cell's energy factories work, as an idea to test.
key_finding: Proposes that chronic psychological stress causes structural and functional recalibrations of mitochondria ('mitochondrial allostatic load'), which may be a subcellular mechanism through which psychosocial experiences become biological changes. Framed as an emerging concept.

title: Psychological Stress and Mitochondria: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Evidence that stress harms mitochondria comes mostly from male lab animals; human studies were few and indirect.
key_finding: All 23 experimental studies were in male laboratory animals; 19 showed adverse effects of psychological stress on mitochondria and 4 found increases in function or size. In humans only six observational studies existed, none experimental, mostly measuring indirect markers such as mtDNA copy number.

title: A Mitochondrial Health Index Sensitive to Mood and Caregiving Stress
plain_language: Mothers under long-term caregiving stress had less efficient energy production in their blood cells, and better mood went with better mitochondrial health.
key_finding: Mothers caring for an autistic child (high-stress caregivers) had lower leukocyte mitochondrial health index (MHI) than control mothers. Higher positive mood at night was associated with higher MHI and mediated the caregiving-MHI association; MHI tracked mood on the days before the blood draw.

title: The energetic cost of allostasis and allostatic load
plain_language: This model proposes that chronic stress costs the body extra energy, leaving less for repair; it still needs testing.
key_finding: Proposes an energetic model of allostatic load in which chronic stress adds an energetic burden; overconsumption of energy (hypermetabolism) competes with growth, maintenance and repair and may drive physiological decline and ageing. Presented as a model making testable predictions.

title: A molecular framework for autistic experiences: Mitochondrial allostatic load as a mediator between autism and psychopathology
plain_language: This paper suggests, as an untested idea, that masking-related stress might strain cell energy systems and lead to autistic burnout.
key_finding: Proposes that social camouflaging could be a form of chronic stress contributing to allostatic overload, experienced as autistic burnout, and that mitochondrial allostatic load may mediate the link between autism and psychopathology. The authors note these mechanisms remain largely unexplored by molecular researchers.

title: The impact of camouflaging autistic traits on psychological and physiological stress: a co-twin control study
plain_language: People who masked more tended to have higher long-term stress hormone levels, but comparing twins suggests family factors explain much of this.
key_finding: Across individuals, camouflaging was associated with higher hair cortisol, particularly in autistic and adult subsamples. Within twin pairs there was no association in the full sample, suggesting familial confounding, and in autistic and adult twin pairs camouflaging was linked to lower hair cortisol.

title: Oxidative Stress and ADHD: A Meta-Analysis
plain_language: An early small review found signs of more oxidative stress in ADHD, but antioxidant levels were normal and the result was fragile.
key_finding: ADHD was significantly associated with oxidative stress, but this lost significance after correcting for intra-study clustering; antioxidant status did not differ. The authors suggest normal antioxidant production with an insufficient response to oxidative stress, and call the results preliminary.

title: Systemic oxidative stress in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis of oxidative and antioxidant biomarkers
plain_language: Children with ADHD showed somewhat higher markers of oxidative stress and lower overall antioxidant capacity on some, not all, blood and urine tests.
key_finding: Children and adolescents with ADHD had higher blood total oxidant status (SMD 0.94) and urinary 8-OHdG (SMD 0.21) and lower blood total antioxidant status (SMD -0.53). Blood 8-OHdG, MDA, NO and SOD did not differ.

title: The SIRT-1/Nrf-2/HO-1 antioxidant defense axis in adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: In one study, adults with ADHD had lower blood levels of proteins that switch on the body's antioxidant defences.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD had lower serum SIRT-1, Nrf-2 and HO-1 (antioxidant-regulatory proteins) than controls, and these correlated negatively with symptom severity; TNF-alpha did not differ, CRP was modestly higher and ferritin lower in ADHD.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in autism spectrum disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Some autistic children show signs of strained cell energy production in blood tests; about 1 in 20 had diagnosable mitochondrial disease.
key_finding: Mitochondrial disease prevalence in children with ASD was 5.0% (95% CI 3.2-6.9%), far above the ~0.01% general-population rate. Abnormal mitochondrial biomarker values were much more common than mitochondrial disease, and lactate, pyruvate, carnitine and ubiquinone differed between ASD and controls; studies had small samples and referral biases.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction as a neurobiological subtype of autism spectrum disorder: evidence from brain imaging
plain_language: About 1 in 8 autistic participants, and 1 in 5 autistic adults, had a lactate signal in the brain, compared with 1 in 100 controls.
key_finding: Brain lactate doublets were present in 13% of participants with ASD vs 1% of controls; in the ASD group they were more common in adults (20%) than children (6%) and did not correlate with sex, subtype, IQ or ADOS scores.

title: Increased cerebral lactate levels in adults with autism spectrum disorders compared to non-autistic controls: a magnetic resonance spectroscopy study
plain_language: 9.4% of autistic adults had raised lactate in one brain region, and this did not match their blood lactate levels.
key_finding: Mean posterior cingulate lactate was higher in autistic adults (p = 0.028; d = 0.40), and 9.4% of the autistic group had elevated levels versus 0% of controls. Serum lactate did not correlate with brain lactate. The authors urge caution given the p value and the many scans excluded for poor quality; prevalence was lower than the 20% expected.

title: Association Between Methylphenidate and Amphetamine Use in Pregnancy and Risk of Congenital Malformations
plain_language: Methylphenidate taken in early pregnancy may slightly raise the chance of a heart defect in the baby. Amphetamines did not show this. The authors describe the increase as small.
key_finding: First-trimester methylphenidate: adjusted RR 1.11 (95% CI 0.91-1.35) for any malformation and 1.28 (95% CI 0.94-1.74) for cardiac malformations; pooled US-Nordic cardiac estimate 1.28 (95% CI 1.00-1.64). Amphetamines showed no increased risk (RR 1.05 for any; 0.96 for cardiac malformations). The authors conclude there may be a small increase in cardiac malformations with methylphenidate but not with amphetamines.

title: Placental Complications Associated With Psychostimulant Use in Pregnancy
plain_language: Stimulants in pregnancy were linked to a small rise in preeclampsia and, if continued late, preterm birth. The authors say the extra risk is small and is not by itself a reason to stop treatment.
key_finding: Stimulant use in the first half of pregnancy was associated with preeclampsia (adjusted RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.11-1.49) but not clearly with placental abruption, small for gestational age or preterm birth. Continuing stimulants after 20 weeks (vs discontinuing) was associated with preterm birth (adjusted RR 1.30, 1.10-1.55). Atomoxetine was not associated with the outcomes. The authors state that the absolute increases are small and that women with significant ADHD should not be counselled to stop treatment on the basis of these findings.

title: Prescription Stimulant Use During Pregnancy and Risk of Neurodevelopmental Disorders in Children
plain_language: Children exposed to stimulants in the womb looked more likely to get ADHD or autism at first, but this mostly disappeared once the mother's own ADHD and other factors were taken into account.
key_finding: Unadjusted analyses showed a 2- to 3-fold higher risk of neurodevelopmental outcomes after exposure in the second half of pregnancy, but after adjustment amphetamine/dextroamphetamine was not associated with autism (HR 0.80, 0.56-1.14) or ADHD (HR 1.07, 0.89-1.28). Methylphenidate was associated with child ADHD (HR 1.43, 1.12-1.82), but this did not persist with stricter control for maternal ADHD. The authors conclude in utero stimulant exposure is not likely to meaningfully increase childhood neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: In utero exposure to ADHD medication and long-term offspring outcomes
plain_language: Among Danish mothers with ADHD, children of those who kept taking medication in pregnancy did not have more developmental conditions than children of those who stopped.
key_finding: Comparing children of mothers who continued ADHD medication in pregnancy with children of mothers who stopped before pregnancy, there was no increased risk of any developmental disorder (aHR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.17) or of any subcategory, including in negative-control and sibling analyses.

title: In utero exposure to methylphenidate, amphetamines and atomoxetine and offspring neurodevelopmental disorders – a population-based cohort study and meta-analysis
plain_language: A large Swedish study, combined with Danish data, found no higher rate of ADHD or autism in children exposed to ADHD medicines before birth.
key_finding: Compared with children whose mothers stopped medication before conception, in utero exposure to methylphenidate, amphetamines or atomoxetine was not associated with any neurodevelopmental disorder (adjusted HR 0.95, 0.82-1.11), ADHD (0.92, 0.78-1.08) or autism (0.86, 0.63-1.18); results held in sibling comparisons. The pooled Swedish-Danish HR for any neurodevelopmental disorder was 1.00 (0.83;1.20).

title: Methylphenidate and Atomoxetine in Pregnancy and Possible Adverse Fetal Outcomes
plain_language: Pooling ten studies, methylphenidate and atomoxetine in pregnancy were not linked to more birth defects or miscarriages.
key_finding: Congenital anomalies (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.83-1.55) and miscarriages (OR 1.01, 0.70-1.47) were not more frequent with methylphenidate or atomoxetine in pregnancy compared with unexposed mothers with ADHD, nor compared with the general population. The authors conclude continuation appears safe for these outcomes but call for further studies.

title: Maternal and offspring outcomes associated with prescribed ADHD medication in pregnancy: a systematic review
plain_language: A review of twelve recent studies found mostly reassuring results for ADHD medicines in pregnancy, except modafinil, which was linked to birth defects.
key_finding: Seven of twelve studies found no significant negative maternal or offspring effect; one found continuing reduced several negative outcomes; one found stopping may increase threatened abortion; three reported associations with pre-eclampsia, gastroschisis, omphalocele or transverse limb deficiency. Modafinil significantly increased congenital malformations. The authors conclude women taking modafinil should consider stopping before pregnancy, and that for other ADHD medications the benefits of continuing where effective are likely to outweigh the risks.

title: Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Medication Use in Pregnancy and Risk of Preterm Birth: A Population‐Based Cohort Study
plain_language: Among women already taking ADHD medicine before pregnancy, longer use during pregnancy was linked to a slightly higher chance of an early birth.
key_finding: Two or more filled prescriptions in early pregnancy were associated with preterm birth (aRR 1.29, 95% CI 1.08, 1.53), but one or more was not (aRR 1.08, 0.93, 1.25). In late pregnancy each 30 days of cumulative exposure raised risk (aHR 1.07, 1.02, 1.12). The authors conclude ADHD medication may modestly increase preterm birth risk, especially with longer use.

title: Investigating maternal and neonatal health outcomes associated with continuing or ceasing dexamphetamine treatment for women with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder during pregnancy: a retrospective cohort study
plain_language: Continuing dexamphetamine was no worse than stopping partway through pregnancy, but women who were off it for the whole pregnancy had fewer complications.
key_finding: Continuing dexamphetamine throughout pregnancy was not associated with more adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes than ceasing; ceasers had higher odds of threatened abortion (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.00, 5.15). Women unexposed in pregnancy had lower odds of preeclampsia (OR 0.58) and neonatal special care admission (OR 0.16) than continuers. The authors suggest stopping before pregnancy may be advisable where possible, and note small samples.

title: Parental ADHD in pregnancy and the postpartum period – A systematic review
plain_language: A review pulling together what is known about ADHD in pregnancy and the first years of parenting, which found that much is still unknown.
key_finding: Reviews evidence on maternal ADHD and pregnancy and birth outcomes, health behaviour in pregnancy, early parent-child interaction and child development to age 3, and the risks of stimulant and non-stimulant treatment in pregnancy and lactation. The abstract notes that data on how parental ADHD affects early parent-child interaction are lacking.

title: Association of maternal attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and preterm birth: a cohort study
journal: BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
plain_language: Women with ADHD were slightly more likely to give birth early, mostly because of risk factors that can be changed.
key_finding: Women with ADHD had more preterm births than women without (7.3 versus 5.8%; aOR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05-1.30), particularly very preterm (<32 weeks) births, with both spontaneous and medically indicated onset. The authors add that most of the excess risk is due to modifiable risk factors.

title: Pregnancy Outcomes in Women Diagnosed With Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Population‐Based Register Study
plain_language: The higher early-birth rate in women with ADHD largely disappeared once other mental health conditions and smoking were accounted for.
key_finding: Preterm birth was 6.6% vs 4.9% (crude OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.25, 1.42), but this attenuated to non-significance after adjusting for maternal age, education and comorbid mental disorders (adjOR 1.06, 0.99, 1.13). Maternal ADHD remained associated with large-for-gestational-age babies (adjOR 1.16) and planned caesarean section (adjOR 1.16).

title: Maternal attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and adverse obstetrical and perinatal outcomes: A population-based cohort study in Ontario, Canada
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM
plain_language: In Ontario, women diagnosed with ADHD before pregnancy had somewhat more serious complications for themselves and their babies, whether or not they took stimulants.
key_finding: Severe maternal morbidity occurred in 2.8% vs 2.3% (aRR 1.31, 1.21-1.42) and severe neonatal morbidity in 15.7% vs 12.5% (aRR 1.25, 1.21-1.29). Maternal ADHD was also associated with preeclampsia (1.28), preterm birth (1.41) and small for gestational age (1.21), but not gestational diabetes. Findings were largely unchanged after removing people who filled a psychostimulant prescription in pregnancy.

title: Pregnancy outcomes in women with autism: a nationwide population-based cohort study
plain_language: Autistic women were somewhat more likely to have an early birth (mostly planned by doctors), a planned caesarean and preeclampsia.
key_finding: Maternal autism was associated with preterm birth (OR 1.30, 1.10-1.54), especially medically indicated preterm birth (OR 1.41, 1.08-1.82), elective caesarean (OR 1.44) and preeclampsia (OR 1.34), but not emergency caesarean, low Apgar, gestational diabetes or stillbirth.

title: The bidirectional association between premenstrual disorders and perinatal depression: A nationwide register-based study from Sweden
plain_language: Women who had a premenstrual disorder before pregnancy were much more likely to be diagnosed with depression around pregnancy, and the link also ran the other way.
key_finding: Premenstrual disorders before pregnancy were recorded in 2.9% of women with perinatal depression vs 0.6% of controls (OR 4.76, 95% CI 4.52,5.01). Women with perinatal depression were later more likely to be diagnosed with premenstrual disorders (HR 1.81, 1.74,1.88). Sibling comparisons attenuated but did not remove the associations. The authors interpret this as a bidirectional association consistent with shared aetiology.

title: History of premenstrual syndrome and development of postpartum depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Women who had PMS before pregnancy had more than double the odds of postpartum depression, though the studies were not high quality.
key_finding: Women with a pre-pregnancy history of PMS had more than double the odds of postpartum depression (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.81-2.68). Evidence quality was low: five studies had moderate, eleven serious and three critical risk of bias.

title: Association between premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perinatal depression: a systematic review
plain_language: Most of the small number of studies found that women with PMDD were more likely to develop depression after giving birth.
key_finding: One study linked PMDD with depression during pregnancy; that study and five others found a positive association between PMDD and postpartum depression (assessed from 2 to 4 days to 1 year after birth); only one found no significant association at 4 weeks postpartum. The authors recommend routinely asking about PMDD in perinatal care.

title: Maternal Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Perinatal Depression: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Across ten studies, women with ADHD were more likely to have depression around pregnancy than women without ADHD.
key_finding: Perinatal depression prevalence in women with ADHD ranged from 16.76% to 57.6%, with higher odds than in women without ADHD (OR 1.8-2.63); ADHD symptoms correlated with perinatal depressive symptoms. Most studies were of medium quality and the authors call for higher-quality replication.

title: Maternal ADHD Diagnoses Before and After Childbirth: A Danish Population-Based Cohort Study
plain_language: In Denmark, mothers were most likely to be newly diagnosed with ADHD 2 to 5 years after giving birth, often after first being treated for other mental health problems.
key_finding: Incident ADHD diagnoses fell during pregnancy (IRR 0.28), stayed below pre-pregnancy levels up to 2 years postpartum (IRR 0.82) and rose above them 2 to 5 years postpartum (IRR 1.24). Among mothers diagnosed postpartum, 53.9% had psychiatric service contact or other psychotropic prescriptions between childbirth and their ADHD diagnosis. The authors suggest the postpartum years may be a window of symptom worsening.

title: Psychostimulant Continuation and Postpartum Mental Health in Pregnant People With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Continuing ADHD stimulants during pregnancy was not linked to worse mental health after birth. Overall, 16.2% had a new mood or anxiety diagnosis in the year after birth.
key_finding: 41.4% stopped stimulants in pregnancy. Overall 16.2% had a new postpartum mood or anxiety diagnosis. A crude excess among continuers (19.3% vs 12.8%) disappeared after adjustment: continuation was not associated with postpartum mental health admissions (RR 1.01, 0.59-1.71) or new mood/anxiety diagnoses (RR 1.30, 0.97-1.74). Pre-existing mental health diagnoses were the strongest predictor of admissions (RR 2.60).

title: Associations between self-reported ADHD symptoms and depression and anxiety in mothers and fathers during the postpartum period: A Canadian nationwide longitudinal study
plain_language: New mothers with likely ADHD were more likely to be depressed or anxious in the first two years, and each parent's ADHD symptoms affected the other's mental health.
key_finding: Mothers with possible ADHD (self-report) had higher odds of depression (aOR 1.70, 1.13-2.56) and anxiety (aOR 1.74, 1.30-2.34) at 3-24 months postpartum. Fathers' ADHD symptoms were associated with mothers' depression (aOR 1.05 per symptom unit), and mothers' ADHD symptoms with fathers' anxiety (aOR 1.03).

title: Methylphenidate use in pregnancy and lactation: a systematic review of evidence
plain_language: Very few breastfed babies exposed to methylphenidate have been studied; those reported developed normally.
key_finding: In the few breastfeeding cases identified, children developed normally and no adverse effects were reported; pregnancy data were small and confounded by co-exposures. The authors conclude data are scarce and that interrupting ADHD treatment in pregnancy and lactation may itself carry significant risk.

title: A comparative study of autistic and non-autistic women’s experience of motherhood
plain_language: Autistic mothers reported more depression around birth and more trouble being understood by professionals, while still putting their children first.
key_finding: Autistic mothers were more likely to report pre- or postpartum depression, difficulty multitasking and coping with domestic responsibilities, feeling misunderstood by professionals, anxiety, and isolation in motherhood, yet reported acting in their child's best interest.

title: Autistic mothers’ perinatal well-being and parenting styles
plain_language: Autistic parents were more stressed, depressed and anxious during pregnancy and after birth, but parented just as positively in most ways.
key_finding: Autistic parents had higher stress, depression and anxiety scores than non-autistic parents across the perinatal period, with no differences in life satisfaction, parenting confidence or most parenting styles (lower scores only on parenting discipline).

title: Efficacy of Transdermal Estradiol and Micronized Progesterone in the Prevention of Depressive Symptoms in the Menopause Transition
plain_language: Over a year, fewer women on estrogen patches plus progesterone developed depression than on placebo (17.3% vs 32.3%), with the benefit seen in early perimenopause.
key_finding: Twelve months of transdermal estradiol plus intermittent micronized progesterone reduced onset of clinically significant depressive symptoms vs placebo (17.3% vs 32.3%; OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.1-5.7). Benefit was seen in the early menopause transition but not the late transition or postmenopause.

title: Guidelines for the evaluation and treatment of perimenopausal depression: summary and recommendations
plain_language: Experts agree perimenopause raises depression risk. Standard treatments come first; estrogen may help some women, especially those with hot flushes.
key_finding: Perimenopause is a window of vulnerability for depressive symptoms and major depression; most women with a perimenopausal major depressive episode have had a prior episode. Antidepressants and psychotherapy are front-line. Estrogen is not approved for perimenopausal depression but has evidence of antidepressant effects in perimenopausal women, particularly with vasomotor symptoms; estrogen-plus-progestin data are sparse.

title: Hormones and Menopausal Status as Predictors of Depression in Womenin Transition to Menopause
plain_language: Depressive symptoms rose during the move into menopause and fell afterwards, linked to changing hormone levels.
key_finding: Depressive symptoms were more likely during the transition to menopause and less likely after menopause, after adjusting for other predictors including history of depression and severe premenstrual syndrome, poor sleep and employment. Hormone patterns gave corroborating evidence that the changing hormonal milieu contributes to dysphoric mood.

title: Premenstrual Symptoms and Perimenopausal Depression
plain_language: Some, but not all, women depressed in perimenopause also had premenstrual mood symptoms, and they could not reliably report this from memory.
key_finding: On prospective daily ratings, 21% of depressed vs 3% of nondepressed perimenopausal women met criteria for premenstrual dysphoria, but it was not an invariant accompaniment of perimenopausal depression, and self-reports did not predict it.

title: Cognitive effects of estradiol after menopause
plain_language: Estrogen taken after menopause did not improve or worsen memory or thinking skills, whenever it was started.
key_finding: Oral 17β-estradiol for a mean 57 months had no effect on verbal memory (estradiol-placebo difference -0.06, 95% CI -0.22 to 0.09), executive functions or global cognition, whether started within 6 years or 10+ years after menopause. The authors conclude estradiol neither benefits nor harms these abilities.

title: Menopause hormone therapy and risk of mild cognitive impairment or dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Hormone therapy at menopause did not raise or lower the risk of dementia.
key_finding: No significant association between menopause hormone therapy and mild cognitive impairment or dementia, with no effects by timing, duration or type; certainty ranged from moderate to very low. The authors conclude MHT should be prescribed for other benefits and risks, not dementia prevention.

title: Examining the Link Between ADHD Symptoms and Menopausal Experiences
plain_language: Women with ADHD did not report worse menopause symptoms than other women in this survey, though ADHD symptoms and menopause complaints went together in everyone.
key_finding: After FDR correction, women with ADHD did not report more menopausal complaints than women without at any menopause stage, with or without medication. ADHD symptoms correlated with menopausal complaints across all participants, less strongly within the ADHD group, which the authors suggest may reflect different symptom attribution.

title: Self-Reported Psychological, Somatic, and Vasomotor Symptoms at Different Stages of the Menopause for Autistic and Non-autistic People
plain_language: Autistic people found psychological and physical menopause symptoms more troublesome than others did, but hot flushes were similar.
key_finding: Autistic people reported significantly more bothersome psychological and somatic menopause symptoms than non-autistic people, but no difference in vasomotor symptoms. Autistic people also reported more bothersome symptoms before menopause, which the authors say needs longitudinal study.

title: The course of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder through midlife
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
plain_language: Most adults with ADHD still had it thirteen years later in midlife, and women were more likely to keep their symptoms.
key_finding: Of those assessed three times, 68.8% had a stable, 25.5% an unstable and 5.7% a remitting ADHD trajectory. Women, more severe ADHD, more comorbidity and genetic liability to depression predicted a stable trajectory.

title: Time after time: failure to identify and support females with ADHD – a Swedish population register study
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Girls and women with ADHD were diagnosed about 4 years later than boys and men, and had more other mental health problems first.
key_finding: Females were older than males at first ADHD diagnosis or medication (23.5 vs 19.6 years), about 4 years later, and had higher rates of psychiatric comorbidity, pharmacological treatment and health-care use than both males with ADHD and female controls, before and after diagnosis.

title: Childhood predictors and moderators of lifetime risk of self-harm in girls with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Self-harm in girls with ADHD was concentrated in the teenage years and was predicted by childhood behaviour problems, adversity and low self-esteem.
key_finding: Most self-harm occurred in adolescence and desisted by adulthood, and came largely from the combined-type ADHD group. Non-suicidal self-injury was predicted by early externalizing symptoms, executive functioning and father's negative parenting; suicide attempts by early externalizing symptoms, adverse childhood experiences and low self-esteem.

title: Teenage Parenthood and Birth Rates for Individuals With and Without Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Nationwide Cohort Study
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Teenage girls with ADHD were much more likely to become young mothers.
key_finding: Females with ADHD were more likely to become parents at 12 to 16 years (IRR 3.62, 95% CI 2.14-6.13) and 17 to 19 years (IRR 1.94, 1.62-2.33) than females without ADHD. The authors suggest targeted sexual education and contraceptive counselling.

title: Adolescent Mediators of Unplanned Pregnancy among Women with and without Childhood ADHD
journal: Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology
plain_language: Girls with ADHD who struggled at school in early adolescence were more likely to take sexual risks and have unplanned pregnancies later.
key_finding: The link between childhood ADHD and unplanned pregnancy by early adulthood ran through low academic achievement in early adolescence leading to risky sexual behaviour in late adolescence, after adjusting for age, IQ and family SES.

title: A meta-analytic review of the association between pubertal timing and psychopathology in adolescence: Are there sex differences in risk?
plain_language: Starting puberty early was linked to slightly more mental health problems in both girls and boys.
key_finding: Early pubertal timing had small but robust associations (ds ∼.20) with all domains of adolescent psychopathology in both sexes; adolescent sex did not moderate the effect.

title: Early Pubertal Timing and Testosterone Associated With Higher Levels of Adolescent Depression in Girls
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Girls who started puberty early, and those with higher testosterone, were more likely to become depressed.
key_finding: Early pubertal timing (OR 5.8, 95% CI 1.9-17.9 after age 12) and higher testosterone (OR 2.0, 1.1-3.8) were the only significant predictors of depression during puberty; estradiol, age and Tanner stage per se were not.

title: Pubertal Timing During Early Adolescence: Advanced Pubertal Onset in Females with Autism Spectrum Disorder
plain_language: Autistic girls in this study started puberty and periods earlier than other girls.
key_finding: Autistic girls showed advanced pubertal onset relative to autistic boys and typically developing girls, and earlier onset of menses than typically developing girls.

title: Assessing causal links between age at menarche and adolescent mental health: a Mendelian randomisation study
plain_language: Getting a first period earlier slightly raised the risk of teenage depression, but not of other mental health problems.
key_finding: Earlier menarche was associated with more depressive symptoms, and one-sample MR suggested a small causal effect (0.06 SD per earlier year) and a 29% increase in odds of a depression diagnosis per earlier year. There was little consistent evidence of effects on other domains of mental health.

title: Genetics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: ADHD is highly heritable, so when a child is diagnosed it is common for a parent to have it too.
key_finding: Family, twin and adoption studies show ADHD runs in families, with heritability of 74%. About a third of heritability is due to a polygenic component of many common variants, and rare copy number variants account for part.

title: Parenting in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
plain_language: This review explains how ADHD difficulties with memory, planning and self-control can make day-to-day parenting harder.
key_finding: Proposes how ADHD-related deficits in cognitive processes (working memory, planning, inhibition), self-regulation and motivation could impair parents' behavioural control and emotional responsiveness, and notes the limited existing studies.

title: Parental ADHD symptoms and parenting behaviors: A meta-analytic review
plain_language: Parents with more ADHD symptoms were a little more likely to be harsh or inconsistent, but the effect was small.
key_finding: Parental ADHD symptoms accounted for 2.9%, 3.2% and 0.5% of the variance in harsh, lax and positive parenting respectively, with effect sizes similar to other parental psychopathologies and relatively small.

title: The Relation Between Maternal ADHD Symptoms & Improvement in Child Behavior Following Brief Behavioral Parent Training is Mediated by Change in Negative Parenting
plain_language: Mothers with more ADHD symptoms got less benefit from parenting programmes for their child, so treating the mother's ADHD may help both.
key_finding: Higher maternal ADHD symptoms predicted less improvement in children's disruptive behaviour after brief behavioural parent training, mediated by change in observed negative parenting. The authors suggest combining treatment of adult ADHD with parent training.

title: “Until I Had My Son, I Did Not Realise That These Characteristics Could Be Due to Autism”: Motherhood and Family Experiences of Spanish Autistic Mothers
plain_language: Autistic mothers often realised they were autistic only after their child was diagnosed.
key_finding: Themes included mothers being diagnosed after their autistic children or close relatives, the role of partners and children in self-acceptance, and sensory reactivity and anxiety intensifying experiences from pregnancy to intimacy.

title: Racial and Ethnic Disparities in ADHD Diagnosis and Treatment
plain_language: Black and Latino children with the same symptoms were less likely than white children to be diagnosed with or treated for ADHD.
key_finding: Controlling for ADHD symptoms and other factors, African-American and Latino children had lower odds of an ADHD diagnosis and of ADHD medication than white children at every wave. The authors conclude disparities more likely reflect underdiagnosis and undertreatment of minority children than overdiagnosis of white children.

title: Trends in the Prevalence and Incidence of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Among Adults and Children of Different Racial and Ethnic Groups
plain_language: Among insured US adults, ADHD was diagnosed far less often in Black, Hispanic and Asian American people than in white people.
key_finding: Adult ADHD prevalence rose from 0.43% to 0.96%. White adults consistently had the highest prevalence (0.67%-1.42%) vs Black (0.22%-0.69%), Hispanic (0.25%-0.65%) and Asian American adults (0.11%-0.35%). Women had slightly lower odds of diagnosis (OR 0.943). Eating disorders (OR 5.192), depression (OR 4.118) and anxiety (OR 2.438) were associated with an ADHD diagnosis.

title: Racial Disparities in Diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in a US National Birth Cohort
plain_language: Asian, Black and Hispanic children were less likely to be diagnosed with ADHD than White children, and Asian children were least likely to be treated.
key_finding: Compared with White children, the hazard of ADHD diagnosis was lower for Asian (HR 0.48), Black (HR 0.83) and Hispanic children (HR 0.77). Asian children had the highest odds of receiving no treatment after diagnosis.

title: Prevalence and Risk Factors Associated With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Among US Black Individuals
plain_language: This review found ADHD was common among Black Americans, suggesting it may be missed rather than truly rarer.
key_finding: Pooled ADHD prevalence among US Black individuals was 14.54% (95% CI 10.64%-19.56%). The authors argue this contradicts the DSM-5 statement of lower prevalence and call for more assessment and culturally appropriate care.

title: Association of Race/Ethnicity and Social Disadvantage With Autism Prevalence in 7 Million School Children in England
plain_language: In English schools, autism was recorded much less often in girls, and rates differed by ethnic group and home language.
key_finding: Autism prevalence was 1.76%: 2.81% in male and 0.65% in female pupils (male-to-female ratio 4.32:1). It was highest in Black pupils (2.11%) and lowest in Roma/Irish Traveller pupils (0.85%). Pupils speaking English as an additional language were less likely to have an autism record (adjusted PR 0.64), and the ethnicity effect was mediated mostly through social disadvantage. The authors suggest differences in detection or referral.

title: Diagnosis and Treatment of ADHD in the United States: Update by Gender and Race
plain_language: Black adults were much less likely than white adults to be diagnosed with ADHD in US doctors' offices.
key_finding: ADHD diagnoses rose 36% in adults; diagnosis plus medication rose 29% in female youths. In 2012-2013 ADHD diagnosis was 77% less likely among Black than White adults but 24% more likely among Black than White youths.

title: Neurodevelopmental disorders in children aged 2–9 years: Population-based burden estimates across five regions in India
plain_language: In a survey across India, 9.2% to 13.6% of young children had a neurodevelopmental condition, with no significant difference between girls and boys.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence of any neurodevelopmental disorder was 9.2% at 2-<6 years and 13.6% at 6-9 years, with no significant difference by gender, rural/urban residence or religion; ADHD was assessed in 6-9 year olds. Most identified risk factors were modifiable.

title: Adult ADHD presentations in an Indian tertiary care setting: Gender perspectives
plain_language: In an Indian clinic, women with ADHD were more severely affected but more often diagnosed with something else.
key_finding: Women had higher ASRS scores, more mind-wandering, hyperfocusing and mood lability, lower self-esteem and higher illness severity, often identified on screening. Women were more likely to be diagnosed with personality disorder than ADHD, with a trend to low help-seeking and atypical primary complaints.

title: Prevalence of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in India: a systematic review and a cross-sectional study among young adults in Delhi-NCR
plain_language: Studies in India suggest adult ADHD is common, but most figures come from screening questionnaires rather than diagnoses.
key_finding: Indian studies reported adult ADHD prevalence ranging from 5.48 to 25.7%; 14% of Delhi-NCR students screened positive on the ASRS (a screen, not a diagnosis). The authors call for awareness of adult ADHD in India.

title: Burden of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in Indian Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Across Indian studies, 63.2 per 1000 children had ADHD on average, but estimates varied widely.
key_finding: Pooled ADHD prevalence was 63.2 per 1000 children overall: 75.1 per 1000 in school-based and 18.6 per 1000 in community-based studies, with significant heterogeneity.

title: The prevalence of adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A global systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Worldwide, about 2.58% of adults have ADHD that started in childhood, and 6.76% have ADHD symptoms.
key_finding: Adjusted to the 2020 global population, prevalence of persistent adult ADHD (childhood onset) was 2.58% and of symptomatic adult ADHD 6.76%, about 139.84 million and 366.33 million adults; both decreased with age.

title: Elevated rates of autism, other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diagnoses, and autistic traits in transgender and gender-diverse individuals
plain_language: Trans and gender-diverse people were more likely than cisgender people to have autism and other neurodevelopmental diagnoses.
key_finding: Compared with cisgender individuals, transgender and gender-diverse individuals had higher rates of autism and other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diagnoses, and on average higher autistic traits, systemizing and sensory sensitivity and lower self-reported empathy, in both autistic and non-autistic groups.

title: Autism Spectrum Disorder and Gender Dysphoria/Incongruence. A systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Across studies, 11% of people with gender dysphoria had an autism diagnosis.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence of autism diagnoses in people with gender dysphoria/incongruence was 11%, and autistic traits were higher than in controls (g = 0.67), with high heterogeneity. The authors conclude a link is very likely but its size is uncertain.

title: Prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Amongst Individuals with Gender Dysphoria: A Systematic Review
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Autism seems more common in trans people than in the general population, but ADHD has hardly been studied.
key_finding: Studies using diagnostic criteria suggest autism prevalence of 6-26% in transgender populations, higher than the general population but no different from people attending psychiatry clinics. Few studies examined ADHD. The authors rate the evidence for a link as low-level.

title: Initial Clinical Guidelines for Co-Occurring Autism Spectrum Disorder and Gender Dysphoria or Incongruence in Adolescents
journal: Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology
plain_language: Experts agreed that autistic teenagers questioning their gender need careful, longer assessment and support across several areas of life.
key_finding: With a 75% consensus cutoff, experts recommended assessing gender dysphoria in autistic adolescents and vice versa, often with an extended diagnostic period in which assessment and treatment overlap, and addressing social functioning, medical safety, victimisation, school and transition to adulthood.

title: Hormone Therapy, Mental Health, and Quality of Life Among Transgender People: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Hormone therapy for trans people was linked to better quality of life and less depression and anxiety, but the studies were weak.
key_finding: Gender-affirming hormone therapy was associated with increased quality of life and decreased depression and anxiety, but certainty is limited by high risk of bias, small samples and confounding; no conclusions could be drawn about suicide.

title: Prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: About 2.18% of older adults have ADHD-level symptoms on validated scales, but far fewer are diagnosed (0.23%) or treated (0.09%).
key_finding: Pooled ADHD prevalence in older adults was 2.18% using validated scales, 0.23% using clinical diagnosis and 0.09% using treatment rates, with significant heterogeneity. The authors highlight under-diagnosis and under-treatment in older adults.

title: Prevalence of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in older adults in the Netherlands
plain_language: About 2.8% of older Dutch adults met criteria for ADHD.
key_finding: Weighted prevalence was 2.8% for syndromatic and 4.2% for symptomatic ADHD; younger elderly adults (60-70 years) reported more symptoms than older elderly adults (71-94 years).

title: Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and the Risk of Dementia
plain_language: Older people with an adult ADHD diagnosis were more likely to develop dementia later, though this does not prove ADHD causes it.
key_finding: Adult ADHD was associated with increased dementia risk (adjusted HR 2.77, 95% CI 2.11-3.63), robust in most sensitivity analyses, with no clear increase among those who received psychostimulants and only mild evidence of reverse causation.

title: Attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder and Alzheimer's disease and any dementia: A multi‐generation cohort study in Sweden
plain_language: Parents of people with ADHD were somewhat more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease, suggesting the conditions share family risk.
key_finding: Parents of individuals with ADHD had a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.26-1.89), attenuating in grandparents and aunts/uncles, with similar results for any dementia. The authors suggest shared familial risk.

title: Adult ADHD: Risk Factor for Dementia or Phenotypic Mimic?
plain_language: In older adults, lifelong ADHD can look like early memory decline, and doctors cannot always tell them apart.
key_finding: ADHD symptoms (sustained attention, organisation, forgetfulness) can closely resemble mild cognitive impairment, particularly over age 50, and both share sleep, depression and anxiety symptoms. It is unclear whether ADHD is linked to incipient dementia or being misdiagnosed as MCI.

title: No lower cognitive functioning in older adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Older adults with ADHD did not have worse memory or thinking overall; small attention differences were explained by depression.
key_finding: ADHD diagnosis and severity were associated only with lower attention/working memory, and this was no longer significant after adjusting for depression; memory, processing speed and executive function did not differ.

title: Childhood Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Predicts Intimate Partner Victimization in Young Women
plain_language: Young women who had ADHD as girls were much more likely to have been physically hurt by a partner (30.7% vs 6.3%).
key_finding: Young women with childhood ADHD experienced more physical intimate partner violence than comparisons (30.7% vs 6.3%), highest with persistent ADHD (37.3%) vs transient (19.0%) and never-diagnosed (5.9%). Adolescent academic achievement partially mediated the link.

title: ADHD in Childhood and/or Adulthood as a Risk Factor for Domestic Violence or Intimate Partner Violence: A Systematic Review
plain_language: A small number of studies link ADHD symptoms with partner violence, partly explained by other behaviour disorders.
key_finding: Three case-control studies found positive associations between ADHD and adult domestic/partner violence, though two did not adequately control for conduct disorder or antisocial personality disorder; cohort studies identified hyperactive, impulsive and inattentive symptoms as risk factors for adult IPV.

title: Prevalence of Victimisation in Autistic Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Across studies, 44% of autistic people had been victimised and 40% had experienced sexual victimisation.
key_finding: Pooled prevalence of any victimisation in autistic individuals was 44%, including 47% for bullying, 40% for sexual victimisation, 16% for child abuse and 84% for multiple forms; heterogeneity was high.

title: Evidence That Nine Autistic Women Out of Ten Have Been Victims of Sexual Violence
plain_language: In a French online survey, most autistic women reported having experienced sexual violence, often as children.
key_finding: 68.9% (open question) and 88.4% (standardised questionnaire) reported sexual victimisation; of 199 victims, 135 were first assaulted at 18 or younger. The authors argue autism is a vulnerability factor and that prevention must target offenders and culture rather than victims.

title: Prevalence of attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder in adult prisoners: An updated meta‐analysis
plain_language: About 1 in 12 adults in prison has ADHD, and the rate is similar in women and men.
key_finding: In random-sampling studies, pooled ADHD prevalence was 8.3% (95% CI 3.8-12.8), with no difference between men and women; the authors note earlier meta-analyses may have overestimated prevalence by including selected samples.

title: A meta-analysis of the prevalence of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in incarcerated populations
plain_language: An earlier review estimated that 25.5% of people in prison have ADHD.
key_finding: Using diagnostic interviews, estimated ADHD prevalence in incarcerated populations was 25.5%, with no significant differences by gender or age.

title: An Epidemiological Study of ADHD, Substance Use, and Comorbid Problems in Incarcerated Women in Sweden
plain_language: Twenty-nine percent of women assessed in a Swedish prison had ADHD, often alongside drug use.
key_finding: Twenty-nine percent of assessed women met DSM-IV criteria for adult ADHD, comparable to male offenders; illicit stimulant use and antisocial personality disorder were more common in women with ADHD. The ASRS had sensitivity 1.0 and specificity 0.66 as a screener.

title: Autism spectrum disorder in individuals with anorexia nervosa and in their first- and second-degree relatives: Danish nationwide register-based cohort-study
plain_language: Autism was more common in people with anorexia and their families, but so were other mental health conditions.
key_finding: Autism comorbidity was increased in people with anorexia nervosa and autism aggregated in their relatives, but the increase did not differ significantly from comorbid and familial depression or any psychiatric disorder, suggesting a non-specific relationship.

title: Using the Autism-Spectrum Quotient to Measure Autistic Traits in Anorexia Nervosa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: People with anorexia scored higher on an autism-traits questionnaire.
key_finding: People with anorexia nervosa had higher self-reported autistic traits on the AQ than controls; the authors note the cause of these traits is unclear and robust clinical measures are needed.

title: Anorexia nervosa and autism: a prospective twin cohort study
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Children who later developed anorexia did not show more autistic traits beforehand; the traits appeared mainly during acute illness.
key_finding: Children later diagnosed with anorexia did not have elevated autistic traits at age 9; at 18 restricted/repetitive traits were markedly elevated only in those with acute anorexia. The authors discuss female-phenotype masking or an acute-illness effect as explanations.

title: Investigating the Presence of Autistic Traits and Prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder Symptoms in Anorexia Nervosa: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
plain_language: People with anorexia had more autistic traits, and 29% scored above an autism cut-off.
key_finding: Autistic traits were higher in anorexia than controls (g = 0.88), modestly correlated with eating-disorder severity (r = 0.28), and 29% scored above the ADOS cutoff for autism.

title: Diagnosis and management of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
plain_language: POTS is diagnosed only when the heart rate rises a lot within 10 minutes of standing, symptoms have lasted at least 3 months, blood pressure does not fall significantly, and nothing else explains the fast heart rate.
key_finding: All criteria must be met: a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 beats/min (at least 40 beats/min at age 12-19) within 10 minutes of upright posture; absence of significant orthostatic hypotension (a blood pressure drop of at least 20/10 mm Hg); very frequent orthostatic-intolerance symptoms that are worse upright and improve rapidly on lying down; symptom duration of at least 3 months; and absence of other conditions that could explain sinus tachycardia. Transient initial orthostatic hypotension does not preclude the diagnosis, and another explanation for the tachycardia (including anaemia, dehydration, hyperthyroidism, anxiety, prolonged bed rest or heart-rate-raising medicines such as stimulants) precludes it.

title: N-Acetylcysteine in the Treatment of Excoriation Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial
plain_language: In one trial in adults with skin-picking disorder, about half of those who finished on NAC improved a lot, compared with about one in five on placebo; everyday functioning did not differ.
