key_finding: In a 12-week double-blind trial in 66 adults with excoriation disorder, N-acetylcysteine was associated with significant improvement in skin-picking severity compared with placebo (NE-YBOCS 11.5 vs 14.1 at 12 weeks, P = .048; CGI-Severity 3.0 vs 4.2, P = .003). Among the 53 completers, 15 of 32 (47%) on NAC vs 4 of 21 (19%) on placebo were much or very much improved (P = .03). There were no significant differences in psychosocial functioning. NAC was well tolerated.

title: Diagnosis, Classification and Management of Mast Cell Activation Syndromes (MCAS) in the Era of Personalized Medicine
plain_language: Experts define MCAS as recurrent symptoms in more than one body system, plus a lab-measured rise in tryptase above your own baseline, plus a response to mast-cell treatment.
key_finding: Consensus criteria for MCAS are met when mast cell activation is shown by a substantial increase in serum tryptase above the person's own baseline during severe systemic reactions, and the symptoms are recurrent, involve more than one organ system and respond to mast-cell-stabilising or mediator-targeting drugs. MCAS is classified as primary (KIT-mutated clonal mast cells), secondary (an underlying IgE-dependent allergy or other trigger) or idiopathic.

title: Amphetamine use for attention deficit hyperactive disorder during breastfeeding and children's neurodevelopmental outcomes: A pilot study
plain_language: Thirteen children whose mothers took amphetamine-type ADHD medicine while breastfeeding were checked for development and quality of life, and the study reported no significant problems. It is a small pilot study, so it cannot rule out uncommon effects.
key_finding: In 13 children exposed to amphetamine stimulants through breastfeeding, assessed with the Pediatric Quality of Life inventory and the Denver Developmental Scale, the study reported normal neurodevelopment with no significant adverse effects. The authors conclude amphetamines are likely compatible with breastfeeding but that larger studies are needed.

title: Does intensive multimodal treatment for maternal ADHD improve the efficacy of parent training for children with ADHD? A randomized controlled multicenter trial
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Treating mothers' ADHD with group therapy and medication helped the mothers' own ADHD more than supportive counselling did, but children's behaviour improved about the same in both groups once everyone had parent training.
key_finding: Mothers with ADHD were randomised to multimodal ADHD treatment (group psychotherapy plus open methylphenidate) or clinical management (supportive counselling) for 12 weeks before parent-child training for all. After 6 months there was no significant between-group difference in change in children's externalizing symptoms (adjusted mean difference 1.1, 95% CI -0.5 to 2.7; p = .1854), although maternal psychopathology improved more in the treatment group. Adverse events were more frequent in treated mothers; no severe treatment-related harms were found. Gains were stable at 1 year.

title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
plain_language: SSRI antidepressants probably ease premenstrual symptoms. On average, trials of daily dosing showed a larger benefit than trials of luteal-only dosing, but both beat placebo; side effects such as nausea, low energy and sleepiness are more common than on placebo.
key_finding: SSRIs probably reduce overall self-rated premenstrual symptoms in women with PMS and PMDD (SMD -0.57, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.42; 12 studies, 1742 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). In a subgroup comparison (P = 0.03 for subgroup difference), SSRIs were probably more effective when taken continuously (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.88 to -0.51; 7 studies, 1055 participants) than in the luteal phase only (SMD -0.39, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.21; 6 studies, 687 participants), both moderate-certainty evidence. SSRIs probably increase adverse events, most commonly nausea (OR 3.30), asthenia or decreased energy (OR 3.28) and somnolence/decreased concentration (OR 3.26, low-certainty). Overall certainty was moderate; reporting of methods was poor, publication bias was suspected for response rate, and 68% of included studies were funded by pharmaceutical companies.

title: Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone for premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: A combined pill containing drospirenone may ease PMDD symptoms a little to moderately over three cycles, but placebo helped too, side effects were more common, and the evidence is low quality.
key_finding: Combined pills containing drospirenone and ethinylestradiol may improve overall premenstrual symptoms versus placebo (SMD -0.41, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.24; 2 RCTs, N = 514; low-quality evidence) and functional impairment in productivity, social activities and relationships (low-quality evidence); the effects may be small to moderate, and the placebo also had a significant effect. They may increase withdrawal due to adverse effects (OR 3.41, 95% CI 2.01 to 5.78; low-quality) and adverse effects overall (OR 2.31); probably more breast pain, and may be more nausea, intermenstrual bleeding and menstrual disorder. No included study reported rare serious adverse effects such as venous thromboembolism. Effect on premenstrual mood symptoms measured with non-premenstrual tools is uncertain. Evidence quality was very low to moderate. Unknown whether it works after three cycles, helps less severe symptoms, or is better than other combined pills.

title: The Relationship between Sensory Sensitivity and Autistic Traits in the General Population
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Adults with more autistic traits reported many more everyday sensory difficulties, both over- and under-sensitivity.
key_finding: In 212 adults from the general population, the number of autistic traits correlated strongly with the frequency of sensory processing problems (r = .775, p < .001), covering over- and under-responsiveness. The authors suggest a strong link between sensory processing and autistic traits across the population.

title: The relation between procrastination and symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in undergraduate students
journal: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research
plain_language: In a small student study, putting things off went with inattention symptoms, not with impulsivity; the finding needs confirming.
key_finding: In 54 students, partial correlations showed that only inattention (not hyperactivity or impulsivity) was correlated with general procrastination; the authors note procrastination is not an officially recognised ADHD symptom and call the finding specific and preliminary.

title: Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism
plain_language: A theory that autistic attention tends to go deep into a few things at a time, and that this can explain many other autistic features.
key_finding: The authors argue from the literature and personal experience (one author is autistic) that atypical allocation of attention is central to autism, and that the social and communication criteria follow from the restricted range of interests.

title: Motor Coordination in Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Synthesis and Meta-Analysis
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Across many studies, autistic people had much more difficulty with coordination, balance and movement than non-autistic people.
key_finding: Meta-analysis found a large standardised mean difference of 1.20 (p < 0.0001) in motor coordination between autistic and typically developing groups across arm movements, gait and postural stability; the authors conclude motor coordination deficits are pervasive and a cardinal feature of autism.

title: Sleep in adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of subjective and objective studies
plain_language: Autistic adults took longer to fall asleep and woke more in the night, both by their own report and on sleep measurements.
key_finding: Autistic adults were more impaired than controls in six of 11 subjective sleep parameters (e.g. lower sleep efficiency, SMD = -0.87) and 10 of 17 objective outcomes, including longer sleep onset latency on polysomnography (SMD = 0.86) and more wake after sleep onset on actigraphy (SMD = 0.57).

title: Sleep in adults with autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Autistic adults and adults with ADHD both tend to take longer to fall asleep, wake more and sleep less well.
key_finding: Adults with autism and adults with ADHD shared a similar sleep-impaired profile: higher sleep onset latency, poorer sleep efficiency, more awakenings and lower self-perceived sleep quality than controls; a higher proportion of N1 sleep was found in autism and more periodic limb movements in ADHD.

title: Anxiety and depression in adults with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: About four in ten autistic adults have had an anxiety disorder and over a third have had depression at some point.
key_finding: Pooled current and lifetime prevalence in autistic adults were 27% and 42% for any anxiety disorder and 23% and 37% for depressive disorder; questionnaire measures and intellectual disability influenced estimates, and heterogeneity was high with over-reliance on clinical samples.

title: Prevalence of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in substance use disorder patients: A meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis
plain_language: Almost one in four people in treatment for alcohol or drug problems also has ADHD.
key_finding: Overall, 23.1% (CI 19.4-27.2%) of people with substance use disorders met DSM criteria for ADHD; prevalence varied with the substance (lower in cocaine dependence) and with the assessment instrument.

title: The lived experience of meltdowns for autistic adults
plain_language: Autistic adults described meltdowns as total overwhelm, with intense emotion and trouble thinking, which they try hard to prevent or hide.
key_finding: Qualitative analysis of 32 autistic adults: meltdowns were described as being overwhelmed by information, sensory input and social and emotional stress, with extreme emotions, difficulty thinking and remembering, efforts to stay in control, feeling 'not themselves', and a release of emotion; people tried to avoid triggers or be alone to prevent harm.

title: The Co-Occurrence of Autism and Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID): A Prevalence-Based Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Autism and ARFID (very restricted eating not driven by body image) often occur together.
key_finding: Prevalence of autism was 16.27% (95% CI 8.64%-28.53%) in people with ARFID, and ARFID prevalence in autistic groups was 11.41% (95% CI 2.89%-35.76%); the authors suggest screening each group for the other.

title: Quantifying and exploring camouflaging in men and women with autism
plain_language: Autistic women, on average, appeared less autistic in a clinical assessment than their inner traits would predict, suggesting more masking.
key_finding: Camouflaging, operationalised as the discrepancy between observed social presentation (ADOS) and internal traits/social cognition, was higher on average in autistic women than men (Cohen's d = 0.98), with large variability; greater camouflaging was associated with more depressive symptoms in men.

title: The Role of Emotion Regulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Big, hard-to-control emotions are common in autism and may be part of autism itself rather than a separate problem.
key_finding: Review concluding that autism is associated with amplified emotional responses and poor emotional control; some mechanisms are shared with other conditions while others may be specific (information processing, rigidity, less goal-directed behaviour), and poor emotion regulation may be inherent in autism.

title: Autistic peer-to-peer information transfer is highly effective
plain_language: Autistic people communicated as well with each other as non-autistic people did; problems showed up mostly between the two groups.
key_finding: Autistic people shared information with other autistic people as effectively as non-autistic people did with each other, but information transfer and rapport were lower in mixed autistic/non-autistic chains.

title: Face identity recognition in autism spectrum disorders: A review of behavioral studies
plain_language: Autistic people, on average, are less good at remembering faces, particularly after a delay.
key_finding: No strong evidence of qualitatively different face processing in autism, but quantitatively autistic people perform worse at remembering and discriminating facial identity, especially in tasks with a memory delay.

title: Gender Differences in the Social Motivation and Friendship Experiences of Autistic and Non-autistic Adolescents
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Autistic girls wanted and had friendships much like other girls, but struggled more with conflict inside those friendships.
key_finding: Autistic girls showed similar social motivation and friendship quality to non-autistic girls, while autistic boys differed; autistic girls reported high relational aggression within friendships, suggesting difficulty identifying and handling conflict.

title: What is the evidence of impaired motor skills and motor control among children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)? Systematic review of the literature
plain_language: Over half of children with ADHD have trouble with coordination or fine motor skills such as handwriting.
key_finding: More than half of children with ADHD had difficulties with gross and fine motor skills; the inattentive presentation showed more fine-motor impairment and slower reaction time. Medication normalised motor skills in 28% to 67% depending on the study, and those with persisting deficits might meet criteria for developmental coordination disorder.

title: Increased Risk for Substance Use-Related Problems in Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Population-Based Cohort Study
journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
plain_language: Autistic people, and especially those who also have ADHD, had higher rates of alcohol and drug problems.
key_finding: Autism without ADHD or intellectual disability was associated with a doubled risk of substance use-related problems, highest in people with both autism and ADHD; relatives also had raised risk, suggesting shared familial liability.

title: The lived experience of rejection sensitivity in ADHD - A qualitative exploration
plain_language: Five students with ADHD described how feeling rejected hit them physically and emotionally, and how hiding it led to loneliness.
key_finding: Thematic analysis gave three themes: withdrawal, masking and bodily sensations. Perceived rejection or criticism brought unpleasant bodily sensations, anxiety and misery; participants masked these feelings, which led to feeling dissociated from themselves, withdrawal and loneliness.

title: The Kind Nature Behind the Unsocial Semblance: ADHD and Justice Sensitivity-A Pilot Study
plain_language: In a pilot study, adults with ADHD, especially the inattentive type, were more bothered by unfairness than other adults.
key_finding: Participants with ADHD scored higher than controls on observer and profiteer justice sensitivity, with no difference in perpetrator sensitivity; on the questionnaire, the inattentive subtype scored higher than other subtypes and controls on all dimensions. The authors suggest justice sensitivity may be a coping strategy for inferring appropriate social behaviour.

title: Criteria for Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
plain_language: Daily diaries showed the worst days usually run from a few days before a period into its first few days, and that irritability-type symptoms are more common in PMDD than low mood.
key_finding: Daily ratings showed mood and physical symptoms, with impairment, were most severe from 4 days before through the first 2 days of menses (self-identified group) and 3 days before through the first 3 days of menses (community sample); the DSM-IV symptoms were the most problematic, but depressed mood was less frequent than other affective symptoms. In the combined sample, 4 or more symptoms was the optimal cutoff for predicting impairment.

title: Premenstrual syndrome
plain_language: Mild premenstrual changes are common; a smaller group have severe symptoms, mostly mood-related, that disrupt daily life.
key_finding: Most women of reproductive age have some premenstrual physical discomfort or dysphoria; about 5-8% have severe PMS, most of whom also meet PMDD criteria. Mood and behavioural symptoms (irritability, tension, depressed mood, tearfulness, mood swings) are the most distressing, while somatic complaints such as breast tenderness and bloating can also be problematic; fluctuations in gonadal hormones trigger the symptoms.

title: The prevalence, impairment, impact, and burden of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMS/PMDD)
plain_language: Premenstrual symptoms can seriously affect life even when they don't add up to the full PMDD count.
key_finding: Estimates 3-8% of reproductive-age women meet strict PMDD criteria and 13-18% may have premenstrual dysphoric symptoms severe enough to cause impairment and distress without reaching the 5-symptom count; impairment and lowered quality of life in PMDD are similar to dysthymic disorder and not much lower than major depressive disorder.

title: Cognition and behaviour across the menstrual cycle in individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder - A systematic review
plain_language: Tests of memory and attention don't reliably change in PMDD, but a pull toward negative thoughts and information seems to be a key feature.
key_finding: Cognitive performance was most often tested, but evidence of change with PMDD was limited and inconsistent; studies of cognitive processes and content suggest a negative attentional bias is central to the psychological experience of PMDD. The authors conclude cognitive process, content and behaviour are likely more informative than absolute cognitive abilities.

title: Cognition, The Menstrual Cycle, and Premenstrual Disorders: A Review
plain_language: Research has not settled whether thinking skills really change across the cycle or in premenstrual disorders.
key_finding: Concludes there is a lack of consistent findings on cognitive functioning across the menstrual cycle; cognitive research in premenstrual disorders is in its infancy, and it remains unclear whether any cognitive disturbances reflect negative mood or a more direct effect of hormonal dysregulation or sensitivity.

title: Menstrual Cycle Effects on Sleep
plain_language: Sleep often gets worse before and during periods, especially for people with premenstrual symptoms or painful periods.
key_finding: Subjective and objective sleep changes occur during the menstrual cycle; poorer sleep quality in the premenstrual phase and menstruation is common in women with premenstrual symptoms or painful cramps. Luteal changes include blunted temperature rhythm amplitude and reduced REM sleep; menstrual cycle phase and menstrual disorders should be considered when assessing women's sleep complaints.

title: The high-sweet-fat food craving among women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder: emotional response, implicit attitude and rewards sensitivity
plain_language: Cravings for sweet, fatty foods rose before periods, and more so in women with PMDD.
key_finding: The luteal phase was associated with higher food and high-sweet-fat food cravings; women with PMDD had higher reward sensitivity and greater emotional, implicit and craving responses to high-sweet-fat foods than controls.

title: Perimenstrual exacerbation of symptoms in borderline personality disorder: evidence from multilevel models and the Carolina Premenstrual Assessment Scoring System
plain_language: In a small daily-diary study, borderline personality symptoms tended to worsen around periods, without the women having PMDD.
key_finding: Most symptoms showed midluteal worsening, a perimenstrual peak and resolution in the follicular or ovulatory phase; depressive symptoms showed a delayed pattern with exacerbations in both the perimenstrual and follicular phases. Most participants met C-PASS criteria for clinically significant (30% or more) exacerbation, and none met DSM-5 PMDD criteria. The authors conclude females with BPD may be at elevated risk for perimenstrual worsening of emotional symptoms.

title: Exacerbation of Psychosis During the Perimenstrual Phase of the Menstrual Cycle: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
plain_language: People with psychotic disorders were admitted to hospital more often around their periods than would be expected by chance.
key_finding: Psychiatric admission rates in the perimenstrual phase were 1.48 times higher than expected (95% CI 1.31-1.67); 4 of 6 symptom-score studies reported perimenstrual worsening, and self-reported menstrual exacerbation prevalence ranged from 20% to 32.4%. The authors call for more precise research.

title: Effects of the menstrual cycle on bipolar disorder
plain_language: Some women with bipolar disorder notice mood episodes linked to their cycle, which can look like PMDD.
key_finding: Retrospective studies suggest 25-77% of women with bipolar disorder meet PMS criteria and 15-27% PMDD criteria; menstrual cycle-related mood changes were displayed by 44-65% of women in prospective studies, and 64% of case reports involved premenstrual hypomanic or manic episodes. A subgroup may experience cycle effects on depressive, hypomanic and manic episodes.

title: Why are women so vulnerable to anxiety, trauma-related and stress-related disorders? The potential role of sex hormones
plain_language: Ovarian hormones may help explain why anxiety disorders are more common and persistent in women.
key_finding: Proposes that oestradiol and progesterone influence sex differences in anxiety disorders through two broad mechanisms: augmenting vulnerability factors for developing anxiety disorders and facilitating maintenance of anxious symptoms after development.

title: What we know about primary dysmenorrhea today: a critical review
plain_language: Painful periods are common, often dismissed, and linked to wider pain sensitivity, poorer mood and poorer sleep during periods.
key_finding: Primary dysmenorrhea affects between 45 and 95% of menstruating women and is often poorly treated or disregarded. Women with dysmenorrhea have greater sensitivity to experimental pain, even outside menstruation, and dysmenorrhea is a risk factor for fibromyalgia; they have reduced quality of life, poorer mood and poorer sleep during menstruation.

title: Does pain vary across the menstrual cycle? A review
plain_language: Existing pain conditions can vary across the cycle, but healthy women don't reliably feel pain differently at different cycle phases.
key_finding: Several clinical pain conditions show variation in symptom severity across the menstrual cycle, but most recent well-controlled studies show cycle phase has no effect on experimental pain perception in healthy, pain-free women.

title: Menstrual Cycle Effects on Mental Health Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Serious mental health crises cluster around and just before periods.
key_finding: Found 26% greater risk of suicide deaths, 17% greater risk of suicide attempts and 20% greater risk of psychiatric admissions at menstruation, and 13% greater risk of psychiatric admissions in the premenstrual phase; suicidal ideation was unrelated to cycle stage.

title: Menstrual cycle-driven vs noncyclical daily changes in sexual desire
plain_language: Sexual desire shifts across the cycle differently for different people.
key_finding: On average there was a small midcycle increase in sexual desire, but large individual differences: some showed a midcycle increase, others a perimenstrual increase and others no change; psychological changes predicted sexual desire more than physical changes.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the comorbidity of premenstrual dysphoric disorder or premenstrual syndrome with mood disorders: prevalence, clinical and neurobiological correlates
plain_language: Around four in ten people with depression or bipolar disorder also have premenstrual disorders in these studies.
key_finding: Pooled comorbidity between PMDD/PMS and mood disorders was consistently high, from 42% (95% CI 30-55%) to 49% (95% CI 38-60%) across sampling strategies; limitations include heterogeneity, cross-sectional designs and provisional PMDD/PMS diagnoses.

title: Prospective daily evidence of cyclic suicidality and self-harm in premenstrual disorders
plain_language: Daily tracking showed suicidal and self-harm thoughts rose before periods, eased when bleeding began and could return around ovulation.
key_finding: Suicidal (deviance explained = 38%) and self-harm (21.6%) ideation showed significant menstrual cyclicity, peaking in the late luteal phase, improving by menses onset and re-emerging around ovulation; cyclicity was significant only in participants above PMD diagnostic threshold, and psychosocial factors shaped the pattern.

title: Perceived associations between the menstrual cycle and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A qualitative interview study exploring lived experiences
plain_language: People with ADHD described their ADHD getting worse in the second half of their cycle.
key_finding: Participants perceived ADHD symptoms as more severe during the mid-luteal phase, reported uncertainty about ADHD medication in relation to the cycle, varied healthcare experiences and heightened challenges with menstrual health management.

title: Burden of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder on Health-Related Quality of Life
plain_language: Quality of life for people at risk of PMDD was well below average, similar to some chronic physical illnesses.
key_finding: Six SF-12v2 scales and both summary measures were significantly below adjusted US norms; the burden was greater on mental/emotional than physical health-related quality of life and comparable to osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis on all scales. The authors conclude PMDD is associated with substantial physical and mental burden.

title: Premenstrual syndrome and alcohol consumption: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Drinking alcohol was linked to higher odds of PMS, more so with heavy drinking; direction of cause is not established.
key_finding: Alcohol intake was associated with a moderate increase in the risk of PMS (OR=1.45, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.79), and heavy drinking with a larger increase (OR=1.79, 1.39 to 2.32); the authors call for non-cross-sectional designs.

title: Thyroid function in women with premenstrual syndrome
journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
plain_language: A minority of women with PMS had thyroid problems, but thyroid medicine did not treat PMS.
key_finding: 13 women (10.5%) had basal evidence of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism and eight (13%) had elevated thyroid autoantibodies; L-T4 was not superior to placebo for PMS. The authors conclude PMS is not simply masked hypothyroidism, though thyroid abnormalities appear more often than expected.

title: Female sex steroids and epilepsy: Part 2. A practical and human focus on catamenial epilepsy
plain_language: Some people's seizures cluster at certain points of the cycle; tracking seizures against the cycle is the main way to see this.
key_finding: Catamenial epilepsy is the best described sex steroid-specific seizure exacerbation, yet there are no evidence-based treatments or accepted diagnostic tool; tracking seizures over menstrual cycles is the best current tool, and seizure severity as well as frequency can be tracked.

title: How does premenstrual dysphoric disorder relate to depression and anxiety disorders?
plain_language: PMDD looks most like irritability and mood swings, not just depression or anxiety arriving monthly.
key_finding: Concludes PMDD is neither a variant of depression nor an anxiety disorder but a distinct entity, with irritability and affect lability rather than depressed mood or anxiety as the most characteristic features, while noting similarities with panic disorder.

title: Understanding premenstrual dysphoric disorder from a psychosomatic and a sensory perspective
plain_language: A review suggests sensory sensitivity and trauma history may shape how intense PMDD feels; this is a proposal, not settled evidence.
key_finding: Proposes a trauma-informed sensory framework in which heightened sensory processing and altered interoceptive awareness amplify symptom severity in the luteal phase, and recommends assessing trauma history and sensory reactivity.

title: Menstrual Cycle-Related Hormonal Fluctuations in ADHD: Effect on Cognitive Functioning-A Narrative Review
plain_language: Small studies suggest attention and self-control dip in the second half of the cycle for women with ADHD or premenstrual disorders.
key_finding: Four studies in women with ADHD and six in women with PMS or PMDD consistently observed impairments in attention, executive function and impulsivity during the mid-luteal and premenstrual phases, paralleling subjective reports of worsened cognition, heightened mood symptoms and diminished medication efficacy; findings remain preliminary and sometimes contradictory.

title: Changes in ADHD Symptoms and Mood Across the Menstrual Cycle in Females Treated With Stimulants: A Pilot Study
plain_language: In a small pilot, ADHD symptoms on stimulants were worst during periods and best in the week or so after.
key_finding: ADHD symptoms were significantly associated with cycle phase, most severe in the menstruation phase and comparatively milder in the mid-follicular phase; the difference correlated with changes in negative mood.

title: The effects of intermittent escitalopram treatment on impulsivity and inattention in women with premenstrual irritability and anger
plain_language: In women with strong premenstrual irritability, impulsive urgency was higher before periods.
key_finding: Escitalopram reduced self-rated luteal irritability and anger and, on a continuous performance test, lowered anticipatory responses and increased response-speed consistency; on placebo, participants reported higher urgency and lower sensation seeking in the luteal than follicular phase.

title: Autism, menstruation and mental health- a scoping review and a call to action
plain_language: Research on periods and mental health in autistic people is thin but points to real difficulties.
key_finding: Key themes were the mental health impact of menstruation, menstrual disorders among autistic individuals, and support strategies and healthcare use; knowledge is scant but raises significant concerns, framed within a biopsychosocial model.

title: Risk factors for premenstrual asthma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Some people's asthma gets worse before their period.
key_finding: Premenstrual asthma is deterioration of asthma symptoms or peak flow in the premenstrual phase; women with it are older, have more severe asthma, higher BMI and longer asthma duration, and more often have dysmenorrhea, premenstrual syndrome, shorter cycles and longer bleeding.

title: Females with ADHD: An expert consensus statement taking a lifespan approach providing guidance for the identification and treatment of attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder in girls and women
plain_language: A panel of experts agreed that ADHD in girls and women is often quieter and hidden by coping strategies, so doctors need to look for it differently and keep looking across a woman's life.
key_finding: UK ADHD Partnership expert consensus: barriers to recognising ADHD in girls and women include symptom differences, gender bias, comorbidities and compensatory strategies that mask symptoms; recommends attending to the subtler, internalised presentation and a lifespan model of care.

title: Updated European Consensus Statement on diagnosis and treatment of adult ADHD
plain_language: Sixty-three European experts agreed that ADHD often lasts into adulthood, is often missed in adults, and can be diagnosed and treated effectively.
key_finding: Consensus of 63 experts (European Network Adult ADHD/EPA): ADHD often persists as a lifelong impairing condition but is under-diagnosed and under-treated in adults; validated screening/diagnostic instruments and effective evidence-based treatments exist; more research needed on gender differences.

title: The World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement: 208 Evidence-based conclusions about the disorder
plain_language: Eighty experts from 27 countries listed 208 facts about ADHD that are backed by large, strong studies, to counter common myths.
key_finding: World Federation of ADHD consensus of 208 empirically supported statements, drawn only from meta-analyses or studies with >2,000 participants, approved by 80 authors from 27 countries; intended to correct common misconceptions about the nature, course, causes and treatment of ADHD.

title: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: A major overview concludes ADHD is mostly inherited, can be reliably diagnosed, and while there is no cure, treatments substantially reduce symptoms.
key_finding: Disease Primer: ADHD has a predominantly genetic aetiology; diagnosis is reliable and valid with standard criteria; no cure exists, but medications are effective for core symptoms and usually well tolerated, and some non-drug treatments help adaptive functioning.

title: Adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: key conceptual issues
plain_language: Experts argue that adult ADHD should be recognised like other common adult mental health conditions, and that missing it harms many people who seek help for common mental health problems.
key_finding: Conceptual review: ADHD symptoms and impairments affect adults, who respond to medication and psychosocial treatment similarly to children; argues adult ADHD should be recognised like other common adult mental disorders, as failure to treat it harms many patients seeking help for common mental health problems.

title: Annual Research Review: Attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder in girls and women: underrepresentation, longitudinal processes, and key directions
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Girls meet ADHD criteria at just under half the rate of boys, but by adulthood the ratio is much closer to equal, and women with ADHD face serious risks such as self-harm and problems in close relationships.
key_finding: Narrative review: girls meet ADHD criteria at just under half the rate of boys, approaching parity by adulthood; females show more inattention and internalising problems, are often overlooked because of less overt symptoms and compensatory strategies, and are at heightened risk of self-harm, relationship problems, intimate partner violence and unplanned pregnancy.

title: Why are females less likely to be diagnosed with ADHD in childhood than males?
plain_language: This paper explores why girls are diagnosed later and less often than boys, considering biology, how diagnosis is done, and social factors such as differences in presentation and compensating behaviours.
key_finding: Personal View (conceptual review): females are diagnosed with ADHD less often and later than males and are less often prescribed medication; considers biological explanations, diagnostic practices (criteria suitability, diagnostic overshadowing, thresholds) and sociocultural factors (presentation, compensatory behaviours).

title: Gender differences in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A narrative review
plain_language: Across 73 studies, gender was linked to several features of adult ADHD, but many of these differences may partly come from how studies were done or from social and cultural influences rather than real differences in ADHD itself.
key_finding: Review of 73 studies on gender and adult ADHD: many observed gender differences (prevalence, comorbidity, impairment, cognition, treatment response) may be partly due to methodological artefacts or social/cultural influences rather than fundamental differences in how ADHD is expressed in men and women.

title: Meta-Analysis of Sex Differences in ADHD Symptoms and Associated Cognitive Deficits
plain_language: In children with ADHD, boys tend to be more physically restless than girls, but girls and boys have similar thinking and planning difficulties.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of studies (1997-2017) in children and adolescents: boys with ADHD were more hyperactive and had more difficulty with motor response inhibition and cognitive flexibility than girls with ADHD; executive deficits relative to non-ADHD peers did not differ by sex.

title: Sex differences in predicting ADHD clinical diagnosis and pharmacological treatment
plain_language: In a study of 19,804 Swedish children, disruptive behaviour predicted diagnosis and treatment more strongly in girls than in boys, suggesting girls without such behaviour may be more easily missed.
key_finding: In 19,804 Swedish twins assessed at age 9, hyperactivity/impulsivity and conduct problems were stronger predictors of clinical ADHD diagnosis (conduct OR 1.43) and medication (conduct OR 2.20) in girls than boys; females with ADHD may be more easily missed unless they have prominent externalising problems.

title: The Prevalence and Correlates of Adult ADHD in the United States: Results From the National Comorbidity Survey Replication
plain_language: An estimated 4.4% of US adults aged 18-44 had current ADHD, and most of them were untreated for it.
key_finding: Nationally representative US survey (n=3,199 aged 18-44; 154 clinical reappraisal interviews): estimated current adult ADHD prevalence 4.4%; highly comorbid and impairing; most cases untreated for ADHD although many had received treatment for other mental or substance disorders.

title: Is Adult ADHD a Childhood-Onset Neurodevelopmental Disorder? Evidence From a Four-Decade Longitudinal Cohort Study
plain_language: In one New Zealand group followed for 38 years, 90% of adults with ADHD had no history of childhood ADHD, raising the possibility that adult ADHD is not always a childhood-onset condition; the authors say this needs replication.
key_finding: In the Dunedin birth cohort (n=1,037, followed to age 38), childhood ADHD (6%) and adult ADHD (3%) groups were almost non-overlapping: 90% of adult cases had no history of childhood ADHD and showed no childhood neuropsychological deficits or polygenic risk for ADHD.

title: Evaluation of the Persistence, Remission, and Emergence of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Young Adulthood
plain_language: In a large British twin study, 21.9% of children with ADHD still met criteria at 18, and 67.5% of 18-year-olds with ADHD had not met criteria at any childhood assessment yet had comparable symptoms and impairment.
key_finding: In the E-Risk twin cohort (2,040 analysed), 21.9% of 247 children with ADHD still met criteria at 18, while 67.5% of 166 young adults with ADHD had not met criteria at any childhood assessment; these late-onset cases had comparable symptoms, impairment and mental health problems at 18.

title: Late-Onset ADHD Reconsidered With Comprehensive Repeated Assessments Between Ages 10 and 25
plain_language: When people were followed carefully from childhood, most adults who seemed to develop ADHD late actually had other explanations, so ADHD that truly starts in adulthood looks rare.
key_finding: Among 239 people without childhood ADHD assessed 8 times from mean age 9.89 to 24.40 years, approximately 95% of those who initially screened positive were excluded from a late-onset ADHD diagnosis; among those with impairing late-onset symptoms the most common reason for exclusion was symptoms occurring only with heavy substance use; there was no evidence for adult-onset ADHD independent of a complex psychiatric history.

title: Variable Patterns of Remission From ADHD in the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD
plain_language: Following 558 children into their mid-20s showed ADHD usually comes and goes rather than simply disappearing, and only 9.1% recovered for good.
key_finding: In 558 children with ADHD followed to mean age 25, ~30% fully remitted at some point but 60% of those later recurred; only 9.1% showed sustained recovery and 63.8% had fluctuating remission and recurrence; 90% still had residual symptoms in young adulthood.

title: Mind wandering perspective on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Researchers suggest that a constantly wandering mind may be at the heart of ADHD, but this is an idea still being tested.
key_finding: Review proposing the mind-wandering hypothesis: altered default mode network deactivation and its interaction with executive control networks lead to excessive spontaneous mind wandering, which may underpin ADHD symptoms and impairments.

title: Validation of the Mind Excessively Wandering Scale and the Relationship of Mind Wandering to Impairment in Adult ADHD
plain_language: A short questionnaire about a restless, wandering mind picked out adults with ADHD well, and this mind wandering added to their day-to-day difficulties.
key_finding: Using data from two adult ADHD studies, the Mind Excessively Wandering Scale showed good internal consistency (alpha >.9) and ~.9 sensitivity and specificity for ADHD diagnosis; excessive mind wandering contributed to impairment independently of core ADHD symptoms.

title: Living “in the zone”: hyperfocus in adult ADHD
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: Adults with more ADHD traits reported more episodes of getting deeply absorbed in tasks, hobbies or screens, based on a new questionnaire.
key_finding: New Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire tested in a pilot (n=251) and preregistered replication sample (n=372): higher ADHD symptoms were associated with more total and dispositional hyperfocus and more frequent hyperfocus at school, in hobbies and during screen time.

title: The dual pathway model of AD/HD: an elaboration of neuro-developmental characteristics
plain_language: This theory says ADHD can arise through two routes: difficulties controlling thinking and behaviour, and a strong motivation to escape or avoid waiting.
key_finding: Theoretical paper elaborating the dual-pathway model: executive dysfunction (fronto-dorsal striatal circuits) and delay aversion (a motivational style of escaping delay, linked to fronto-ventral striatal reward circuits) as complementary routes to ADHD with different developmental pathways.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Monetary Delay Discounting: A Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies
journal: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
plain_language: Across many studies, people with ADHD more often preferred a smaller reward now over a bigger one later.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 25 case-control comparisons (21 studies, N=3,913): people with ADHD discounted delayed monetary rewards more steeply than controls (d=0.43, described as medium), with no differences by age, real vs hypothetical rewards or comorbidity and minimal heterogeneity.

title: Timing deficits in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): Evidence from neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies
plain_language: People with ADHD often have real difficulties sensing and judging time, and this seems to be its own problem, not just a side effect of poor attention.
key_finding: Review: people with ADHD are consistently impaired in motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight (most consistently sensorimotor synchronisation, duration discrimination/reproduction and delay discounting), with fronto-striato-cerebellar network dysfunction; deficits appear independent of other executive functions and methylphenidate attenuates most of them.

title: Report of a Work Group on Sluggish Cognitive Tempo: Key Research Directions and a Consensus Change in Terminology to Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Experts renamed 'sluggish cognitive tempo' as 'cognitive disengagement syndrome' and concluded it is now recognised as a distinct syndrome, though much about it is still unclear.
key_finding: International work group reviewed research on sluggish cognitive tempo and renamed it cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS), concluding it has reached the threshold of recognition as a distinct syndrome while its exact nature (separate disorder, transdiagnostic factor or specifier) remains unclear.

title: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
plain_language: Pooling 133 trials showed ADHD medicines outperform placebo in the short term, with methylphenidate preferred for children and amphetamines for adults, though long-term evidence is lacking.
key_finding: Network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind RCTs: in adults (clinician ratings) amphetamines, methylphenidate, bupropion and atomoxetine but not modafinil beat placebo at timepoints closest to 12 weeks; weighing efficacy and safety, methylphenidate is the preferred first choice for children and adolescents and amphetamines for adults short term; data for 26 and 52 weeks were insufficient.

title: Comparative efficacy and acceptability of pharmacological, psychological, and neurostimulatory interventions for ADHD in adults: a systematic review and component network meta-analysis
plain_language: Across 113 adult trials, stimulant medicines and atomoxetine were the treatments that most clearly reduced ADHD symptoms in the short term; talking therapies showed mixed results.
key_finding: Component network meta-analysis of 113 RCTs (14,887 adults, 45.6% female): only stimulants and atomoxetine reduced core symptoms at 12 weeks on both self- and clinician-rated scales; CBT, mindfulness, psychoeducation, cognitive remediation and tDCS helped only on clinician ratings; atomoxetine was less acceptable than placebo; longer-term evidence is lacking.

title: ADHD Pharmacotherapy and Mortality in Individuals With ADHD
plain_language: In a Swedish study of 148,578 people with ADHD, those who started ADHD medication had a lower risk of dying in the next two years, particularly from unnatural causes such as injuries, suicide and accidental poisonings; this is an association from observational data.
key_finding: Swedish target-trial emulation (n=148,578; 41.3% female): starting ADHD medication within 3 months of diagnosis was associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality (39.1 vs 48.1 per 10,000; HR 0.79), driven by unnatural causes (HR 0.75) but not natural causes.

title: Mortality in children, adolescents, and adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a nationwide cohort study
plain_language: In Denmark, people with ADHD had about double the death rate of people without it (rate ratio 2.07), mostly from accidents, and the excess was larger for girls and women once other conditions were accounted for.
key_finding: Danish national cohort (1.92 million, 32,061 with ADHD): mortality rate 5.85 vs 2.21 per 10,000 person-years (fully adjusted MRR 2.07), mainly driven by unnatural causes, especially accidents; MRR was highest for those diagnosed at age 18 or older (4.25); after excluding people with ODD, conduct disorder and substance use disorder, MRR remained raised (1.50) and was higher in girls and women (2.85) than boys and men (1.27).

title: An evidenced-based perspective on the validity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in the context of high intelligence
plain_language: A review found limited but consistent evidence that ADHD is a valid diagnosis in very bright people too; their coping strategies may make it easier to miss.
key_finding: Systematic review: limited evidence suggests ADHD is a valid construct in high-intelligence individuals, with characteristic clinical features, course, outcome and treatment response (hyperactivity possibly less specific); compensatory strategies may increase risk of a missed diagnosis, and ADHD and IQ are negatively correlated on nearly all constructs.

title: Is attention deficit hyperactivity disorder a valid diagnosis in the presence of high IQ? Results from the MGH Longitudinal Family Studies of ADHD
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Very bright children with ADHD still struggled more than other bright children, and their ADHD looked like ADHD in other children.
key_finding: Among high-IQ (>=120) children, 49 with ADHD vs 92 without showed more familial ADHD, grade repetition, comorbid psychopathology and functional impairment, a pattern consistent with ADHD in average-IQ children, supporting diagnostic validity.

title: Is adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder a valid diagnosis in the presence of high IQ?
plain_language: Very bright adults with ADHD had more problems at work, at home and on the road than equally bright adults without ADHD.
key_finding: Among high-IQ (>=120) adults, 64 with ADHD vs 53 without had lower quality of life, poorer family and occupational functioning, more speeding tickets, accidents and arrests, more depression, OCD and GAD, and more ADHD in relatives, paralleling average-IQ adult ADHD.

title: Executive functioning in high-IQ adults with ADHD
plain_language: Bright adults with ADHD scored lower on planning and attention tests than other bright adults, even though their scores looked 'normal' compared with everyone else.
key_finding: High-IQ adults with ADHD (n=64) performed worse than high-IQ controls (n=53) on several executive function tests (WCST, Stroop, ROCF, CVLT, CPT), although their scores were in the average range; several test scores predicted real-world functioning.

title: Executive Function Impairments in High IQ Adults With ADHD
plain_language: Most very bright adults with ADHD in this study (73%) had clear executive function impairments despite their high IQ.
key_finding: In 157 adults with ADHD and IQ >=120, 73% were significantly impaired on at least 5 of 8 normed executive function measures (test indices and self-report), with impairment rates higher than in the general population on all 8.

title: High IQ May “Mask” the Diagnosis of ADHD by Compensating for Deficits in Executive Functions in Treatment-Naïve Adults With ADHD
plain_language: In a small study, adults with ADHD and higher IQ looked almost normal on thinking tests, which could make their ADHD harder to spot.
key_finding: 51 treatment-naive adults with ADHD split by IQ (>=110 vs <110) were compared with 33 healthy controls: the standard-IQ group was impaired on many executive tests, whereas the higher-IQ group differed from controls only on CPT commission errors, suggesting higher IQ may compensate and complicate diagnosis.

title: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder in Children With High Intelligence Quotient: Results From a Population-Based Study
plain_language: Children with ADHD and high IQ had much the same ADHD-related problems as other children with ADHD, though they read better.
key_finding: In a population birth cohort (N=5,718; 379 with ADHD), children with ADHD and high IQ (n=34) did not differ from normal- or low-IQ peers with ADHD in age at meeting criteria, comorbid learning, psychiatric or substance disorders, or stimulant treatment, but had better reading achievement.

title: Empirical Investigation of Twice-Exceptionality: Where Have We Been and Where Are We Going?
plain_language: Research shows gifted students can also have ADHD or other conditions, but we know little about how best to help them.
key_finding: 20-year review of empirical research on gifted students with learning disabilities, ADHD or autism: research strongly suggests gifted students can have a coexisting disability and need comprehensive, individualised diagnosis; little is known about effective interventions.

title: Skills and compensation strategies in adult ADHD – A qualitative study
plain_language: Adults with ADHD described many self-made coping strategies they used before diagnosis, several of which they found helpful; knowing about them may help explain why ADHD is sometimes diagnosed late.
key_finding: Interviews with 32 adult outpatients with ADHD: before diagnosis they used diverse compensatory strategies (organisational, motoric, attentional, social, psychopharmacological) of varying effectiveness, several perceived as helpful, and sometimes saw ADHD symptoms as useful; such coping may help explain late or under-diagnosis.

title: Miss. Diagnosis: A Systematic Review of ADHD in Adult Women
plain_language: Women who learned they had ADHD as adults described strain on emotional wellbeing, difficult relationships and feeling out of control, with self-acceptance after diagnosis emerging as a theme.
key_finding: Thematic synthesis of 8 studies on women living with undiagnosed ADHD and adult diagnosis: four themes were impacts on social-emotional wellbeing, difficult relationships, lack of control, and self-acceptance after diagnosis.

title: A Review of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Women and Girls
journal: The Primary Care Companion For CNS Disorders
plain_language: Doing well at school does not rule out ADHD in girls and women, whose symptoms are often quieter and mixed up with anxiety or depression.
key_finding: Review (41 articles from a 2012 search of the previous 10 years): girls' inattentive presentation is often considered 'subthreshold'; females may develop coping strategies that mask symptoms; comorbid anxiety and depression can lead to missed or misdiagnosis; hormonal effects raise unique issues; satisfactory academic achievement should not rule out ADHD.

title: Gender differences in psychiatric comorbidity: a population‐based study of 40 000 adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: In Norway, the extra burden of anxiety, depression, bipolar and personality disorders linked to ADHD was larger in women, while the extra burden of substance problems and schizophrenia was larger in men.
key_finding: Norwegian registry study of 40,103 adults with ADHD (44% women) vs 1,661,103 adults: prevalence differences associated with ADHD were larger in women for anxiety, depression (24.4 vs 13.1), bipolar and personality disorders, and larger in men for schizophrenia and substance use disorder.

title: Anxiety, mood, and substance use disorders in adult men and women with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A substantive and methodological overview
plain_language: Adults with ADHD had 4.5 to 8.7 times higher odds of also having anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder or substance problems, and this held for both women and men.
key_finding: Overview of large studies (n>10,000) with meta-analysis (550,748 with vs 14,546,814 without ADHD): pooled ORs 5.0 for anxiety, 4.5 for major depression, 8.7 for bipolar and 4.6 for substance use disorders; sex did not moderate these, with women showing higher anxiety, depression and bipolar prevalence and men higher SUD, as in the general population.

title: Differential diagnosis, comorbidity, and treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in relation to bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder in adults
plain_language: ADHD can look like bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder, and this paper explains the differences so people get the right diagnosis and treatment.
key_finding: Expert review: ADHD co-occurs in ~20% of adults with bipolar disorder or BPD; BD is episodic whereas ADHD and BPD are chronic and trait-like; BPD but not ADHD involves frantic avoidance of abandonment, suicidal behaviour, self-harm, chronic emptiness and stress-related paranoia/dissociation; recommends treating BD episodes first in comorbid cases.

title: Differential diagnosis and comorbidity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) in adults
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
plain_language: ADHD and borderline personality disorder share several features and often occur together, and some researchers think they may be related.
key_finding: Review: adult ADHD and BPD share impulsivity, emotional dysregulation and cognitive impairment, frequently co-occur, and both respond to DBT-based therapy; raises the hypothesis that in some patients they may be two dimensions of one disorder.

title: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) revisited – a review-update on common grounds and subtle distinctions
journal: Borderline Personality Disorder and Emotion Dysregulation
plain_language: ADHD and borderline personality disorder overlap a lot, especially in impulsiveness and emotional difficulties, but differ in subtle ways that may call for different treatment approaches.
key_finding: Review update: impulsivity and emotion dysregulation feature in both ADHD and BPD and are highest in people with both; BPD impulsivity is more stress-dependent while ADHD involves more motor impulsivity; adverse childhood events are linked to both; a population study confirmed high co-occurrence and familial co-aggregation.

title: Emotion dysregulation in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and borderline personality disorder
journal: Borderline Personality Disorder and Emotion Dysregulation
plain_language: This review looks at how emotional ups and downs show up in both ADHD and borderline personality disorder, and how tracking moods in daily life might help tell them apart.
key_finding: Narrative review of ADHD-BPD overlap focusing on emotion dysregulation: discusses unique and shared diagnostic criteria, ecological momentary assessment as a way to distinguish the disorders, shared and unique genetic/environmental risk factors, and treatment implications.

title: Emotion Dysregulation in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Strong emotional reactions are common in ADHD at every age and cause real problems, and ADHD treatment often helps with them.
key_finding: Review: emotion dysregulation is prevalent in ADHD across the lifespan and a major contributor to impairment; it may arise from deficits in orienting to and processing emotional stimuli (striato-amygdalo-medial prefrontal network); ADHD treatments often help it; three models of the overlap are proposed.

title: Practitioner Review: Emotional dysregulation in attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder – implications for clinical recognition and intervention
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Experts say emotional difficulties are a common and lasting part of ADHD, and some argue they should count as a core symptom.
key_finding: Practitioner review: emotional symptoms are common, persistent and impairing in youth and adults with ADHD; emotional impulsivity and deficient emotional self-regulation may be specific enough to serve as diagnostic criteria, but there is no consensus on how to define them.

title: Emotion dysregulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis
plain_language: Pooling 13 studies, adults with ADHD had much more trouble managing emotions than other adults, especially quick mood changes.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 13 studies (N=2,535): adults with ADHD had higher general emotion dysregulation than healthy controls (Hedges' g=1.17), strongest for emotional lability (g=1.20); ADHD severity correlated with ED (r=0.54).

title: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and children's emotion dysregulation: A meta-analysis
plain_language: Across 77 studies, children with ADHD had much bigger and harder-to-manage emotional reactions than other children.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 77 studies (n=32,044 youths): youth with ADHD showed the greatest impairment in emotion reactivity/negativity/lability (d=.95), then emotion regulation (d=.80), with smaller effects for empathy/callous-unemotional traits (d=.68) and emotion recognition (d=.64).

title: ADHD and Emotion Dysregulation Among Children and Adolescents
journal: Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review
plain_language: Early evidence links emotional difficulties in young people with ADHD to social problems and risk-taking, but many basic questions are still open.
key_finding: Critical review of ADHD and emotion dysregulation in youth: preliminary evidence links ED to social impairment and risky behaviours and to treatment response, but the proportion of youth with ADHD who have ED, its role in impairment and whether it is changeable remain unclear.

title: Emotional lability, comorbidity and impairment in adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: In a small study of men, quick mood changes seemed to come from ADHD itself rather than other conditions and made daily life harder.
key_finding: Comparing 41 men with ADHD (no comorbidity, medication or frequent substance use) with 47 healthy men: emotional lability was elevated, best predicted by hyperactivity-impulsivity rather than subsyndromal comorbid symptoms, and contributed independently to everyday impairment.

title: Everyday emotional experience of adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: evidence for reactive and endogenous emotional lability
plain_language: When men with ADHD tracked their moods several times a day, they felt more irritation and frustration, sometimes triggered by events and sometimes not.
key_finding: Eight-times-daily ambulatory ratings over a working week in 41 men with ADHD vs 47 controls: ADHD group reported more bad events and greater intensity and instability of irritability and frustration and greater anger; findings suggest both a reactive component (to bad events) and an endogenous component of emotional lability.

title: Emotional dysregulation is a primary symptom in adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
plain_language: In one clinic sample, emotional difficulties and self-image problems fit alongside classic ADHD symptoms as part of the adult picture.
key_finding: Confirmatory factor analysis in 213 newly diagnosed adults (62.9% male): a 7-factor model treating affect, self-concept problems and emotion regulation skills as distinct but correlated with inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity fitted well; the sample was highly comorbid (47.9%).

title: Pharmacotherapy of emotional dysregulation in adults with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: ADHD medicines had small-to-moderate effects on adults' emotional regulation, and may be less effective for emotions than for core ADHD symptoms.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 21 double-blind RCTs in adults: ADHD medications had small-to-moderate effects on emotional dysregulation (methylphenidate SMD 0.34, atomoxetine 0.24, lisdexamfetamine 0.50), suggesting they may be less effective for ED than for core symptoms.

title: Effects of stimulants and atomoxetine on emotional lability in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: ADHD medicines eased mood swings in adults, but only about half as much as they eased core ADHD symptoms.
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 9 placebo-controlled RCTs in adults with ADHD: stimulants and atomoxetine moderately reduced emotional lability (SMD -0.41) versus a twice-as-large effect on core ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.8), suggesting adjunctive psychotherapy may be needed for some.

title: Implications of rejection sensitivity for intimate relationships.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
plain_language: This classic study (not about ADHD) showed that people who expect rejection tend to see it in ambiguous situations, which can strain relationships.
key_finding: Four studies defined rejection sensitivity as a disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive and overreact to rejection, developed a measure, showed high-RS people perceive intentional rejection in ambiguous or insensitive behaviour, and found RS linked to relationship dissatisfaction in both partners. (Not an ADHD study.)

title: Rejection Sensitivity and Social Outcomes of Young Adult Men With ADHD
plain_language: In a small study of college men, those with ADHD were not more sensitive to rejection, though they had lower self-esteem.
key_finding: In undergraduate men (31 combined-type ADHD, 22 inattentive-type, 25 controls), the hypothesis that men with ADHD would have elevated rejection sensitivity was not supported; both ADHD groups reported lower self-esteem than controls, and inattentive-type men reported more negative relational outcomes than combined-type peers.

title: Justice and rejection sensitivity in children and adolescents with ADHD symptoms
plain_language: Teenagers with more ADHD symptoms felt more hurt by unfairness and rejection, which may partly explain their other difficulties.
key_finding: In 1,235 German 10-19-year-olds, those with ADHD symptoms reported higher victim justice sensitivity, more perceived injustice and higher anxious and angry rejection sensitivity; justice and rejection sensitivity partially mediated links between ADHD symptoms and comorbid problems.

title: Experiences of criticism in adults with ADHD: A qualitative study
plain_language: Adults with ADHD said they were often criticised, especially for being forgetful or distracted, and that this hurt their sense of self-worth.
key_finding: Thematic analysis of written responses from 162 adults with ADHD or high ADHD traits: inattentive behaviours were perceived as most criticised; criticism harmed self-worth and wellbeing; coping included avoidance or changing reactions; feeling understood shaped whether criticism was perceived.

title: Adult ADHD and romantic relationships: What we know and what we can do to help
journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
plain_language: Research suggests adults with ADHD often have shorter and more troubled romantic relationships, and this review looks at why and what might help.
key_finding: Review: much research indicates adults with ADHD have short-lived and discordant romantic relationships; summarises established ADHD vs non-ADHD differences and distal/proximal risk factors for relationship distress, and identifies gaps and implications for prevention and intervention.

title: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms and loneliness among adults in the general population
plain_language: Adults who screened positive for ADHD symptoms had 2.48 times the odds of feeling lonely, and over one-third of this link was explained by common mental disorders such as anxiety and depression.
key_finding: In the 2007 English Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (N=7,403), screening positive for ADHD symptoms (ASRS >=14) was strongly associated with loneliness (OR 2.48), with a dose-response by severity; over one-third of the association was explained by common mental disorders.

title: The self-esteem of adults diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a systematic review of the literature
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: Adults with ADHD tend to have lower self-esteem, and therapy may help improve it to some extent, though the evidence is limited.
key_finding: Systematic review of 13 studies (1980-2013): despite few studies and methodological concerns, ADHD is associated with lower self-esteem in adulthood, and self-esteem can be improved to some extent by psychotherapeutic work.

title: Self-Esteem in Adults With ADHD Using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale: A Systematic Review
plain_language: Most studies found adults with ADHD have lower self-esteem, and this was similar for women and men.
key_finding: Systematic review of 11 studies using the Rosenberg scale (2010-2022): 5 of 6 controlled studies found lower self-esteem in adults with ADHD; ADHD symptoms correlated negatively with self-esteem; no gender differences; confounders were rarely controlled.

title: Prospective follow-up of girls with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder into early adulthood: Continuing impairment includes elevated risk for suicide attempts and self-injury.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
plain_language: Girls with ADHD followed into young adulthood had higher rates of suicide attempts and self-injury, concentrated in those with the combined type.
key_finding: 10-year follow-up (95% retention) of 140 girls with ADHD and 88 matched comparisons into ages 17-24: the ADHD group had more symptoms and impairment and higher rates of suicide attempts and self-injury (medium to very large effects), concentrated in combined type; no differences in eating pathology, substance use or driving.

title: Girls with childhood ADHD as adults: Cross-domain outcomes by diagnostic persistence.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
plain_language: Women who had ADHD as girls faced more problems as adults, and even those whose symptoms faded still had some lasting disadvantages.
key_finding: 16-year follow-up of 140 girls with ADHD and 88 comparisons: childhood ADHD, whether remitted or persistent, predicted lower education, unplanned pregnancy, higher BMI and clinician-rated impairment; persistent ADHD added externalising, internalising, self-injury, occupational and social problems; no association with objective employment, substance use or driving.

title: Association between suicidal spectrum behaviors and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: ADHD was associated with higher odds of suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts and of death by suicide (odds ratio 6.69 for completed suicide).
key_finding: Meta-analysis of 57 studies: ADHD was associated with suicide attempts (OR 2.37), suicidal ideation (3.53), suicide plans (4.54) and completed suicide (6.69); results held when pooling adjusted ORs, though heterogeneity was high for most outcomes.

title: The lived experiences of adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A rapid review of qualitative evidence
plain_language: Adults with ADHD describe experiences that overlap with other conditions, which can lead to being misdiagnosed or diagnosed late.
key_finding: Rapid review of 35 qualitative studies on adults' lived experience of ADHD (adult diagnosis, symptoms, adaptive skills, substance use, self-perception, social interactions); many reported symptoms overlap with other psychiatric conditions and may contribute to misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis.

title: Peripheral blood inflammatory markers in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A systematic review and meta-analysis
journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
plain_language: Blood tests showed higher IL-6 and lower TNF-alpha in ADHD, but these results depended on single studies and need confirming in larger studies.
key_finding: IL-6 higher (g=0.71) and TNF-alpha lower (g=-0.16) in ADHD vs controls; no differences in CRP, IL-1β, IL-10 or interferon-γ; the overall effects were no longer significant after removing single studies.

title: Environmental risk factors, protective factors, and peripheral biomarkers for ADHD: an umbrella review
plain_language: A large review of reviews found that childhood eczema and asthma are among the most consistently reported factors linked to ADHD.
key_finding: Childhood eczema (OR 1.31) reached 'convincing' (class I) and childhood asthma (OR 1.51) 'highly suggestive' (class II) evidence of association with ADHD; of 23 peripheral biomarkers (median 175 cases), only serum vitamin D reached class II.

title: Association of atopic diseases and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and meta-analyses
plain_language: Children with asthma, eczema or hay fever are somewhat more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD later.
key_finding: Longitudinal studies: atopic disease precedes ADHD with pooled OR 1.34 for asthma, 1.32 for eczema and 1.52 for allergic rhinitis.

title: Allergic diseases in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Children with ADHD are more likely to have asthma and some other allergies, though the evidence is limited.
key_finding: Children with ADHD had higher odds of asthma (OR 1.80) and modestly higher odds of rhinitis, eczema and conjunctivitis; no association with food allergy (OR 1.13, NS); evidence quality low.

title: Association between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and asthma: a systematic review and meta-analysis and a Swedish population-based study
plain_language: Asthma and ADHD go together more often than chance, even after accounting for many other factors.
key_finding: Pooled adjusted OR 1.53 for ADHD-asthma; in Swedish registers the association held after simultaneous adjustment for all identified confounders (OR 1.45).

title: Associations Between Autoimmune Diseases and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Nationwide Study
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: People with an autoimmune disease, or whose mother has one, are a little more likely to have ADHD.
key_finding: Personal autoimmune disease raised ADHD risk (IRR 1.24) and maternal autoimmune disease raised offspring risk (IRR 1.12); paternal autoimmune disease did not.

title: Associations between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and autoimmune diseases are modified by sex: a population-based cross-sectional study
plain_language: ADHD was linked to some autoimmune conditions such as psoriasis, and some gut inflammatory diseases only in women.
key_finding: ADHD associated with psoriasis (adjOR 1.57 females, 1.31 males); in females only, with Crohn's (1.44) and ulcerative colitis (1.28), whereas males with ADHD had lower odds of Crohn's.

title: Association of Maternal Autoimmune Disease With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children
plain_language: Children whose mothers have an autoimmune disease are slightly more likely to have ADHD.
key_finding: Maternal autoimmune disease associated with offspring ADHD (cohort HR 1.30; meta-analysis HR 1.20); in the meta-analysis type 1 diabetes (HR 1.53), hyperthyroidism (1.15) and psoriasis (1.31) were also associated.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Offspring of Mothers With Inflammatory and Immune System Diseases
plain_language: Children of mothers with certain immune or inflammatory conditions were somewhat more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD.
key_finding: Maternal MS (OR 1.8), rheumatoid arthritis (1.7), type 1 diabetes (1.6), asthma (1.5) and hypothyroidism (1.2) linked to offspring ADHD; hypertension and type 2 diabetes were not.

title: Fever and infections in pregnancy and risk of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in the offspring
journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
plain_language: Having a fever or infection during pregnancy was not, overall, linked to ADHD in children.
key_finding: No overall association between fever or infection in pregnancy and offspring ADHD (aHR 1.03 and 1.01); only isolated timing-specific signals (fever weeks 9-12, aHR 1.33).

title: Maternal immune activation and neuroinflammation in human neurodevelopmental disorders
plain_language: This review describes how a mother's immune system during pregnancy might influence brain development, mostly based on early and animal research.
key_finding: Synthesises human evidence linking maternal obesity, asthma, autoimmunity, infection and stress during pregnancy with offspring NDDs incl. ADHD, plus animal mechanisms (placental signalling, microglial priming).

title: Neuroinflammation as a risk factor for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: Several lines of early evidence suggest inflammation might play a part in ADHD, but none is conclusive.
key_finding: Summarises five lines of evidence (immune comorbidity, serum cytokines, inflammatory gene variants, early-life exposures, MIA animal models) for neuroinflammation as an ADHD risk factor; most human strands are initial or preliminary.

title: In vivo imaging of dopamine D1 receptor and activated microglia in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a positron emission tomography study
plain_language: A small brain-scan study found signs of immune-cell activity in some brain areas of people with ADHD.
key_finding: PET showed increased activated-microglia signal ([11C]PK11195) in DLPFC and OFC and decreased D1 receptor in ACC in psychotropic-naive individuals with ADHD; microglial activation correlated with slower processing speed and poorer attention.

title: Histamine in the Nervous System
plain_language: The brain chemical histamine helps keep us awake and alert.
key_finding: Histaminergic neurons of the tuberomammillary nucleus are active only during waking and maintain wakefulness and attention via H1/H2/H3 receptors.

title: The effects of antihistamines on cognition and performance
journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
plain_language: Older 'drowsy' antihistamines can dull attention and memory, sometimes into the next day, while newer non-drowsy ones mostly do not.
key_finding: First-generation (brain-penetrant) H1 antihistamines impair divided attention, working memory, vigilance and speed, with next-day carryover; second-generation agents largely do not.

title: Effects of Fexofenadine, Diphenhydramine, and Alcohol on Driving Performance
plain_language: A common drowsy antihistamine affected simulated driving more than alcohol at about 0.1% blood alcohol, even when people did not feel sleepy.
key_finding: Diphenhydramine 50 mg impaired simulated driving more than alcohol at ~0.1% BAC; fexofenadine was indistinguishable from placebo; self-rated drowsiness did not predict impairment.

title: Increased attention‐deficit/hyperactivity symptoms in atopic dermatitis are associated with history of antihistamine use
plain_language: Children with eczema who had used antihistamines had more ADHD-like symptoms, which may be an effect of the medicine rather than the skin condition.
key_finding: In children with atopic dermatitis without ADHD, prior antihistamine use was associated with higher ADHD symptoms (OR 1.88); current eczema severity was not.

title: Definitions, Criteria and Global Classification of Mast Cell Disorders with Special Reference to Mast Cell Activation Syndromes: A Consensus Proposal
journal: International Archives of Allergy and Immunology
plain_language: Experts set out how to diagnose mast cell activation syndrome, which requires lab evidence and not just symptoms.
key_finding: Defines MCAS by typical symptoms, a substantial transient rise in tryptase or other mast-cell mediators, and response to mast-cell-directed therapy.

title: Mast cell activation and autism
journal: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Molecular Basis of Disease
plain_language: This is a theory that mast-cell activity may contribute to brain inflammation in some autistic children; it is not yet tested well.
