key_finding: Proposes perinatal non-allergic mast cell activation as a contributor to brain inflammation in a subgroup of autism, based largely on parent-reported 'allergic-like' symptoms.

title: Joint Hypermobility Links Neurodivergence to Dysautonomia and Pain
plain_language: Neurodivergent adults were more often very flexible in their joints, which was linked to dizziness on standing and pain.
key_finding: 51% of neurodivergent adults had generalised joint hypermobility vs 20% in the general population (OR 4.51, greater odds in females); the number of hypermobile joints mediated links to orthostatic intolerance and pain.

title: Association between adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and generalised joint hypermobility: A cross-sectional case control comparison
plain_language: Adults with ADHD were much more likely to have very flexible joints than adults without ADHD.
key_finding: Adult ADHD associated with generalised joint hypermobility on examination (adjOR 4.7) and symptomatic hypermobility (adjOR 6.9).

title: Nationwide population-based cohort study of psychiatric disorders in individuals with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome or hypermobility syndrome and their siblings
plain_language: People with Ehlers-Danlos or hypermobility syndromes, and their siblings, were more likely to have ADHD.
key_finding: EDS associated with ADHD (RR 5.6) and autism (RR 7.4); unaffected siblings also had elevated ADHD risk (RR 2.1); similar results for hypermobility syndrome.

title: Joint hypermobility and the heritable disorders of connective tissue: clinical and empirical evidence of links with psychiatry
plain_language: This review describes links between very flexible joints and anxiety, depression, ADHD, autism and eating disorders.
key_finding: Reviews evidence linking joint hypermobility/HDCT with anxiety, depression, neurodevelopmental conditions (autism, ADHD, DCD) and eating disorders.

title: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, joint hypermobility-related disorders and pain: expanding body-mind connections to the developmental age
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: This paper suggests that clumsiness, tiredness, pain and dizziness may connect ADHD and very flexible joints.
key_finding: Proposes coordination/proprioception problems, fatigue, chronic pain and dysautonomia as bridges between ADHD and joint hypermobility/hEDS.

title: A Prospective Evaluation of Undiagnosed Joint Hypermobility Syndrome in Patients With Gastrointestinal Symptoms
plain_language: A third of people referred to a gut clinic had unrecognised joint hypermobility, which came with more indigestion-type symptoms.
key_finding: 33% of new GI-clinic referrals had undiagnosed joint hypermobility syndrome, with more heartburn, water brash and postprandial fullness.

title: No association between joint hypermobility, musculoskeletal pain and neurodevelopmental problems in a school-based sample of 11-year-old children
plain_language: In ordinary 11-year-olds, very flexible joints were not linked to ADHD or autism traits.
key_finding: In a school sample, high Beighton scores were not associated with neurodevelopmental problems, unlike adult clinical cohorts.

title: The Association Between Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: People with ADHD have more gut symptoms like IBS and constipation; this review did not look at gut diseases such as IBD.
key_finding: ADHD associated with more total GI symptoms (OR 1.48), IBS (OR 1.58), constipation (OR 1.97) and encopresis (OR 4.32); studies of diagnosed organic GI disease (e.g., IBD) were excluded.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and gastrointestinal morbidity in a large cohort of young adults
plain_language: Young adults with ADHD had more IBS, constipation and indigestion than their peers.
key_finding: Young adults with ADHD had more IBS (OR 1.67), chronic constipation (OR 1.64) and dyspepsia (OR 1.48), but not IBD or coeliac disease, and more referrals to GI specialists (RR 1.96).

title: Association of Constipation and Fecal Incontinence With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: Children with ADHD were more likely to have constipation and soiling.
key_finding: Children with ADHD had more constipation (4.1% vs 1.5%) and fecal incontinence (0.9% vs 0.15%); stimulant treatment did not change visit rates.

title: Perturbations in Gut Microbiota Composition in Psychiatric Disorders
plain_language: Gut bacteria differences in several psychiatric conditions are mostly shared across conditions rather than specific to one; the shared pattern was reported for depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis and anxiety, not specifically ADHD.
key_finding: Microbiome differences across psychiatric disorders were largely transdiagnostic (fewer butyrate producers such as Faecalibacterium/Coprococcus) rather than disorder-specific.

title: The gut-microbiome in adult Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder - A Meta-analysis
plain_language: Gut bacteria in adults with ADHD differ somewhat, but results vary a lot between studies.
key_finding: Beta diversity associated with adult ADHD but with large between-cohort heterogeneity; a few genera (e.g., Ruminococcus torques group) were robustly associated.

title: Gut microbiota profiles of autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic literature review.
plain_language: Studies of gut bacteria in ADHD have not found a consistent pattern.
key_finding: ADHD microbiome findings were highly heterogeneous with no clear consistent differences.

title: Gut microbiome and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review
plain_language: Studies hint at some gut bacteria differences in ADHD, but overall findings were inconclusive.
key_finding: Across 11 studies, diversity and higher-level taxa findings were inconclusive; at genus level, Odoribacter and Eggerthella were increased (two studies each) and Faecalibacterium decreased (three studies) in ADHD, and one study linked Bacteroides to hyperactivity/impulsivity.

title: Gut microbiome in ADHD and its relation to neural reward anticipation
plain_language: A small study linked certain gut bacteria to how the brain responds to rewards in ADHD.
key_finding: Nominally increased Bifidobacterium in ADHD, with higher predicted dopamine-precursor (phenylalanine) synthesis function, which was associated with lower ventral-striatal reward-anticipation responses on fMRI (subset of 28, independent of diagnosis).

title: Endometriosis
plain_language: Endometriosis is common, affecting roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 20 women of reproductive age.
key_finding: Endometriosis affects ~5-10% of reproductive-age women (176 million); involves altered immunity and inflammation; reliable diagnosis requires surgical visualisation with histology, though endometrioma and deep nodular disease can be seen on ultrasound and MRI.

title: ESHRE guideline: endometriosis
plain_language: European specialists' guideline on how to diagnose and treat endometriosis, which no longer treats surgery as the only way to diagnose it.
key_finding: The ESHRE guideline gives 109 recommendations on diagnosis, pain and infertility treatment, recurrence, adolescents and postmenopausal women; it challenges laparoscopy/histology as the gold-standard diagnostic test, and notes that evidence was insufficient for firm recommendations on the most appropriate treatments.

title: Clinical diagnosis of endometriosis: a call to action
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: Experts argue endometriosis can often be diagnosed from symptoms and examination without waiting for surgery.
key_finding: Argues for clinical (non-surgical) diagnosis of endometriosis to reduce the 4-11 year delay from symptom onset.

title: Diagnostic delay for endometriosis in Austria and Germany: causes and possible consequences
plain_language: Women in Austria and Germany waited about 10 years for an endometriosis diagnosis, often after a misdiagnosis or after treating period pain as normal.
key_finding: Median 10.4 years from symptoms to diagnosis; 74% received at least one false diagnosis; misdiagnosis and normalisation of dysmenorrhoea prolonged delay.

title: Impact of endometriosis on quality of life and work productivity: a multicenter study across ten countries
plain_language: Women with endometriosis waited an average of almost 7 years for diagnosis and lost about 11 hours of work productivity a week.
key_finding: Women with endometriosis had a mean 6.7-year delay between symptom onset and surgical diagnosis, mainly in primary care (8.3 vs 5.5 years in mainly state-funded vs other settings), and lost on average 10.8 hours (SD 12.2) of work weekly, mainly through reduced effectiveness while working.

title: Can symptomatology help in the diagnosis of endometriosis? Findings from a national case–control study—Part 1
journal: BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
plain_language: Pelvic pain, painful or heavy periods and IBS diagnoses were more common in women with endometriosis than in other women.
key_finding: Compared with controls, women with endometriosis had more abdominopelvic pain (OR 5.2), dysmenorrhoea (8.1), menorrhagia (4.0) and IBS diagnoses (1.6); endometriosis may coexist with or be misdiagnosed as PID or IBS.

title: Endometriosis and its coexistence with irritable bowel syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease: findings from a national case–control study—Part 2
journal: BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
plain_language: Women with endometriosis were more likely to have been diagnosed with IBS, sometimes perhaps wrongly.
key_finding: Women with endometriosis were 3.5x more likely to have received an IBS diagnosis, and 2.5x more likely to get a new IBS diagnosis even after endometriosis was confirmed.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the associations between endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome
journal: European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology
plain_language: Women with endometriosis are about two to three times more likely to also meet the criteria for IBS, though whether this is true comorbidity is uncertain.
key_finding: Endometriosis associated with ~2-3x IBS risk (summary RR 2.39); authors question whether Rome criteria can separate IBS from endometriosis-related visceral hypersensitivity.

title: Endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Women with endometriosis are about three times more likely to have IBS.
key_finding: Prevalence of IBS in women with endometriosis OR 3.26; history of IBS OR 3.10, with low heterogeneity.

title: Endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome: similarities and differences in the spectrum of comorbidities
plain_language: Endometriosis and IBS often occur together but each has its own pattern of other health problems.
key_finding: 9.0% of women with IBS had endometriosis and 13.6% of women with endometriosis had IBS; each condition had a broad, partly distinct comorbidity profile.

title: Psychiatric comorbidity among women with endometriosis: nationwide cohort study in Sweden
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: Women with endometriosis had higher risks of depression, anxiety and ADHD, and the links ran in both directions.
key_finding: Endometriosis followed by raised risk of depression, anxiety, substance use and ADHD (sibling-adjusted HR up to 1.98 for ADHD); prior ADHD also predicted later endometriosis.

title: Epidemiologic and Genetic Associations of Endometriosis With Depression, Anxiety, and Eating Disorders
plain_language: Endometriosis was linked to depression, anxiety and eating disorders, partly through shared genes.
key_finding: Endometriosis associated with depression (OR 3.61), eating disorders (2.94), anxiety (2.61), supported by genetic correlations and MR evidence for depression/anxiety liability.

title: Chronic Pain And Health-Related Quality Of Life In Women With Autism And/Or ADHD: A Prospective Longitudinal Study
plain_language: Most women diagnosed with ADHD or autism as girls reported chronic pain as adults.
key_finding: 76.6% of women diagnosed with ADHD and/or autism in childhood reported chronic pain; those on stimulants had less chronic widespread pain.

title: Screening for Adult ADHD in Patients with Fibromyalgia Syndrome
plain_language: Almost half of people with fibromyalgia screened positive for possible adult ADHD.
key_finding: 44.72% of fibromyalgia patients screened positive for adult ADHD (ASRS v1.1), with higher fibromyalgia impact and more self-reported cognitive impairment.

title: Genetic Interplay Between Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Pain Suggests Neurodevelopmental Pathways and Comorbidity Risk
plain_language: Genetic studies suggest ADHD and chronic pain share some genetic roots.
key_finding: Strong genetic/biological overlap between ADHD and multisite chronic pain (weaker with migraine); causal-inference analyses showed stronger effects of pain liability on ADHD than the reverse; pain PRS related to ADHD severity and brain structure.

title: Iron Status in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
plain_language: Children with ADHD tend to have lower iron stores (ferritin), though their serum iron did not differ.
key_finding: Serum ferritin lower in children with ADHD (SMD -0.40), but serum iron not different (SMD -0.026).

title: Peripheral iron levels in children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Children with ADHD tend to have slightly lower iron stores, and low iron was linked to more severe symptoms.
key_finding: Ferritin modestly lower in ADHD (g=-0.246); iron deficiency associated with ADHD (OR 1.636) and with more severe symptoms.

title: Iron and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: what is the empirical evidence so far? A systematic review of the literature
plain_language: Studies on iron and ADHD are mixed, with only small treatment trials so far.
key_finding: Mixed ferritin findings; one MRI study of low thalamic iron; two small trials with partial benefit; iron deficiency may reduce stimulant response and links to RLS.

title: Iron Deficiency in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: In a small study, most children with ADHD had low iron stores compared with other children.
key_finding: Ferritin <30 ng/mL in 84% of children with ADHD vs 18% of controls; lower ferritin correlated with symptom severity (r=-0.34).

title: Effects of Iron Supplementation on Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder in Children
plain_language: In a very small trial, iron tablets improved ADHD symptoms in children with low iron stores.
key_finding: 12 weeks of ferrous sulfate 80 mg/day reduced ADHD-RS scores (-11.0) vs no change on placebo; parent/teacher Conners changes not significant.

title: Multimodal MR Imaging of Brain Iron in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Noninvasive Biomarker That Responds to Psychostimulant Treatment?
plain_language: A small brain-scan study found lower brain iron in unmedicated young people with ADHD.
key_finding: Medication-naive ADHD had lower striatal and thalamic brain iron on magnetic field correlation (MFC) MRI than controls and medicated patients; other MRI relaxation measures and serum iron did not differ.

title: Effect of iron supplementation on fatigue in nonanemic menstruating women with low ferritin: a randomized controlled trial
plain_language: Women with low iron stores but no anaemia felt less tired after taking iron tablets for 12 weeks.
key_finding: 12 weeks of oral iron reduced fatigue by 47.7% vs 28.8% on placebo (difference -18.9%); no effect on mood or quality of life.

title: Iron supplementation for unexplained fatigue in non-anaemic women: double blind randomised placebo controlled trial
plain_language: Iron reduced unexplained tiredness in women, but only in those with low iron stores.
key_finding: Iron reduced fatigue by 29% vs 13% on placebo over 4 weeks; benefit confined to women with ferritin <=50 ug/L.

title: Efficacy of iron supplementation on fatigue and physical capacity in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials
plain_language: In iron-deficient adults without anaemia, iron supplements eased tiredness a little but did not improve physical fitness.
key_finding: In iron-deficient non-anaemic adults, iron reduced self-reported fatigue (SMD -0.38) but did not improve objective physical capacity.

title: Iron deficiency
plain_language: Low iron can affect how you feel and function even before it causes anaemia.
key_finding: Lancet seminar: iron deficiency can cause clinical and functional impairment even without anaemia; hepcidin upregulation limits absorption of high-dose oral iron; modern IV iron enables rapid, safe total-dose replacement.

title: Iron Deficiency in Adults
plain_language: Low iron can cause tiredness and poor concentration and is diagnosed with a blood test for iron stores.
key_finding: Iron deficiency may cause fatigue, exercise intolerance and difficulty concentrating; diagnosis requires ferritin and/or transferrin saturation; oral iron first line, IV for blood loss or malabsorption.

title: Prevalence of Iron Deficiency and Iron-Deficiency Anemia in US Females Aged 12-21 Years, 2003-2020
plain_language: About 4 in 10 US teenage girls and young women had low iron stores, and about 6 in 100 had iron-deficiency anaemia.
key_finding: Using ferritin <25 ug/L, 38.6% (95% CI 35.8-40.9) of US females aged 12-21 had iron deficiency (17% at <15 ug/L) and 6.3% (5.2-7.4) had iron-deficiency anaemia.

title: The relationship between heavy menstrual bleeding, iron deficiency, and iron deficiency anemia
journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
plain_language: Heavy periods are a common, under-recognised cause of low iron and anaemia.
key_finding: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a major, under-recognised cause of iron deficiency and anaemia, with effects on cognition, work and school.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and restless leg syndrome across the lifespan: A systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Restless legs symptoms are common in people with ADHD, affecting roughly a fifth to a third of adults.
key_finding: RLS symptoms present in 20-33.0% of adults with ADHD (11-42.9% of children); sleep fragmentation and dopaminergic dysfunction proposed as shared pathways.

title: Restless legs syndrome and iron deficiency in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: About a third of adults with ADHD had restless legs syndrome, often alongside low iron stores.
key_finding: RLS in 33.0% of adults with ADHD; iron deficiency (ferritin <50 ng/mL) in 35.5%, more frequent in those with RLS, who also had earlier, more severe ADHD.

title: Restless Legs Syndrome and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: a Review of the Literature
plain_language: An early review suggesting restless legs and ADHD often occur together and may share causes such as dopamine dysfunction.
key_finding: Early review: up to 44% of clinical ADHD samples had RLS or RLS symptoms and up to 26% of RLS samples had ADHD symptoms; proposed mechanisms include sleep disruption, RLS mimicking ADHD, and shared dopamine dysfunction.

title: Evidence-based and consensus clinical practice guidelines for the iron treatment of restless legs syndrome/Willis-Ekbom disease in adults and children: an IRLSSG task force report
plain_language: Guidelines say iron treatment, especially through a drip, can help restless legs when iron stores are low.
key_finding: IV ferric carboxymaltose effective for moderate-severe RLS in adults with ferritin <300 ug/L; oral iron possibly effective with ferritin <=75 ug/L; insufficient evidence in children.

title: Delayed Circadian Rhythm in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Chronic Sleep-Onset Insomnia
plain_language: Adults with ADHD who had trouble falling asleep had a later-running body clock.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD and sleep-onset insomnia (31 of 40) had delayed dim-light melatonin onset and sleep timing vs controls and ADHD without insomnia.

title: Adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with alterations in circadian rhythms at the behavioural, endocrine and molecular levels
plain_language: A study found the body clock of adults with ADHD ran differently at several levels.
key_finding: Adult ADHD showed loss of rhythmic BMAL1/PER2 clock-gene expression, phase-delayed cortisol and altered activity rhythms.

title: A systematic review of circadian function, chronotype and chronotherapy in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: People with ADHD tend to be 'night owls' with a later body clock.
key_finding: Consistent evidence for later chronotype and delayed DLMO/sleep onset in ADHD; melatonin may help sleep; few other chronotherapy studies.

title: The role of the circadian system in the etiology and pathophysiology of ADHD: time to redefine ADHD?
journal: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders
plain_language: Some ADHD symptoms may partly come from a delayed body clock and lack of sleep.
key_finding: Proposes that in a substantial subgroup some ADHD symptoms result from chronic delayed circadian rhythm and sleep loss, warranting sleep treatment alongside ADHD treatment.

title: The circadian rhythm in adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: current state of affairs
plain_language: Adults with ADHD are often night owls, and melatonin and morning light may help shift sleep earlier.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD are often 'evening types' with delayed rhythms; treatments are sleep hygiene, afternoon or evening melatonin and morning bright light.

title: Sleep in adults with ADHD: Systematic review and meta-analysis of subjective and objective studies
plain_language: Adults with ADHD report worse sleep, though lab sleep studies do not always show differences.
key_finding: Adults with ADHD reported worse sleep on 7 of 9 subjective measures (SMD 0.56-1.55); actigraphy showed longer sleep latency (SMD 0.80) and lower efficiency, but polysomnography showed no differences.

title: Sleep in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Meta-Analysis of Subjective and Objective Studies
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Children with ADHD have more trouble going to bed, falling asleep and staying awake in the day.
key_finding: Children with ADHD had more bedtime resistance, sleep-onset difficulty, night waking and daytime sleepiness, and objectively longer sleep latency.

title: Assessment and Management of Sleep Problems in Youths With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: For children with ADHD, good sleep habits and behavioural approaches come first, with melatonin as an option for falling asleep.
key_finding: Healthy sleep practices first; behavioural interventions first-line for insomnia; RCTs support melatonin for sleep-onset delay.

title: Sleep and Circadian Rhythmicity in Adult ADHD and the Effect of Stimulants
plain_language: Adults with ADHD often fall asleep late; stimulants can push the body clock later while light therapy can help bring it earlier.
key_finding: Adult ADHD shows longer sleep latency, eveningness and delayed DLMO resembling delayed sleep phase disorder; stimulants may delay rhythms while light therapy advances them.

title: Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Insomnia: an Update of the Literature
plain_language: Insomnia is very common in adults with ADHD, and some ADHD medicines can make it worse.
key_finding: Insomnia affects 43-80% of adults with ADHD; treatment-emergent insomnia reported in 10-45% on various stimulants and some on atomoxetine.

title: ADHD, circadian rhythms and seasonality
plain_language: Adults with more ADHD symptoms were more likely to have winter depression, partly explained by going to sleep late.
key_finding: Probable seasonal affective disorder in 9.9% with ADHD symptoms vs 3.3% without; late sleep onset mediated the association.

title: Effect of Melatonin on Sleep, Behavior, and Cognition in ADHD and Chronic Sleep-Onset Insomnia
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
plain_language: Melatonin helped children with ADHD fall asleep earlier but did not change behaviour or thinking.
key_finding: Melatonin advanced sleep onset by 26.9 min and DLMO by 44.4 min and increased total sleep time, but did not improve behaviour, cognition or quality of life.

title: Melatonin for the management of sleep problems in children with neurodevelopmental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
plain_language: Melatonin helped children with neurodevelopmental conditions sleep longer and fall asleep faster.
key_finding: In children with neurodevelopmental disorders melatonin increased total sleep by 48.26 min and reduced sleep-onset latency by 28.97 min, with no medication-related serious adverse events; evidence quality limited by heterogeneity.

title: Effects of chronotherapy on circadian rhythm and ADHD symptoms in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and delayed sleep phase syndrome: a randomized clinical trial
plain_language: Low-dose melatonin shifted the body clock earlier and slightly eased ADHD symptoms in adults, but the effect wore off after stopping.
key_finding: Low-dose melatonin 0.5 mg advanced DLMO by 1 h 28 min and reduced self-reported ADHD symptoms by 14%; melatonin plus bright light did not reduce symptoms; effects disappeared 2 weeks after stopping.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Delayed Sleep Phase Syndrome in Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial on the Effects of Chronotherapy on Sleep
plain_language: Melatonin and light shifted the body clock but did not, on their own, make adults with ADHD go to sleep earlier.
key_finding: Despite advancing DLMO, melatonin with or without bright light did not advance actual sleep times or improve sleep; the authors conclude behavioural coaching is needed.

title: Correcting delayed circadian phase with bright light therapy predicts improvement in ADHD symptoms: A pilot study
plain_language: In an uncontrolled study, morning bright light shifted the body clock earlier and this went with fewer ADHD symptoms.
key_finding: Morning bright light advanced DLMO by 31 min and mid-sleep by 57 min; phase advance correlated with reduced ADHD symptoms.

title: An Open Trial of Light Therapy in Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
plain_language: In a small open study, morning light therapy reduced ADHD symptoms in adults in autumn and winter.
key_finding: In fall/winter, morning light reduced subjective and objective ADHD measures; improvement tracked a shift toward morning preference rather than mood.

title: Stimulant Medications and Sleep for Youth With ADHD: A Meta-analysis
plain_language: Stimulant medicines can make it harder for children to fall asleep and shorten sleep, though the effect on sleep quality was smaller in children who had taken them longer.
key_finding: Stimulants lengthened sleep latency (ES 0.54), reduced sleep efficiency (ES -0.32) and shortened total sleep (ES -0.59); the sleep-efficiency effect was smaller in youth on medication longer.

title: Understanding the Impact of Stimulants on Sleep in ADHD: Evidence from Systematic Assessment of Sleep in Adults
plain_language: In adults, the effect of stimulant medicines on sleep is mixed and sometimes sleep improves.
key_finding: In adults, systematic sleep measurement during stimulant treatment shows mixed effects, with some studies finding improved sleep quality or architecture.

title: The sleep–circadian connection: pathways to understanding and supporting autistic children and adolescents and those with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
plain_language: A review of how sleep and the body clock affect autistic and ADHD young people, and what treatments may help.
key_finding: Lancet Child Adolesc Health review of sleep-circadian mechanisms in autism and ADHD and pharmacological/non-pharmacological interventions, including light therapy evidence in adults.

title: Endometriosis is a chronic systemic disease: clinical challenges and novel innovations
plain_language: A review describing endometriosis as a whole-body inflammatory condition, not only a pelvic one, that is often diagnosed late.
key_finding: Endometriosis affects 5-10% of reproductive-age women, diagnosis is typically delayed by years and misdiagnosis is common; the review argues it is a systemic disease (systemic inflammation, altered liver and fat metabolism, brain changes causing pain sensitisation and mood disorders), and notes progestins and low-dose oral contraceptives fail in a third of symptomatic women, with oral GnRH antagonists as an alternative.

title: Iron deficiency anaemia
plain_language: A review of iron-deficiency anaemia: who gets it, how it is tested for and how it is treated.
key_finding: Lancet Seminar: anaemia affects roughly a third of the world's population, half due to iron deficiency, with women of childbearing age at particular risk; serum ferritin, transferrin saturation and soluble transferrin receptor measures diagnose iron deficiency anaemia more accurately than red-cell indices; oral iron is usually first line, and recent IV formulations seem to replenish stores safely and effectively.
